title: Sustained alpha-dominated magnetic-confinement operation
subfield: Energy gain, ignition, and burning plasmas
open: Can a magnetically confined plasma sustain itself once the fusion alpha particles become the dominant heat source, with density, impurity content, pressure, and current profile all held under control? In other words, can reactor-like burning-plasma operation be maintained stably for the durations a power plant requires?
status: Decades of externally heated experiments support extrapolation, but the cited gain surveys (Wurzel and Hsu 2022, DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990; arXiv:2105.10954) distinguish these results from sustained reactor-like burning operation.
solved_when: A magnetically confined plasma is demonstrated in which alpha-particle heating supplies most of the plasma heating, while density, impurity levels, pressure, and current are actively controlled — sustained rather than transiently achieved.
why: With external heating, instabilities and power-balance problems can stay hidden; when the plasma heats itself, those feedbacks surface, and a solution is what separates today's experiments from a genuine power-producing reactor.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2022), *Progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criterion*, DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990; arXiv:2105.10954.

title: Alpha-particle redistribution under overlapping modes
subfield: Energy gain, ignition, and burning plasmas
open: Can we predict how alpha particles are redistributed, and how many are lost to the wall, when several energetic-particle modes are simultaneously excited in a burning plasma? A complete theory must capture nonlinear saturation of the overlapping modes together with the evolving background profiles.
status: Single-mode theory is well developed and backed by extensive experiments, but the extrapolation to burning plasmas with multiple overlapping modes remains a central uncertainty; see Chen and Zonca (2016), *Physics of Alfvén waves and energetic particles in burning plasmas*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.88.015008. Related mathematical foundations lie in Hamiltonian resonance overlap and transport in near-integrable dynamical systems.
solved_when: A predictive theory (validated against simulation or experiment) exists that yields alpha-particle redistribution and wall-loss estimates for the case of multiple overlapping energetic-particle modes, including nonlinear saturation effects and evolving background profiles.
why: Alpha losses cut both ways at once: they reduce the self-heating that sustains the burn while concentrating damaging power loads on the first wall, so an unquantified extrapolation to burning plasmas directly threatens reactor viability.
key_works: Chen and Zonca (2016), *Physics of Alfvén waves and energetic particles in burning plasmas*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.88.015008.

title: Reactor-geometry Dimits-shift prediction
open: Can we predict how far above the linear instability threshold the turbulence onset actually sits — the Dimits shift — in realistic reactor plasmas? That is, develop a quantitatively reliable theory of the nonlinear turbulence threshold in electromagnetic, multispecies, shaped-geometry configurations.
status: Reduced-model explanations and three-dimensional studies exist, notably Ivanov et al. (2020), *Zonally dominated dynamics and Dimits threshold in curvature-driven ITG turbulence* (DOI: 10.1017/S0022377820000938; arXiv:2004.04047), but a quantitatively reliable reactor-geometry theory remains incomplete.
solved_when: A theory predicts the nonlinear threshold (and hence the Dimits shift) for realistic electromagnetic, multispecies, shaped plasmas, with quantitative agreement against nonlinear simulations or experiment in reactor geometry.
why: The gap between linear and nonlinear thresholds strongly affects predicted confinement, so reliable threshold prediction directly constrains reactor performance estimates.
key_works: Ivanov et al. (2020), *Zonally dominated dynamics and Dimits threshold in curvature-driven ITG turbulence*, DOI: 10.1017/S0022377820000938; arXiv:2004.04047.

title: Predictive ion–electron turbulence coupling
open: When does electron-scale turbulence materially alter ion-scale transport, and when do ion-scale fluctuations feed back on electron-scale heat loss? A predictive characterization is sought across reactor-relevant gradients, magnetic geometry, and beta.
status: Multiscale simulations demonstrated enhanced transport from cross-scale coupling by 2014–2016, notably Howard et al. (2016), *Multi-scale gyrokinetic simulations: Comparison with experiment and implications for predicting turbulence and transport*, *Physics of Plasmas* 23, 056109; economical predictive coverage remains limited.
solved_when: A predictive criterion (or model) exists that quantifies cross-scale coupling between ion- and electron-scale turbulence and is validated over reactor-relevant gradient regimes, magnetic geometries, and beta values.
why: Simulating either scale in isolation can give the wrong heat loss, so single-scale transport predictions may be unreliable precisely where reactor design needs them.
key_works: Howard et al. (2016), *Multi-scale gyrokinetic simulations: Comparison with experiment and implications for predicting turbulence and transport*, *Physics of Plasmas* 23, 056109.

title: Hydrogen-isotope confinement effect
open: Why does energy confinement depend on which hydrogen isotope fuels the plasma, and can we predict how confinement shifts across hydrogen, deuterium, tritium, and their mixtures once heating, profiles, wall conditions, and operating regime are held fixed?
status: The effect has decades of experimental history; the 2023 review by Ida (*Isotope effect of transport and key physics in the isotope mixture plasmas*, DOI: 10.1007/s41614-023-00126-3) documents multiple candidate mechanisms and highlights the physics of isotope mixtures as unresolved.
solved_when: A validated theory exists that quantitatively predicts confinement (transport levels) for hydrogen, deuterium, tritium, and arbitrary isotope mixtures under controlled, otherwise-identical conditions, including the previously unresolved mixture physics.
why: Present-day devices run mostly on deuterium; extrapolating to deuterium–tritium operation — as needed for burning plasmas and reactor design — is unreliable without such a theory.
key_works: Ida (2023), *Isotope effect of transport and key physics in the isotope mixture plasmas*, DOI: 10.1007/s41614-023-00126-3.

title: Fuel-density peaking without impurity accumulation
open: Can a tokamak operating regime be found in which central fuel density peaks while high-charge impurities are kept from accumulating in the core? More formally, identify controllable regimes in which fuel-density peaking is achieved without unacceptable inward transport of high-charge impurities.
status: Neoclassical and turbulent impurity models exist individually, but their combined reactor operating window is not established. Key work includes Donnel et al. (2018), *Self-consistent gyrokinetic modeling of neoclassical and turbulent impurity transport*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/aa6ebb.
solved_when: A controllable regime is identified and demonstrated in which central fuel density increases without producing unacceptable inward impurity transport, and the combined neoclassical–turbulent reactor operating window for this coexistence is established.
why: Density peaking raises fusion power, while impurity peaking radiates away core power and can terminate the discharge outright.
key_works: Donnel et al. (2018), *Self-consistent gyrokinetic modeling of neoclassical and turbulent impurity transport*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/aa6ebb.

title: Neoclassical-tearing-mode seed threshold
subfield: Magnetohydrodynamic stability, disruptions, and runaway electrons
open: Can we predict, from first principles, the minimum magnetic perturbation that seeds a damaging neoclassical tearing mode in a reactor with evolving pressure and current profiles? More precisely, what is the critical seed-island width (or perturbation amplitude) for NTM onset as a function of the evolving profiles?
status: The 2006 review by La Haye (*Neoclassical tearing modes and their control*, DOI: 10.1063/1.2180747) established the major framework, but seed formation and its extrapolation to reactors remain distinct, unsolved problems beyond linear stability theory.
solved_when: A validated predictive criterion or theory gives the minimum seed perturbation for neoclassical tearing mode onset under realistic evolving reactor pressure and current profiles, with demonstrated extrapolation from present experiments to reactor conditions.
why: Avoiding the formation of a seed island may require far less control power than suppressing a mature island, so a predictive threshold would directly set cheaper disruption-avoidance strategies in reactors.
key_works: La Haye (2006), *Neoclassical tearing modes and their control*, DOI: 10.1063/1.2180747.

title: Out-of-distribution disruption prediction
subfield: Magnetohydrodynamic stability, disruptions, and runaway electrons
open: Can a disruption predictor trained on existing machines reliably forecast disruptions on a new device or an unfamiliar operating regime, with honestly calibrated warning times and error rates? Formally, this asks for out-of-distribution generalization with quantified missed-event rates and false-alarm costs.
status: Deep learning demonstrated cross-device progress in 2019 (Kates-Harbeck, Svyatkovskiy, and Tang, *Predicting disruptive instabilities in controlled fusion plasmas through deep learning*, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-019-1116-4), but reliable extrapolation to reactor conditions remains unresolved.
solved_when: A predictor demonstrates reliable disruption prediction on new machines and unfamiliar operating regimes, delivering calibrated warning times, missed-event rates, and false-alarm costs under distribution shift.
why: A predictor that fails on the first unfamiliar dangerous event is not a protection system; reactor safety depends on extrapolating beyond the training data.
key_works: Kates-Harbeck, Svyatkovskiy, and Tang (2019), *Predicting disruptive instabilities in controlled fusion plasmas through deep learning*, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-019-1116-4.

title: Shattered-pellet assimilation
subfield: Magnetohydrodynamic stability, disruptions, and runaway electrons
open: Can we predict — and ultimately control — how the fragments of a shattered pellet ablate, penetrate, mix, and radiate as they are assimilated into a disrupting plasma, including cases where the deposition is strongly asymmetric?
status: Shattered-pellet injection is a developed disruption-mitigation approach, but assimilation at reactor scale remains an active validation need (Lehnen et al. (2015), *Disruptions in ITER and strategies for their control and mitigation*, DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2014.10.075).
solved_when: A validated predictive capability exists for fragment ablation, penetration, mixing, and radiation during shattered-pellet injection in reactor-scale disruptions, verified against experimental data and demonstrated to account for asymmetric deposition.
why: Injecting mitigation material is useful only if it actually reaches and cools the plasma as intended; without reliable assimilation models, shattered-pellet mitigation cannot be confidently extrapolated to reactor scale.
key_works: Lehnen et al. (2015), *Disruptions in ITER and strategies for their control and mitigation*, DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2014.10.075.

title: Runaway seed prediction during thermal quench
subfield: Magnetohydrodynamic stability, disruptions, and runaway electrons
open: Can we predict the size of the runaway-electron seed produced during the rapid cooling of a thermal quench, when hot-tail, Dreicer, radioactive, and externally driven sources all act at once? The goal is a quantitative prediction of the combined seed from these mechanisms under realistic fast-cooling conditions.
status: The 2019 runaway review by Breizman et al. (*Physics of runaway electrons in tokamaks*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/ab1822) synthesizes these generation mechanisms; their combined prediction for reactor conditions remains uncertain.
solved_when: A validated predictive framework yields the total runaway seed from hot-tail, Dreicer, radioactive, and externally driven sources during realistic rapid cooling, at reactor-relevant conditions.
why: Even a small seed can amplify into a destructive relativistic-electron population that threatens machine integrity.
key_works: Breizman et al. (2019), *Physics of runaway electrons in tokamaks*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/ab1822.

title: Runaway-free startup
subfield: Magnetohydrodynamic stability, disruptions, and runaway electrons
open: Can a tokamak be brought up from startup through waveforms and fueling choices that never produce runaway electrons, even when the prefill pressure, impurity content, and wall conditions are uncertain? Formally, the goal is a startup design that is robust to this realistic operational variability rather than tuned to a nominal scenario.
status: Startup runaway generation was modeled explicitly by Hoppe et al. (2022), *Runaway electron generation during tokamak start-up* (DOI: 10.1017/S002237782200054X; arXiv:2203.09900), but avoiding it across realistic operational variability remains open.
solved_when: Startup waveforms and fueling strategies are established that avoid runaway formation across the stated uncertainty in prefill, impurities, and wall conditions — not merely for a nominal case.
why: Dangerous runaway electron populations can form before normal confinement is even established, so the earliest phase of operation can seed the very hazard the rest of the discharge must manage.
key_works: Hoppe et al. (2022), *Runaway electron generation during tokamak start-up*, DOI: 10.1017/S002237782200054X; arXiv:2203.09900.

title: Advanced-divertor reactor scaling
open: Do advanced divertor geometries such as Super-X, snowflake, and X-point-target still deliver their exhaust advantages once a reactor imposes real constraints on coil placement, shielding, pumping, and control? In other words, can their heat-spreading benefit survive full power-plant integration?
status: Advanced divertor geometries have experimental and modeling support, but full integration into a power plant remains unresolved; see Leonard (2018), *Plasma detachment in divertor tokamaks*, and NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991. Constrained topology optimization is a related direction.
solved_when: A demonstrated plant-level design (or equivalent integrated analysis) shows that an advanced divertor geometry retains its exhaust performance under reactor-grade constraints on coils, shielding, pumping, and control.
why: Spreading the heat load geometrically could relax the most severe material requirements facing a fusion power plant, easing a central bottleneck on the path to practical fusion energy.
key_works: Leonard (2018), *Plasma detachment in divertor tokamaks*; NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991.

title: Exact force-free toroidal equilibria with nested surfaces
open: Do exact analytic force-free magnetic fields in a torus — with no axisymmetry assumed — exist that also have the desired nested magnetic surfaces? A sharper version: construct or rule out nonaxisymmetric toroidal solutions of the force-free (Beltrami) equations whose field lines lie on nested invariant surfaces.
status: Explicitly flagged as unresolved in the September 2026 analytic-equilibrium paper of Landreman (2026), *Analytic toroidal 3D MHD equilibria and steady Euler flows with invariant surfaces*, arXiv:2609.26742; the question is distinct from the finite-pressure families newly constructed there.
solved_when: An exact analytic nonaxisymmetric force-free toroidal equilibrium with nested surfaces is constructed, or such a configuration is proven impossible.
why: It would bridge stellarator geometry and current-carrying low-pressure equilibria, connecting magnetic-surface design to the topology of steady Euler flows.
key_works: Landreman (2026), *Analytic toroidal 3D MHD equilibria and steady Euler flows with invariant surfaces*, arXiv:2609.26742.

title: Piecewise-omnigenous collisional transport
open: How much collisional and finite-orbit-width transport is generated when particles cross the boundaries between approximately omnigenous regions of a stellarator's magnetic field? A quantitative determination of this transition-layer transport would sharpen the question formally.
status: Generalized omnigenity and newer optimization methods enlarge the design space; realistic transport across the boundaries of omnigenous regions still needs validation.
solved_when: The transport coefficients at transitions between approximately omnigenous regions are determined, yielding a validated prediction of collisional and finite-orbit-width transport for piecewise-omnigenous field configurations.
why: A field configuration with good collisionless orbits can still suffer unacceptable thermal transport, so without this analysis omnigenity-based optimization may certify the wrong designs.
key_works: *Magnetic Fields with General Omnigenity* (2024 version), arXiv:2305.08026; *Optimizing omnigenity like quasisymmetry for stellarators* (2025), arXiv:2502.09350.

title: Solenoid-free spherical-tokamak startup
subfield: Spherical tokamaks, reversed-field pinches, spheromaks, and mirrors
open: Can a spherical tokamak be started up — reaching a reactor-relevant plasma current and a closed-flux configuration — without relying on a conventional central solenoid?
status: Alternative startup methods exist, but the complete reactor trajectory remains a development problem. (Menard et al. (2016), *Fusion nuclear science facilities and pilot plants based on the spherical tokamak*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/56/10/106023.)
solved_when: A demonstrated startup route establishes reactor-relevant plasma current and closed magnetic flux surfaces in a spherical tokamak using no central solenoid, and the full trajectory from startup to reactor conditions is developed rather than merely illustrated in parts.
why: The narrow center column of a spherical tokamak leaves little room for a solenoid and its shielding, so conventional inductive startup hardware cannot simply be scaled down; solenoid-free startup is a prerequisite for the configuration's reactor viability.
key_works: Menard et al. (2016), *Fusion nuclear science facilities and pilot plants based on the spherical tokamak*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/56/10/106023.

title: Simultaneous mirror microstability and MHD stability
subfield: Spherical tokamaks, reversed-field pinches, spheromaks, and mirrors
open: Can a mirror plasma be configured so that kinetic loss-cone–type microinstabilities and macroscopic MHD interchange modes are simultaneously stable? Formally, find mirror-confined particle distributions that suppress loss-cone and other kinetic instabilities while also meeting interchange stability criteria.
status: Stabilization mechanisms for the individual instability classes are known, but a reactor-quality combined stability window remains unresolved. Key works: Ivanov and Prikhodko (2013), *Gas-dynamic trap: an overview of the concept and experimental results*.
solved_when: A demonstration — analytic or computational — of a mirror distribution achieving reactor-quality simultaneous suppression of loss-cone/kinetic instabilities and interchange stability, without unacceptable degradation of end losses.
why: Stabilizing one instability class can worsen another or increase end losses, so a reactor-relevant mirror concept requires a combined stability window; without it, no self-consistent operating point exists.
key_works: Ivanov and Prikhodko (2013), *Gas-dynamic trap: an overview of the concept and experimental results*.

title: Positive FRC beam-sustainment balance
subfield: Field-reversed configurations, Z pinches, cusps, and dipoles
open: Can neutral-beam-maintained field-reversed configurations (FRCs) produce more fusion power than the total power needed to sustain them? Formally, the question is whether the beam-sustained configuration achieves a positive net power balance, with fusion output exceeding the full sustainment power draw.
status: Beam-generated FRCs were reported in 2025 (Roche et al., *Generation of field-reversed configurations via neutral beam injection*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-58849-5), so formation itself is no longer the open problem; the power balance remains undemonstrated.
solved_when: An experiment demonstrates a neutral-beam-maintained FRC whose fusion output exceeds the complete power required to sustain the configuration.
why: Strong beam support can improve confinement while masking an unfavorable power balance, so demonstrating net-positive operation is what determines whether this route is viable as a power source rather than a laboratory curiosity.
key_works: Roche et al. (2025), *Generation of field-reversed configurations via neutral beam injection*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-58849-5.

title: Kinetic stabilization of reactor-scale FRCs
subfield: Field-reversed configurations, Z pinches, cusps, and dipoles
open: Does the favorable finite-orbit and energetic-ion stabilization seen in present field-reversed configurations survive the extrapolation to reactor scale — or does it fade as the device size, collisionality, and fusion-product ion populations change? Formally, one wants a predictive account of how these kinetic stabilization mechanisms scale across the relevant parameter space.
status: High-performance beam-supported FRC states have been achieved experimentally, but stability at reactor scale remains an extrapolation rather than a demonstrated or predicted result. Key references include Steinhauer (2011), *Review of field-reversed configurations*, and Roche et al. (2025), DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-58849-5.
solved_when: A theory (or validated model) predicts the stability of FRC equilibria as a function of size, collisionality, and fusion-product populations, correctly indicating whether kinetic stabilization persists or degrades at reactor scale.
why: Stabilization demonstrated in one kinetic regime may simply not survive the scaling to a reactor, so extrapolating current results without such a theory could anchor reactor designs on an unstable configuration.
key_works: Steinhauer (2011), *Review of field-reversed configurations*; Roche et al. (2025), DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-58849-5.

title: Sheared-flow Z-pinch scaling to gain
subfield: Field-reversed configurations, Z pinches, cusps, and dipoles
open: Can shear-flow stabilization of a Z-pinch be maintained under the density, temperature, current, and duration a burning plasma requires, rather than only in present-day experimental conditions?
status: Sustained neutron production and measurements establishing thermonuclear origin have been achieved, but these results do not establish reactor gain. Key works include Shumlak (2020), *Z-pinch fusion*, *Journal of Applied Physics* 127, 200901; and Mitrani et al. (2021), DOI: 10.1063/5.0066257.
solved_when: A sheared-flow Z-pinch demonstrates stable confinement at the density, temperature, current, and duration needed for fusion gain — not merely sustained neutron production.
why: It would validate a potentially simple, magnet-light confinement architecture, offering a lower-complexity path to fusion than conventional magnetic confinement systems.
key_works: Shumlak (2020), *Z-pinch fusion*, *Journal of Applied Physics* 127, 200901; Mitrani et al. (2021), DOI: 10.1063/5.0066257.

title: Plasma-jet liner assembly
subfield: Magnetized inertial fusion and pulsed power
open: Can a large number of supersonic plasma jets be merged into a single imploding liner that stays uniform enough to compress a fusion target? Formally, this asks for a merged liner with acceptably low mass, momentum, and timing variation across its surface, and sufficiently low entropy that it can deliver high-gain compression.
status: Plasma-liner concepts have an established research history, but high-gain target compression with such liners remains unresolved.
solved_when: An experimentally assembled plasma liner is demonstrated with adequate uniformity and sufficiently low entropy — quantified by acceptably small mass, momentum, and timing variation among the contributing jets — such that it can plausibly compress a target toward high gain.
why: Success would enable a standoff driver that keeps all hardware far from the fusion chamber, protecting it from target-generated damage — a key advantage over contact drivers.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2022), *Progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criterion*, DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990.

title: Direct-drive ignition
open: Can a directly laser-driven inertial-confinement target actually ignite and produce useful gain, rather than merely reproducing the conditions of ignition through hydrodynamically scaled equivalence?
status: A hydrodynamically equivalent burning-plasma demonstration was published in 2024 (Gopalaswamy et al., *Demonstration of a hydrodynamically equivalent burning plasma in direct-drive inertial confinement fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/s41567-023-02361-4); that result, while a milestone, is not direct-drive ignition itself.
solved_when: A direct-drive experiment achieves ignition with useful target gain — that is, a self-sustaining burn yielding more fusion energy than delivered to the target, not a hydrodynamically equivalent surrogate.
why: Success would establish direct drive as a real ignition pathway with distinct efficiency and target-manufacturing tradeoffs, opening design space beyond indirect drive.
key_works: Gopalaswamy et al. (2024), *Demonstration of a hydrodynamically equivalent burning plasma in direct-drive inertial confinement fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/s41567-023-02361-4.

title: Predictive cross-beam energy transfer
open: Can cross-beam energy transfer be predicted and controlled in evolving, multidimensional target plasmas over the full pulse? A complete theory would forecast the energy redistribution among crossing laser beams as the target plasma evolves in space and time, and would enable its active control across target designs.
status: Wavelength detuning was demonstrated as a mitigation technique in 2018 (Marozas et al., *First observation of cross-beam energy transfer mitigation for direct-drive inertial confinement fusion implosions using wavelength detuning at the national ignition facility*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.120.085001); complete predictive control across target designs remains open.
solved_when: A predictive, validated capability exists for cross-beam energy transfer in evolving, multidimensional target plasmas over the full pulse, with control demonstrated across target designs.
why: Energy redistributed among beams changes implosion symmetry and reduces useful coupling to the target, so prediction and control directly determine fusion-driver performance.
key_works: Marozas et al. (2018), *First observation of cross-beam energy transfer mitigation for direct-drive inertial confinement fusion implosions using wavelength detuning at the national ignition facility*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.120.085001.

title: Repeatedly demountable HTS joints
open: Can high-temperature superconducting magnet joints be disconnected and reconnected many times while still meeting the electrical, mechanical, and vacuum demands of a reactor magnet system? The goal is a joint design that preserves performance across repeated demount-reconnect cycles.
status: Demountable magnets are a prominent compact-reactor design feature, notably in ARC (Sorbom et al. (2015), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.008), with continuing work by Hartwig et al. (2024), but lifecycle qualification of the joints remains unresolved.
solved_when: A demountable HTS joint design is demonstrated to reconnect repeatedly while maintaining electrical continuity, mechanical integrity, and vacuum tightness at reactor-relevant conditions, with a lifecycle qualification for cycle count and performance established.
why: Demountable magnets would transform maintenance access in compact fusion reactors, but this only matters if the joints stay reliable through many reconnect cycles rather than degrading with use.
key_works: Sorbom et al. (2015), *ARC: A compact, high-field, fusion nuclear science facility and demonstration power plant with demountable magnets*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.008; Hartwig et al. (2024).

title: Rapid outer-cycle tritium recovery
open: How can tritium bred in blanket materials — whether liquid or solid — be extracted fast enough that a burning plasma never starves for fuel? Formally, the recovery time from breeding media must be short enough to satisfy dynamic fuel-self-sufficiency requirements, not merely a favorable steady-state breeding ratio.
status: ARC- and STEP-class models published in 2023 (Meschini et al., DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/acf3fc) show the importance of coupled inventories and processing times.
solved_when: A demonstrated (modeled or engineered) outer-cycle tritium recovery process whose characteristic processing times and coupled inventories meet the dynamic fuel-self-sufficiency requirements of a D-T power plant under realistic operating transients.
why: A plant can have a favorable long-run breeding ratio yet still suffer short-run fuel starvation, so without fast recovery even a well-breeding design cannot sustain operation.
key_works: Meschini et al. (2023), *Modeling and analysis of the tritium fuel cycle for ARC- and STEP-class D-T fusion power plants*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/acf3fc.

title: Rapid remote divertor replacement
open: Can a full divertor replacement cycle — removal, replacement, reconnection, inspection, and recommissioning of representative activated divertor modules — be demonstrated end-to-end under remote handling conditions?
status: Existing DEMO studies estimate substantial maintenance durations, but these are planning estimates, not demonstrated reactor turnaround records (Crofts and Harman, 2014, *Maintenance Duration Estimate for a DEMO Fusion Power Plant*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2014.01.038).
solved_when: A complete removal-through-recommissioning cycle of representative activated divertor modules has been demonstrated remotely, rather than estimated on paper.
why: Divertor replacement frequency may dominate the plant capacity factor, so unproven turnaround times translate directly into lost availability for a fusion power plant.
key_works: Crofts and Harman (2014), *Maintenance Duration Estimate for a DEMO Fusion Power Plant*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2014.01.038.

title: Evidence-based fusion availability models
open: Can the largely assumed component failure and repair rates in fusion availability models be replaced with traceable measurements and dependence models, yielding validated plant-level availability predictions?
status: Maintenance-duration studies and pilot-plant analyses exist, but operating-fleet reliability data do not yet underpin them. Key works include Crofts and Harman (2014), arXiv:1412.4008, and NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*.
solved_when: Fusion availability analyses are built on traceable, measured component failure and repair data with dependence models, and their plant-level availability predictions are validated.
why: Availability assumptions can dominate electricity-cost estimates, so replacing guesses with evidence directly improves the credibility of fusion economic projections.
key_works: Crofts and Harman (2014), arXiv:1412.4008; NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*.

title: Affordable full nonlinear Coulomb collisions
open: Can the full nonlinear gyrokinetic Coulomb collision operator be implemented at production scale in realistic plasma simulations? The target is a computationally affordable implementation of the complete operator in demanding electromagnetic, multispecies simulations, without replacing important velocity-space structure with uncontrolled model collisions.
status: The nonlinear gyrokinetic Coulomb collision operator has already been derived (Jorge, Frei, and Ricci, 2019, *Nonlinear Gyrokinetic Coulomb Collision Operator*, arXiv:1906.03252); the open problem is its computationally affordable use in demanding electromagnetic, multispecies simulations.
solved_when: The full nonlinear gyrokinetic Coulomb operator — already derived — runs at production scale in electromagnetic, multispecies simulations at computationally affordable cost, retaining the velocity-space structure of the true operator rather than substituting model collisions.
why: The choice of collision model can influence transport thresholds, impurity behavior, and irreversible heating, so an affordable exact operator removes an uncontrolled source of error in these predictions.
key_works: Jorge, Frei, and Ricci (2019), *Nonlinear Gyrokinetic Coulomb Collision Operator*, arXiv:1906.03252.

title: Reactive collisions with changing charge states
open: How can gyrokinetic Coulomb collisions be coupled to ionization, recombination, and charge exchange in a way that remains physically consistent as species populations change? Formally, the challenge is to preserve the appropriate particle, momentum, and total-energy balances across reactive events in a partially ionized plasma.
status: A nonlinear Coulomb operator by itself does not supply the reactive collision system required for partially ionized edge plasmas. Relevant work includes Jorge, Frei, and Ricci (2019), *Nonlinear Gyrokinetic Coulomb Collision Operator*, arXiv:1906.03252, and Osborne et al. (2024–2025), arXiv:2410.14403.
solved_when: A coupled gyrokinetic collision–reaction operator exists that exactly preserves particle, momentum, and total-energy conservation in the presence of ionization, recombination, and charge exchange.
why: Incorrect source coupling can create artificial energy or impurity transport near the plasma boundary, corrupting edge-plasma predictions.
key_works: Jorge, Frei, and Ricci (2019), *Nonlinear Gyrokinetic Coulomb Collision Operator*, arXiv:1906.03252; Osborne et al. (2024–2025), arXiv:2410.14403.

title: Conservation and positivity under adaptive remeshing
open: Can kinetic collision discretizations retain positivity, conservation, and the discrete entropy law once combined with the mesh-changing operations of practical adaptive simulations — velocity-grid adaptation, spatial remeshing, and transfers between kinetic representations?
status: Discretizations satisfying these properties already exist for the nonlinear Landau operator — see Hirvijiki, Burby, and Kraus (2018), *Energy-, momentum-, density-, and positivity-preserving spatio-temporal discretizations for the nonlinear Landau collision operator with exact H-theorems*, arXiv:1804.08546 — but maintaining them through the additional operations used by practical adaptive simulations remains unresolved.
solved_when: A scheme is given that preserves positivity, exact conservation, and the discrete H-theorem (exact entropy law) through collision solves together with velocity-grid adaptation, spatial remeshing, and inter-representation transfers, for at least the nonlinear Landau operator.
why: Without it, remeshing can introduce negative populations or erase physically important tails, corrupting the quantities the structure-preserving discretization was built to control.
key_works: Hirvijoki, Burby, and Kraus (2018), *Energy-, momentum-, density-, and positivity-preserving spatio-temporal discretizations for the nonlinear Landau collision operator with exact H-theorems*, arXiv:1804.08546.

title: Three-dimensional gyrokinetic dissipation anomaly
open: Does driven electromagnetic gyrokinetic turbulence in three dimensions retain a finite amount of irreversible entropy production even as the physical collisionality tends to zero, and if so, under what regularity and forcing assumptions?
status: Entropy-cascade theory and reduced gyrokinetic studies, including Tatsuno et al. (2008 preprint), *Nonlinear phase mixing and phase-space cascade of entropy in gyrokinetic plasma turbulence* (arXiv:0811.2538), provide a foundation; the full three-dimensional electromagnetic statement is stronger and remains open.
solved_when: A proof (or rigorous construction) shows finite, nonzero irreversible entropy production in the zero-collisionality limit for the full three-dimensional electromagnetic gyrokinetic system, with explicit regularity and forcing assumptions, or a counterexample ruling it out under those assumptions.
why: It would clarify how nearly collisionless plasma converts turbulent energy into heat, the mechanism behind anomalous transport in magnetized fusion devices.
key_works: Tatsuno et al. (2008 preprint), *Nonlinear phase mixing and phase-space cascade of entropy in gyrokinetic plasma turbulence*, arXiv:0811.2538.

title: Turbulent lifetime distributions near threshold
open: Does near-threshold plasma turbulence decay, persist indefinitely, or exhibit system-size-dependent metastability, and what are the corresponding lifetime distributions?
status: MAST-oriented studies connect subcritical simulations to measurements; distinguishing long transients from genuinely sustained states remains essential, as in van Wyk et al. (2017), *Ion-scale turbulence in MAST: anomalous transport, subcritical transitions, and comparison to BES measurements*, arXiv:1704.02830.
solved_when: The near-threshold regime is classified as decaying, sustained, or metastable, with measured lifetime distributions that distinguish long transients from genuinely sustained turbulent states.
why: A discharge lasting less than a turbulent lifetime can misidentify the underlying stability boundary.
key_works: van Wyk et al. (2017), *Ion-scale turbulence in MAST: anomalous transport, subcritical transitions, and comparison to BES measurements*, arXiv:1704.02830.

title: Staircase survival under reactor scaling
open: Do the transport staircases observed in global simulations persist all the way to reactor scale — that is, under decreasing normalized gyroradius, evolving profiles, electromagnetic turbulence, and realistic sources — or are they finite-domain structures that vanish as devices grow?
status: Global simulations established the staircase phenomenology (Dif-Pradalier et al. 2017, *The E×B staircase of magnetised plasmas*), but reactor-scale persistence remains a separate extrapolation problem that has not been resolved.
solved_when: A demonstration (analytic or simulation-based) shows either that staircases persist under decreasing normalized gyroradius, evolving profiles, electromagnetic turbulence, and realistic sources, or that they disappear in some identifiable limit, with the criterion for persistence made precise.
why: A confinement mechanism that disappears with device size cannot be relied on in reactor design assumptions; settling persistence determines whether staircases are a reactor-relevant feature or an artifact of present-day simulation domains.
key_works: Dif-Pradalier et al. (2017), *The E×B staircase of magnetised plasmas*.

title: Correct isotope scaling of molecular charge exchange
open: Can we replace the crude practice of rescaling hydrogen charge-exchange rates by mass ratios with validated, state-resolved molecular charge-exchange rates for the deuterium–tritium mixtures actually present in reactors?
status: A 2023 SOLPS-ITER investigation (Verhaegh et al. (2023), *Investigating the impact of the molecular charge-exchange rate on detached SOLPS-ITER simulations*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/acd394; arXiv:2301.11298) showed that default rescaling could underestimate molecular-ion production and materially change predicted detachment behavior.
solved_when: A set of validated, state-resolved molecular charge-exchange rates for reactor-relevant isotopic mixtures is available and adopted in edge-code modeling in place of simple hydrogen-to-deuterium/tritium mass rescaling.
why: Incorrect rates can produce the wrong recombination, radiation, and target-current predictions, corrupting the divertor and detachment physics on which reactor design relies.
key_works: Verhaegh et al. (2023), *Investigating the impact of the molecular charge-exchange rate on detached SOLPS-ITER simulations*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/acd394; arXiv:2301.11298.

title: Negative-ion contribution to molecular-assisted recombination
open: Can the recombination mediated by negative hydrogen isotopes be experimentally separated from recombination involving positive molecular ions, and how large is each contribution under strongly detached divertor conditions? In practice, this requires discriminating between these competing molecular-assisted recombination pathways in a detached plasma.
status: MAST-U studies identify molecular channels and possible negative-ion contributions, but their relative importance requires stronger experimental discrimination; see Verhaegh et al. (2023), *Investigations of atomic & molecular processes of NBI-heated discharges in the MAST Upgrade Super-X divertor with implications for reactors*, arXiv:2311.08580.
solved_when: The negative-ion-mediated pathway and the positive-molecular-ion pathway are separately identified and quantified (their relative contributions measured) under strongly detached conditions.
why: The two pathway families respond differently to isotope composition, vibrational excitation, and electron temperature, so knowing their relative weights determines how recombination can be predicted and controlled in reactor-relevant detached regimes.
key_works: Verhaegh et al. (2023), *Investigations of atomic & molecular processes of NBI-heated discharges in the MAST Upgrade Super-X divertor with implications for reactors*, arXiv:2311.08580.

title: Molecular-assisted dissociation power accounting
open: Can we close the power balance for molecular-assisted dissociation in a tokamak edge and divertor, tracing where the energy goes? A complete account should follow fragment kinetic energy, subsequent ionization, radiation, and the energy ultimately deposited on surfaces.
status: MAST-U analyses (Verhaegh et al. (2023), *Investigations of atomic & molecular processes of NBI-heated discharges in the MAST Upgrade Super-X divertor with implications for reactors*, arXiv:2311.08580) infer consequential dissociation-related power sinks; they also show that a reaction's local energy removal is not necessarily its net plant-facing exhaust benefit.
solved_when: A quantitative power accounting exists that tracks all dissociation-related sinks — fragment kinetic energy, subsequent ionization, radiation, and surface-deposited energy — and closes the divertor power balance without unexplained residual power attributable to misallocated chemical energy.
why: Misallocated chemical energy can show up as apparently unexplained divertor power, corrupting interpretation of exhaust measurements and reactor-relevant divertor designs.
key_works: Verhaegh et al. (2023), *Investigations of atomic & molecular processes of NBI-heated discharges in the MAST Upgrade Super-X divertor with implications for reactors*, arXiv:2311.08580.

title: Sub-electronvolt ion–molecule elastic collisions
open: Can we experimentally validate the momentum and energy-transfer operators used for ion–molecule elastic collisions in the very cold plasma regions of detached divertors?
status: Dedicated SOLPS-ITER predictions published in 2023 by Myatra et al. (*Nuclear Fusion* 63, 076030) examine these collisions in strongly detached MAST-U Super-X conditions, but direct discriminating validation against experiment remains needed.
solved_when: Direct discriminating measurements of these collision operators are obtained under strongly detached divertor conditions at temperatures below approximately one electronvolt, sufficient to confirm or refute the SOLPS-ITER model predictions.
why: Processes that are negligible in hotter plasma can control pressure balance below approximately one electronvolt, so unvalidated operators undermine predictive modeling of detached divertor operation.
key_works: Myatra et al. (2023), *SOLPS-ITER predictive simulations of the impact of ion-molecule elastic collisions on strongly detached MAST-U Super-X divertor conditions*, *Nuclear Fusion* 63, 076030.

title: Sheath structure below the critical grazing angle
open: When a grazing-incidence sheath reaches the angle at which monotonic solutions cease to exist, which configuration does nature actually select? The problem is to determine the physically selected sheath structure below this critical grazing angle, with kinetic electrons and finite Debye length included.
status: A 2025 study (Geraldini et al., *Characteristics of monotonic sheaths near a wall with grazing magnetic incidence*, arXiv:2508.09067) characterizes monotonic grazing-incidence sheaths and identifies the critical-angle boundary of their existence; however, this boundary does not describe the state of the plasma below it, which remains undetermined.
solved_when: A characterization is given of the sheath configuration realized below the critical angle — with kinetic electrons and finite Debye length — including the selection principle that picks it out.
why: Reactor divertors deliberately use shallow magnetic incidence to spread heat, so predicting sheath behavior at grazing angles bears directly on divertor heat-load design.
key_works: Geraldini et al. (2025), *Characteristics of monotonic sheaths near a wall with grazing magnetic incidence*, arXiv:2508.09067.

title: Secondary-emission sheath transitions on reactor surfaces
open: When do irradiated, contaminated, or otherwise evolving plasma-facing surfaces in a reactor cross into emission-dominated sheath states, and what does that transition do to the electron heat flux reaching the wall? A sharper formulation asks for transition maps — boundaries in surface-condition and plasma-parameter space separating conventional Debye sheaths from emission-dominated regimes.
status: The absence of a conventional Debye sheath under strong secondary emission was demonstrated theoretically in 2012 by Campanell, Khrabrov, and Kaganovich (*Absence of Debye Sheaths due to Secondary Electron Emission*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.108.255001); reactor-surface transition maps remain a separate, open problem.
solved_when: Transition criteria (maps) are established for realistic reactor surfaces — irradiated, contaminated, or evolving — identifying when emission-dominated sheath states occur, together with a determination of the resulting electron heat flux in those states.
why: Strong surface emission can invalidate the standard wall-potential and heat-transmission assumptions used to predict heat loads, so without these maps reactor wall designs rest on sheath physics that may simply not apply.
key_works: Campanell, Khrabrov, and Kaganovich (2012), *Absence of Debye Sheaths due to Secondary Electron Emission*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.108.255001.

title: Consequences of the unfavorable maximum-J minority
open: Can the small population of particles that violate maximum-J behavior in optimized vacuum quasi-isodynamic fields trigger consequential instabilities or losses, or is its effect negligible?
status: A published construction (Rodríguez, Helander, and Goodman, 2023 preprint, *The maximum-J property in quasi-isodynamic stellarators*, arXiv:2311.14439) gives favorable behavior for 99.6% of trapped particles while identifying an unavoidable unfavorable shallowly trapped population.
solved_when: A determination — analytic or numerical — of whether the unfavorable shallowly trapped minority in a vacuum quasi-isodynamic field (the population outside the 99.6% of trapped particles with favorable behavior) drives consequential instabilities or particle losses.
why: A small phase-space fraction can matter disproportionately if it resonates strongly, so the safety of optimized configurations cannot be certified by favorable behavior on the majority alone.
key_works: Rodríguez, Helander, and Goodman (2023 preprint), *The maximum-J property in quasi-isodynamic stellarators*, arXiv:2311.14439.

title: Uniform treatment of merging neoclassical regimes
open: Can the merged asymptotic description of the superbanana-plateau and square-root-collisionality regimes be extended beyond the restricted setting of nearly quasisymmetric stellarators? In particular, can it be made uniform over realistic plasma profiles, multiple species, and departures from exact quasisymmetry?
status: Catto, Tolman, and Parra (2023) derived a merged treatment for nearly quasisymmetric stellarators (*Merging of the superbanana plateau and √ν transport regimes in nearly quasisymmetric stellarators*, DOI: 10.1017/S0022377822001301); this restricted result should not be mistaken for a universal closure.
solved_when: A uniform asymptotic treatment exists that covers realistic profiles, multiple ion species, and finite departures from near-quasisymmetry, reducing to the Catto–Tolman–Parra result in the quasisymmetric limit.
why: Regime boundaries can fall inside the operating window of an optimized reactor, so a non-uniform description fails precisely where the machine is designed to run.
key_works: Catto et al. (2023), *Merging of the superbanana plateau and √ν transport regimes in nearly quasisymmetric stellarators*, DOI: 10.1017/S0022377822001301.

title: Full flux-surface electrostatic-potential maps
open: Measure the three-dimensional electrostatic-potential variation on a flux surface accurately enough to discriminate competing impurity-transport models. A successful map would resolve the spatial structure of the potential on the surface, not just its magnitude, so that theoretical predictions can be tested point by point.
status: TJ-II measurements reported substantial potential variations and partial agreement with calculations, but local discrepancies remained (Pedrosa et al. 2015, *Electrostatic potential variations along flux surfaces in stellarators*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/55/5/052001; arXiv:1404.0932).
solved_when: A full-flux-surface map of the electrostatic potential exists with sufficient accuracy and spatial resolution to distinguish between competing impurity-transport model predictions, resolving the local discrepancies currently seen against calculations.
why: Potential variations that are small relative to the bulk temperature can strongly affect the transport of high-charge impurities, so these maps directly determine which impurity-segregation physics is actually at play.
key_works: Pedrosa et al. (2015), *Electrostatic potential variations along flux surfaces in stellarators*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/55/5/052001; arXiv:1404.0932.

title: Electric-root transition fronts
open: How do spatial transitions between roots of the ambipolar electric field propagate and stabilize in a stellarator plasma? A theory is needed that predicts front position, propagation speed, and stability while accounting for finite orbit widths and the feedback of evolving radial profiles.
status: Neoclassical theory identifies strong radial-electric-field dependence; selecting a spatially evolving root is more demanding than solving a local ambipolarity equation. Related formalisms include front selection in bistable systems and nonlocal reaction–diffusion dynamics; see Calvo et al. (2017), *The effect of tangential drifts on neoclassical transport in stellarators close to omnigeneity*, arXiv:1610.06016.
solved_when: A predictive theory exists that yields the position, propagation, and stability of electric-root transition fronts, incorporating finite orbit widths and profile feedback, and is checkable against specified profiles.
why: Root transitions can reorganize confinement and impurity transport, so a predictive theory would tell when and where such reorganization occurs in operating stellarators.
key_works: Calvo et al. (2017), *The effect of tangential drifts on neoclassical transport in stellarators close to omnigeneity*, arXiv:1610.06016.

title: Nonlinear significance of stellarator zonal-flow oscillations
open: When does the observed oscillatory relaxation of the radial electric field in stellarator plasmas actually alter sustained turbulence, rather than merely being the response of a linear relaxation experiment?
status: Oscillatory relaxation was observed experimentally in 2017 (Alonso et al., 2017, *Observation of Oscillatory Radial Electric Field Relaxation in a Stellarator Plasma*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.118.185002), and semianalytical frequency calculations exist (Monreal et al., 2017, arXiv:1701.02722).
solved_when: A determination is given of the conditions under which the zonal-flow oscillation materially changes sustained turbulence, distinguishing genuine nonlinear regulation from linear relaxation.
why: A measurable mode is useful for stellarator design only if its nonlinear role in confinement is understood.
key_works: Alonso et al. (2017), *Observation of Oscillatory Radial Electric Field Relaxation in a Stellarator Plasma*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.118.185002; Monreal et al. (2017), arXiv:1701.02722.

title: Self-consistent pressure flattening near stellarator islands
open: How are pressure profiles and their associated currents near magnetic islands in stellarators actually selected when transport and MHD equilibrium are solved together, rather than flattened by assumption? Formally, determine the self-consistent island pressure profile and pressure-driven currents from the coupled transport–equilibrium problem.
status: Pressure-driven currents near islands were analyzed by Reiman et al. (2016), *Pressure driven currents near magnetic islands in 3D MHD equilibria*, *Physics of Plasmas* 23, 072502, but the selection of the self-consistent profile remains a further coupled problem.
solved_when: A solution gives the island pressure profile and its associated currents as outputs of the coupled transport–equilibrium system, with no independently prescribed flattening, and shows how these affect the predicted island structure and stability.
why: Assumed pressure flattening feeds directly into both the predicted island structure and stability assessments, so a self-consistent determination changes what these calculations actually predict.
key_works: Reiman et al. (2016), *Pressure driven currents near magnetic islands in 3D MHD equilibria*, *Physics of Plasmas* 23, 072502.

title: Dynamically accessible island elimination
open: Can a magnetically confined plasma actually be driven into an island-free configuration, or are optimized boundary adjustments merely states that exist on paper? Formally, determine under what conditions boundary shaping that eliminates magnetic islands in equilibrium is dynamically accessible through finite-resistivity evolution.
status: High-pressure free-boundary equilibrium optimization demonstrated island elimination in 2002 (Hudson et al., 2002, *Eliminating Islands in High-Pressure Free-Boundary Stellarator Magnetohydrodynamic Equilibrium Solutions*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.89.275003); however, equilibrium existence does not establish dynamical accessibility, and the question of accessibility remains open.
solved_when: A criterion (analytic or numerical) is established identifying when an island-eliminating equilibrium solution, such as those produced by free-boundary optimization, can be reached by finite-resistivity plasma evolution from a realistic initial state; failing that, a demonstration that specific optimized equilibria are or are not accessible.
why: A numerically optimized topology may not be the state reached by an experiment, so equilibrium optimization alone cannot guarantee that a designed island-free configuration will be realized in practice.
key_works: Hudson et al. (2002), *Eliminating Islands in High-Pressure Free-Boundary Stellarator Magnetohydrodynamic Equilibrium Solutions*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.89.275003.

title: Certified relaxation gaps in coil optimization
open: How large is the gap between an optimized continuous-current representation of a coil design and the best manufacturable discrete-coil realization, and can this gap be bounded even when the global optimum of the relaxation itself is not certified?
status: QUADCOIL (Fu et al., 2024–2025, *Global Stellarator Coil Optimization with Quadratic Constraints and Objectives*, arXiv:2408.08267) provides exact global solutions in some parameter regions and useful approximate solutions elsewhere; extracting certified physical-coil quality from these solutions remains a distinct problem.
solved_when: A bound is established on the difference between the continuous-current optimum and the best discrete physical-coil realization, valid including cases where no certified global optimum of the relaxed problem is available.
why: A favorable mathematical relaxation may conceal expensive discretization losses, so designs that look optimal in the relaxed problem can be far from optimal once realized as manufacturable coils.
key_works: Fu et al. (2024–2025), *Global Stellarator Coil Optimization with Quadratic Constraints and Objectives*, arXiv:2408.08267.

title: Quantified flexibility of optimized stellarators
open: Can stellarator optimization be reformulated to optimize not a single plasma configuration but a sufficiently broad family of configurations reachable with permitted coil currents, while still satisfying conductor-strain and engineering constraints? In other words, can the reachable set of the coil system be built directly into the optimization objective rather than treated as an afterthought?
status: The CSX single-stage design incorporates engineering constraints and possible auxiliary coils (Baillod et al. 2024, *Integrating Novel Stellarator Single-Stage Optimization Algorithms to Design the Columbia Stellarator Experiment*, arXiv:2409.05261), but a general quantitative flexibility–performance tradeoff remains open.
solved_when: A design method exists that jointly optimizes a family of configurations spanning the reachable set of permitted coil currents, with conductor-strain and engineering constraints maintained throughout, and the quantitative tradeoff between flexibility and performance is characterized.
why: An exceptionally optimized but inflexible machine may be difficult to commission or operate; quantifying the flexibility–performance tradeoff would tell designers how much performance must be sacrificed for operational room.
key_works: Baillod et al. (2024), *Integrating Novel Stellarator Single-Stage Optimization Algorithms to Design the Columbia Stellarator Experiment*, arXiv:2409.05261.

title: Experimental discrimination of hydrogen self-clustering
open: Can experiments on tungsten with independently characterized defect populations tell whether hydrogen nucleates bubbles by self-clustering, rather than by trapping at pre-existing vacancies, dislocations, or impurities? A decisive experiment would isolate the contribution of each mechanism under plasma exposure.
status: Density-functional and statistical models predict self-clustering mechanisms [Hou et al. (2017), arXiv:1712.09606], but their quantitative contribution under plasma exposure remains to be isolated.
solved_when: An experimental campaign on tungsten samples with quantified defect populations (vacancies, dislocations, impurities) discriminates self-clustering from defect trapping as the nucleation mechanism.
why: Different nucleation mechanisms imply different retention and blister-prevention strategies.
key_works: Hou et al. (2017), *Hydrogen bubble nucleation by self-clustering: Density Functional Theory and statistical models studies using tungsten as a model system*, arXiv:1712.09606.

title: Self-passivation after preferential alloy erosion
open: Do self-passivating tungsten alloys such as W–Cr–Y still form a protective oxide scale after plasma exposure that preferentially erodes alloying elements from the surface?
status: Self-passivating tungsten alloys have demonstrated favorable oxidation behavior, but surface composition after service remains a separate, unqualified variable. Key work: Calvo et al. (2018), *Self-passivating tungsten alloys of the system W-Cr-Y for high temperature applications*, DOI: 10.1016/j.ijrmhm.2018.01.018.
solved_when: An experiment shows that W–Cr–Y (or a related self-passivating alloy), after plasma exposure with preferential removal of alloying elements, retains protective oxidation behavior under the relevant high-temperature conditions.
why: Accident protection must work on the used component, not just on a freshly manufactured specimen; if erosion depletes the scale-forming elements, the alloy's safety function could fail in service.
key_works: Calvo et al. (2018), *Self-passivating tungsten alloys of the system W-Cr-Y for high temperature applications*, DOI: 10.1016/j.ijrmhm.2018.01.018.

title: Direct validation of RF current condensation
open: Can an experiment directly observe the predicted nonlinear localization of RF-driven heating and current inside a magnetic island, distinguishing condensation from ordinary changes in deposition profile?
status: RF current condensation was proposed in 2018 (Reiman and Fisch, *Suppression of Tearing Modes by Radio Frequency Current Condensation*, PhysRevLett.121.225001; arXiv:1806.09260), with later work developing validation strategies; the mechanism still requires a discriminating experimental test.
solved_when: A measurement demonstrates the nonlinear localization of RF current within a magnetic island in a way that separates it from ordinary deposition changes, as predicted by the condensation theory.
why: Validating the condensation mechanism would confirm a route to reducing the RF power required to suppress dangerous tearing modes.
key_works: Reiman and Fisch (2018), *Suppression of Tearing Modes by Radio Frequency Current Condensation*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.121.225001; arXiv:1806.09260.

title: Robust O–X–B conversion in turbulent edges
open: Can ordinary-to-extraordinary-to-Bernstein wave conversion be kept efficient in a reactor-relevant edge, where density gradients fluctuate, launch angles drift from ideal, and the edge geometry evolves over time?
status: Electron-Bernstein-wave current drive in overdense plasma was demonstrated at the W7-AS stellarator by Laqua et al. (2003), *Electron-Bernstein-Wave Current Drive in an Overdense Plasma at the Wendelstein 7-AS Stellarator*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.90.075003; extending that coupling to robust, reactor-compatible conditions remains unresolved.
solved_when: A coupling scheme maintains efficient O–X–B conversion under realistic fluctuating density gradients, launch angle errors, and evolving edge geometry at reactor scale — not merely under the quiescent, fixed-geometry conditions of past demonstrations.
why: Bernstein waves are the only route for radio-frequency power and current drive to reach overdense plasma, so without a robust coupling pathway this access is lost exactly in the reactor regimes that need it.
key_works: Laqua et al. (2003), *Electron-Bernstein-Wave Current Drive in an Overdense Plasma at the Wendelstein 7-AS Stellarator*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.90.075003.

title: Three-ion heating under changing fuel composition
open: Can efficient three-ion cyclotron heating be sustained in a plasma whose fuel composition is itself changing — as minority populations and fast-ion distributions evolve over time?
status: Three-ion scenarios have substantial experimental and theoretical support, but their efficiency depends sensitively on composition and resonant absorbers (Kazakov et al. (2021), *Physics and applications of three-ion ICRF scenarios for fusion research*, *Physics of Plasmas* 28, 020501).
solved_when: A control scheme (e.g., resonance tracking) maintains efficient three-ion ICRF heating throughout composition evolution and reactor transients, keeping the system within the narrow composition window required for absorption efficiency.
why: A narrow composition window could be difficult to preserve during reactor transients; without active maintenance of the resonant conditions, heating efficiency degrades exactly when the plasma needs controlled energy input.
key_works: Kazakov et al. (2021), *Physics and applications of three-ion ICRF scenarios for fusion research*, *Physics of Plasmas* 28, 020501.

title: Composition-dependent pellet-plasmoid drift
open: Can we predict how far the ablation cloud from a mixed-material pellet will drift radially in a tokamak, when the pellet's changing composition drives evolving ionization states, radiation, magnetic perturbations, and electrical conductivity? A predictive theory would give the drift trajectory as a function of pellet composition and background plasma conditions.
status: Three-dimensional MHD modeling published in 2024 (Kong et al. (2024), *3D MHD modelling of plasmoid drift following massive material injection in a tokamak*, arXiv:2407.01399) advances drift prediction; reliable mixture-dependent assimilation remains a further challenge.
solved_when: A validated model yields the radial drift of the ablation cloud for mixed-material pellets, accounting for ionization, radiation, magnetic perturbations, and composition-dependent electrical conductivity, with reliable mixture-dependent assimilation into the plasma.
why: Pellet material can drift away from the region where it is needed, so fueling and control of the core depend on knowing — and ultimately steering — where injected material actually lands.
key_works: Kong et al. (2024), *3D MHD modelling of plasmoid drift following massive material injection in a tokamak*, arXiv:2407.01399.

title: Predictive non-LTE hohlraum emission
open: Can atomic-kinetics models predict the emission spectrum and drive of an ignition-scale hohlraum from first principles, without experiment-specific correction multipliers? Formally, the goal is a non-LTE model whose predictions match the full hohlraum spectrum and target drive in fully predictive simulations.
status: Improved non-LTE modeling was published in 2025 (Farmer et al., *Toward an improved nonlocal thermodynamic equilibrium model for more predictive simulations of ignition scale hohlraums*, DOI: 10.1063/5.0267536); matching the full spectrum and target drive remains the relevant test.
solved_when: A non-LTE atomic-kinetics model reproduces both the full hohlraum spectrum and the target drive at ignition scale, with no experiment-specific correction multipliers.
why: An incorrect radiation spectrum changes both ablation and preheat, so predictive credibility of ignition-scale hohlraum simulations hinges on getting it right.
key_works: Farmer et al. (2025), *Toward an improved nonlocal thermodynamic equilibrium model for more predictive simulations of ignition scale hohlraums*, DOI: 10.1063/5.0267536.

title: Graded inner shells robust to fabrication uncertainty
open: Can we design graded inner-shell material gradients for double-shell capsules that stay near optimal even when fabricated with realistic imperfections, rather than being tuned only to a nominal simulated yield? In other words, can the optimization objective be reformulated to account for measured uncertainty in thickness, composition, surface finish, and assembly?
status: Multifidelity optimization coupling xRAGE with machine learning (Vazirani et al. (2023), *Coupling multi-fidelity xRAGE with machine learning for graded inner shell design optimization in double shell capsules*, *Physics of Plasmas* 30, 062704) has identified promising graded-shell designs, but these are nominal-yield optimizations; robust experimental realization under fabrication uncertainty remains a further step.
solved_when: A graded-shell design is produced whose performance remains acceptable under the measured distributions of thickness, composition, surface finish, and assembly uncertainties—and this robustness is realized experimentally, not just in simulation.
why: A narrow numerical optimum can collapse into poor manufacturing yield, so designs found by nominal-yield optimization may be unrealizable in practice.
key_works: Vazirani et al. (2023), *Coupling multi-fidelity xRAGE with machine learning for graded inner shell design optimization in double shell capsules*, *Physics of Plasmas* 30, 062704.

title: Chirping criteria far from marginal stability
open: When an energetic-particle-driven mode is pushed far beyond marginal stability on an evolving background with substantial redistribution of energetic particles, when does it chirp in frequency rather than settle into steady saturated oscillations? A criterion is sought that extends existing chirping-versus-steady-frequency discrimination into this strongly nonlinear regime.
status: Existing criteria incorporate collisions and turbulence and have experimental comparisons, but the near-threshold reasoning behind them does not automatically cover strongly nonlinear bursts (Duarte et al., 2017, *Prediction of Nonlinear Evolution Character of Energetic-Particle-Driven Instabilities*, PPPL-5366).
solved_when: A criterion is available that predicts chirping versus steady-frequency behavior for strongly driven modes with evolving backgrounds and significant energetic-particle redistribution, complementing the near-threshold results already validated against experiment.
why: Different nonlinear mode behavior produces very different particle-loss risks, so reliable prediction directly informs how aggressively such modes can be driven in burning plasmas.
key_works: Duarte et al. (2017), *Prediction of Nonlinear Evolution Character of Energetic-Particle-Driven Instabilities*, PPPL-5366.

title: Whistler wave-number and resonance identification
open: Which runaway electrons do whistler waves in a tokamak actually scatter? The goal is to measure the wave-vector distribution and damping of runaway-driven whistler waves well enough to pin down the electron energies and pitch angles at which the waves resonate.
status: Detailed DIII-D characterization published in 2025 (Choudhury et al., DOI: 10.1063/5.0277589) improves frequency and temporal constraints, but frequency measurements alone do not uniquely identify the resonance.
solved_when: The wave-vector distribution and damping of runaway-driven whistler waves are measured sufficiently to determine which electron energies and pitch angles the waves scatter.
why: An observed wave may couple only weakly to the electrons responsible for damage, so frequency measurements alone cannot tell whether mitigation via these waves would actually work.
key_works: Choudhury et al. (2025), *Detailed characterization of runaway electron driven whistler waves in low-density DIII-D discharges*, DOI: 10.1063/5.0277589.

title: Net electricity from an integrated fusion plant
subfield: Energy gain, ignition, and burning plasmas
open: Can a fusion plant, once all its own subsystems are paid for in electricity, deliver more power to the grid than it consumes? Formally, this means demonstrating positive net electricity exported over a complete operating cycle, including drivers, magnets, cryogenics, pumps, fuel processing, startup, and recovery.
status: Target gain above unity is established in inertial confinement, but that is physics-level gain, not plant-level electrical gain. The 2026 DOE roadmap still treats integrated fusion electricity as a development objective.
solved_when: An integrated fusion plant exports positive net electricity to the grid over a complete operating cycle, with the accounting covering drivers, magnets, cryogenics, pumps, fuel processing, startup, and recovery.
why: This is the line that separates a fusion experiment from an electricity-generating technology; no amount of scientific gain matters if the whole plant cannot power itself and still export current.
key_works: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Industrially repeatable isotope-selective adsorption
open: Can an isotope-selective adsorbent survive industrial service? The goal is a material that endures 10,000 separation/regeneration cycles with less than 10% degradation in both working capacity and isotope selectivity.
status: Recent selective-adsorption results — Becker et al. (2025), *Tritium Separation from Gaseous 1,2,3H Isotopologue Mixtures by Selective Adsorption on Ag-Exchanged Zeolite Type Y*, arXiv:2510.03333 — establish promising laboratory separation; the proposed endurance benchmark is not an achieved record or an established universal requirement.
solved_when: A demonstrated run of 10,000 separation/regeneration cycles shows less than 10% degradation in working capacity and less than 10% in isotope selectivity, with full energy and inventory costs reported.
why: Repeatability over industrial cycle counts is what separates a useful process material from a one-time laboratory result.
key_works: Becker et al. (2025), *Tritium Separation from Gaseous 1,2,3H Isotopologue Mixtures by Selective Adsorption on Ag-Exchanged Zeolite Type Y*, arXiv:2510.03333.

title: Exact three-dimensional vacuum equilibria with nested surfaces
open: Does there exist an exact analytic toroidal vacuum magnetic field, with no axisymmetry, whose field lines lie on nested toroidal flux surfaces? A resolution would either exhibit such a curl-free field explicitly or establish a precise obstruction to its existence.
status: Analytic finite-pressure constructions from September 2026 do not settle the curl-free case; that paper (Landreman 2026, *Analytic toroidal 3D MHD equilibria and steady Euler flows with invariant surfaces*, arXiv:2609.26742) explicitly leaves it open.
solved_when: An exact analytic, nonaxisymmetric toroidal vacuum (curl-free) field with nested toroidal flux surfaces is constructed, or a rigorously stated obstruction to such fields is proved.
why: Exact examples would serve as benchmarks for equilibrium codes and clarify what configurations external coils can actually realize.
key_works: Landreman (2026), *Analytic toroidal 3D MHD equilibria and steady Euler flows with invariant surfaces*, arXiv:2609.26742.

title: Robust burn-control stability
subfield: Energy gain, ignition, and burning plasmas
open: Can a controller be established — and validated experimentally — that keeps fusion power stable in a burning plasma against coupled temperature, density, ash, and confinement perturbations, without demanding excessive auxiliary power?
status: Burning-plasma dynamics are modeled, but reactor-scale closed-loop validation remains part of the ITER research program; required R&D in existing fusion facilities is laid out in Loarte et al. (2025), *Required R&D in existing fusion facilities to support the new baseline ITER Research Plan*, ITR-25-005.
solved_when: Such a controller is formulated and demonstrated in reactor-scale closed-loop experiments, stabilizing the burn against the coupled perturbations above at acceptable auxiliary power levels.
why: A favorable equilibrium alone does not guarantee a working reactor; if disturbances repeatedly terminate the burn, net energy production fails in practice.
key_works: Loarte et al. (2025), *Required R&D in existing fusion facilities to support the new baseline ITER Research Plan*, ITR-25-005.

title: Helium-ash removal without fuel loss
subfield: Energy gain, ignition, and burning plasmas
open: Can a burning deuterium–tritium plasma be made to expel its thermalized helium ash without also expelling the fuel it needs? Formally, this asks for a demonstration of selective removal of thermalized helium while retaining sufficient deuterium and tritium and preserving core confinement.
status: Particle-transport and exhaust studies exist, but self-consistent ash removal in a sustained, strongly self-heated reactor plasma remains unvalidated; see Greenfield, Collins, and workshop contributors (2023), *Report of the US ITER Research Program Research Needs Workshop*, arXiv:2303.12094.
solved_when: Selective ash removal is demonstrated experimentally in a sustained, strongly self-heated reactor plasma — that is, helium is extracted while deuterium and tritium are sufficiently retained and core confinement is preserved.
why: Accumulated helium dilutes the fuel mixture and can extinguish an otherwise viable burn, so without validated ash removal no self-heated reactor plasma can be sustained.
key_works: Greenfield, Collins, and workshop contributors (2023), *Report of the US ITER Research Program Research Needs Workshop*, arXiv:2303.12094.

title: Predictive energetic-particle mode saturation
subfield: Energy gain, ignition, and burning plasmas
open: When do energetic-particle instabilities in burning plasmas saturate harmlessly, and when do they chirp in frequency, avalanche, or drive large bursts of energetic-particle transport? The goal is a predictive model, validated across devices, that specifies which saturation outcome occurs from measurable plasma and fast-ion parameters.
status: Nonlinear theories explain important regimes, but no universal reactor-validated saturation rule follows from the existing review literature, e.g. Chen and Zonca (2016), *Physics of Alfvén waves and energetic particles in burning plasmas*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.88.015008.
solved_when: A single saturation rule or model, validated across devices, predicts whether a given energetic-particle instability saturates harmlessly, chirps, avalanches, or produces large transport bursts.
why: Linear instability thresholds alone cannot establish acceptable alpha-particle confinement, so without a validated nonlinear saturation criterion reactor designs cannot ensure energetic-particle losses stay tolerable.
key_works: Chen and Zonca (2016), *Physics of Alfvén waves and energetic particles in burning plasmas*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.88.015008.

title: Useful alpha channeling
subfield: Energy gain, ignition, and burning plasmas
open: Can a substantial fraction of fusion-alpha energy be channeled into useful fuel heating or current drive in an actual plasma, with the full wave-generation power honestly included in the accounting?
status: Theory and proposed operating schemes exist, including Ochs et al. (2022), *Improving the Feasibility of Economical Proton-Boron 11 Fusion via Alpha Channeling with a Hybrid Fast and Thermal Proton Scheme* (DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevE.106.055215; arXiv:2210.08076), but economically useful reactor-scale alpha channeling has not been established by the cited work.
solved_when: A measured energy transfer of alpha power to fuel heating or current drive is demonstrated, at a substantial fraction, with the wave-generation power fully counted in the balance.
why: It would reduce recirculating power in a reactor and improve the prospects of difficult fuels such as proton–boron 11.
key_works: Ochs et al. (2022), *Improving the Feasibility of Economical Proton-Boron 11 Fusion via Alpha Channeling with a Hybrid Fast and Thermal Proton Scheme*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevE.106.055215; arXiv:2210.08076.

title: Low-recirculating-power access to the burning state
subfield: Energy gain, ignition, and burning plasmas
open: Can a fusion plasma be guided from startup to a stable high-gain burning state along a trajectory that is actually achievable in an experiment, without auxiliary systems whose recirculating power cost makes the whole plant uneconomic?
