Formally, this is a reachability question in nonlinear control: which dynamically admissible startup paths terminate at the burning state under realistic engineering constraints?
status: Lawson-condition studies, notably Wurzel and Hsu (2025), *Continuing progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criteria* (arXiv:2505.03834), quantify the gain requirements for burning plasmas; however, satisfying a steady-state condition does not establish an affordable path to reaching that state.
solved_when: An experimentally accessible startup trajectory is identified that reaches a stable high-gain burning state while keeping the recirculating power demanded by auxiliary systems below the level at which the complete plant becomes uneconomic.
why: Startup hardware and repeated failed starts can dominate plant power and availability, so even a plasma that satisfies the gain condition in steady state offers no affordable route to get there.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2025), *Continuing progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criteria*, arXiv:2505.03834.

title: Microtearing saturation and electron heat transport
open: Can we predict the nonlinear electron heat transport produced by microtearing modes, including the overlap of the magnetic islands they generate, collisional effects, electron kinetics, and their interplay with other turbulence channels?
status: Electromagnetic gyrokinetic studies of microtearing turbulence exist (e.g., Garbet et al. 2010, *Gyrokinetic simulations of turbulent transport*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/50/4/043002; and the MGK SciDAC publication program), but predictive extrapolation across collisionality and geometry remains an open research problem.
solved_when: A validated nonlinear (electromagnetic gyrokinetic) prediction of microtearing-driven electron heat transport is available that extrapolates predictively across collisionality regimes and magnetic geometries.
why: Electron heat loss from microtearing turbulence can determine whether high-pressure operating points are viable in a fusion device.
key_works: Garbet et al. (2010), *Gyrokinetic simulations of turbulent transport*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/50/4/043002; MGK SciDAC publication program.

title: Kinetic-ballooning transport beyond onset
open: Can we predict the saturated level of particle and heat transport once kinetic-ballooning modes have gone unstable, rather than merely knowing that they will? That is, derive and validate a theory of the post-onset electromagnetic transport, not just the threshold for instability.
status: Threshold calculations for kinetic-ballooning modes are already incorporated into pedestal models, notably the EPED predictive model of pedestal height and width (Snyder et al. 2011, *Nuclear Fusion* 51, 103016); however, the saturated electromagnetic transport beyond onset remains harder to predict. Related efforts include nonlinear saturation near criticality and reduced-order bifurcation models.
solved_when: A first-principles (or validated reduced) prediction of the saturated, post-threshold kinetic-ballooning transport is derived and shown to agree with experimental or nonlinear-simulation data — replacing threshold-only criteria in pedestal transport modeling.
why: Threshold-based pedestal design can fail if the transport that sets in beyond threshold is unexpectedly strong, degrading confinement in ways the onset condition alone cannot anticipate.
key_works: Snyder et al. (2011), *A first-principles predictive model of the pedestal height and width: development, testing and ITER optimization with the EPED model*, *Nuclear Fusion* 51, 103016.

title: Intrinsic rotation in low-torque reactors
open: Can we predict the sign, magnitude, and radial profile of the toroidal rotation that a tokamak plasma develops on its own, with no strong external momentum injection? In other words, is there a quantitative theory of intrinsic rotation in low-torque reactor regimes?
status: Specific mechanisms — including intrinsic rotation driven by non-Maxwellian equilibrium effects, demonstrated theoretically in Barnes et al. (2013), *Intrinsic Rotation Driven by Non-Maxwellian Equilibria in Tokamak Plasmas*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.111.055005 — have been established, but a universal quantitative prediction of intrinsic rotation remains unavailable.
solved_when: A predictive model yields the sign, magnitude, and radial profile of toroidal rotation without strong external momentum input, validated as a universal quantitative prediction across relevant plasma conditions.
why: Rotation influences plasma stability and transport, but in a reactor the neutral beams may deliver little torque, so the plasma's self-generated rotation must be understood and predicted from first principles.
key_works: Barnes et al. (2013), *Intrinsic Rotation Driven by Non-Maxwellian Equilibria in Tokamak Plasmas*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.111.055005.

title: Momentum-pinch closure
open: Can the diffusive, convective, and residual-stress contributions to momentum transport be separately identified well enough to predict how plasma rotation changes during reactor operating transitions?
status: Theoretical decompositions exist, but their practical identification and extrapolation remain entangled with intrinsic-rotation physics.
solved_when: A decomposition of momentum transport into diffusive, convective, and residual-stress terms, identified from data or experiment, correctly predicts rotation changes under reactor operating transitions.
why: Incorrect momentum transport predictions undermine the stability-control requirements of a reactor.
key_works: Barnes et al. (2013), *Intrinsic Rotation Driven by Non-Maxwellian Equilibria in Tokamak Plasmas*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.111.055005.

title: Non-trace impurity transport
open: How should impurity transport be predicted when the impurities are no longer passive tracers but actively modify the turbulence, collisions, radiation, and equilibrium of the plasma? A theory is needed that treats the impurity as a self-consistent, feedback-coupled species rather than a test particle advected by fields it does not affect.
status: The validity limits of passive-impurity approximations were explicitly examined in 2020 by Lesur et al. (2020), *Validity limits of the passive treatment of impurities in gyrokinetic tokamak simulations*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/ab6e48; reactor mixtures require wider validation beyond those limits.
solved_when: A predictive treatment of impurity transport exists that self-consistently accounts for the impurity's back-reaction on turbulence, collisions, radiation, and equilibrium, and is validated for reactor-relevant impurity mixtures beyond the passive-tracer regime.
why: Trace-species calculations can fail exactly when contamination becomes operationally dangerous, so reliable reactor impurity control depends on closing this gap.
key_works: Lesur et al. (2020), *Validity limits of the passive treatment of impurities in gyrokinetic tokamak simulations*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/ab6e48.

title: Turbulence spreading across stable regions
open: How does turbulence driven in one radial region of a fusion plasma spread into and through regions that are linearly stable, and how does this penetration modify transport barriers? A quantitative account is needed of the nonlocal propagation of turbulent intensity into stable zones and its effect on barrier strength.
status: Global simulations reveal nonlocal behavior that local flux-tube calculations do not by themselves resolve; see Dif-Pradalier et al. (2022), *Transport barrier onset and edge turbulence shortfall in fusion plasmas*, arXiv:2206.04193.
solved_when: A theory or validated model quantitatively predicts the penetration of turbulence into linearly stable regions and the consequent alteration of transport barriers, in agreement with global (non-flux-tube) simulations.
why: Local stability analysis can overstate the protection supplied by a transport barrier, so without such an account barrier design and predictions of confinement rest on incomplete physics.
key_works: Dif-Pradalier et al. (2022), *Transport barrier onset and edge turbulence shortfall in fusion plasmas*, arXiv:2206.04193.

title: Heat avalanches and extreme transport events
open: When do intermittent transport avalanches materially change confinement or wall loading beyond what average-flux predictions would suggest? A sharper formal version asks for the conditions under which extreme heat-transport events dominate global behavior rather than being captured by mean fluxes.
status: Avalanche-like behavior appears in transport studies, but a validated reactor-scale extreme-event model remains missing; related work includes Dif-Pradalier et al. (2022), *Transport barrier onset and edge turbulence shortfall in fusion plasmas*, arXiv:2206.04193.
solved_when: A validated model of avalanche-driven extreme transport events exists at reactor scale, and can be shown to predict (or bound) their effect on confinement and wall loading beyond average-flux-based predictions.
why: Rare avalanche events can dominate safety margins even when average confinement appears acceptable, so missing them risks understating wall loading and confinement threats in reactor design.
key_works: Dif-Pradalier et al. (2022), *Transport barrier onset and edge turbulence shortfall in fusion plasmas*, arXiv:2206.04193.

title: Universal zonal-flow transition law
open: Do turbulence-to-zonal-flow transitions follow a universal law, or are their critical features tied to specific setups? In other words, which characteristics of the transition — its sharpness, thresholds, and scaling — persist when the geometry, drive mechanisms, dissipation, kinetic physics, and system size are varied?
status: Reduced systems exhibit sharp transitions, including the 2025 Hasegawa–Wakatani study by Guillon and Güncan (2025), *Phase transition from turbulence to zonal flows in the Hasegawa–Wakatani system* (DOI: 10.1063/5.0242282); universality in realistic plasmas remains unresolved.
solved_when: A transition law is identified that holds across changes in geometry, drive, dissipation, kinetic physics, and system size, with the surviving features of the transition characterized in realistic plasmas.
why: A robust transition law would turn turbulence suppression into a predictable design variable for plasma confinement, rather than an empirical outcome.
key_works: Guillon and Gürcan (2025), *Phase transition from turbulence to zonal flows in the Hasegawa–Wakatani system*, DOI: 10.1063/5.0242282.

title: Reactor-scale transport similarity
open: Do the gyro-Bohm and empirical confinement scalings we rely on survive extrapolation to reactor conditions, and if not, how must they be corrected as the normalized gyroradius shrinks toward reactor values?
status: Gyrokinetic theory supplies similarity arguments for the scaling (Garbet et al. (2010), *Gyrokinetic simulations of turbulent transport*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/50/4/043002), but no experiment covers the simultaneous reactor values of size, beta, collisionality, and self-heating, so the extrapolation lies outside experimental support.
solved_when: A corrected confinement scaling law is established that remains valid as normalized gyroradius decreases to reactor values, accounting for the simultaneous reactor-level values of device size, beta, collisionality, and self-heating.
why: Small errors in the scaling exponent compound through extrapolation, producing large uncertainties in predicted reactor size and power.
key_works: Garbet et al. (2010), *Gyrokinetic simulations of turbulent transport*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/50/4/043002.

title: Kinetic validation of L–H threshold theory
subfield: Pedestals, confinement transitions, and density limits
open: Do first-principles predictions of the L–H transition power threshold survive contact with physics closer to real tokamak plasmas — kinetic electrons, mixed isotopes, realistic neutral physics, and differing wall materials?
status: A 2026 preprint (De Lucca et al., 2026, *The L-H transition in tokamaks: power threshold, density minimum and toroidal-field asymmetry*, arXiv:2605.00624) derives threshold, density-minimum, and field-asymmetry behavior in a flux-driven two-fluid framework; broader validation remains open.
solved_when: The threshold predictions are tested and shown to remain accurate under kinetic electrons, isotope mixtures, realistic neutrals, and varied wall materials.
why: Heating systems must be sized to cross the L–H threshold reliably without being excessively oversized.
key_works: De Lucca et al. (2026), *The L-H transition in tokamaks: power threshold, density minimum and toroidal-field asymmetry*, arXiv:2605.00624.

title: L–H hysteresis and transition-path prediction
subfield: Pedestals, confinement transitions, and density limits
open: Can the L–H transition be predicted as a path-dependent process — forward and reverse thresholds, waiting times, and sensitivity to perturbation history — rather than through a single average threshold power? Formally, this asks for a theory of the hysteresis loop and transition-path statistics under realistic operating histories.
status: Transition models have advanced, but operating-path dependence remains a separate control and validation problem; see De Lucca et al. (2026), *The L-H transition in tokamaks: power threshold, density minimum and toroidal-field asymmetry*, arXiv:2605.00624.
solved_when: A predictive model reproduces forward and reverse transition thresholds, waiting times, and their dependence on perturbation history, and this path dependence is validated rather than treated as a separate control problem.
why: Hysteresis determines whether a plant can remain in its efficient operating regime during disturbances, so reliable path prediction bears directly on operational resilience.
key_works: De Lucca et al. (2026), *The L-H transition in tokamaks: power threshold, density minimum and toroidal-field asymmetry*, arXiv:2605.00624.

title: Pedestal-width prediction outside fitted regimes
subfield: Pedestals, confinement transitions, and density limits
open: Can the width and height of the H-mode pedestal be predicted from first principles for plasma conditions a model has never been fitted to — unfamiliar shaping, collisionality, isotope composition, and pressure profiles? In other words, is there a predictive model that generalizes beyond its calibrated regime without device-specific retuning?
status: EPED provides an influential first-principles predictive framework for pedestal height and width (Snyder et al. (2011), *A first-principles predictive model of the pedestal height and width*, *Nuclear Fusion* 51, 103016), but extrapolation beyond its validated regimes remains an active problem.
solved_when: A predictive model of pedestal width and height is demonstrated to hold across changes in shaping, collisionality, isotope composition, and pressure profiles without device-specific retuning, including in regimes outside those in which it was validated.
why: The pedestal strongly constrains total fusion performance, so a model that extrapolates reliably would make performance predictions credible for future devices and conditions that cannot be tested in advance.
key_works: Snyder et al. (2011), *A first-principles predictive model of the pedestal height and width*, *Nuclear Fusion* 51, 103016.

title: Pedestal electron-transport closure
subfield: Pedestals, confinement transitions, and density limits
open: What sets electron heat transport across the pedestal, and can a quantitative closure be derived that reproduces observed profiles, including the interplay among candidate instabilities?
status: Existing pedestal models constrain stability, but stability boundaries alone do not supply a complete transport closure. Key works include Garbet et al. (2010), *Gyrokinetic simulations of turbulent transport*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/50/4/043002, and Snyder et al. (2011), EPED study.
solved_when: A model is identified that quantitatively reproduces measured electron temperature (and heat flux) profiles throughout the pedestal from instability physics, including interactions among candidate instabilities — going beyond stability boundaries alone.
why: Accurate electron profiles are the input needed to predict both core performance and edge stability; without a transport closure, pedestal predictions remain incomplete.
key_works: Garbet et al. (2010), *Gyrokinetic simulations of turbulent transport*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/50/4/043002; Snyder et al. (2011), EPED study.

title: Reactor-compatible ELM-free confinement
subfield: Pedestals, confinement transitions, and density limits
open: Can a tokamak sustain a stationary, high-performance confinement regime free of damaging edge-localized modes under fully reactor-relevant conditions — specifically, low torque injection, high density, and metallic plasma-facing components?
status: Several ELM-free regimes exist experimentally, but the complete reactor-compatible combination of low torque, high density, and metallic walls has not been established (Loarte et al. (2025), *Required R&D in existing fusion facilities to support the new baseline ITER Research Plan*, ITR-25-005).
solved_when: A stationary, high-performance, ELM-free regime is demonstrated experimentally while simultaneously meeting reactor-like low-torque, high-density, and metallic-wall conditions.
why: Large, repetitive ELMs can destroy otherwise adequate divertor components, so without such a regime an otherwise viable high-performance operating point cannot be certified for a reactor.
key_works: Loarte et al. (2025), *Required R&D in existing fusion facilities to support the new baseline ITER Research Plan*, ITR-25-005.

title: Predictive resonant-magnetic-perturbation penetration
subfield: Pedestals, confinement transitions, and density limits
open: Can we predict, from first principles, how deeply an applied resonant magnetic perturbation penetrates a tokamak edge plasma — that is, what perturbation amplitude and spectrum actually reach the resonant surfaces? A complete answer must account self-consistently for plasma screening, rotation, magnetic island formation, and the density loss the perturbations themselves induce.
status: RMP control of edge-localized modes is experimentally established in selected operating regimes, but reliable extrapolation to future devices remains a stated ITER research need (Greenfield et al. (2023), *Report of the US ITER Research Program Research Needs Workshop*, arXiv:2303.12094).
solved_when: A validated predictive capability exists that outputs the perturbation amplitude and spectrum required for ELM suppression, incorporating plasma screening, rotation dynamics, island physics, and density loss, and that extrapolates reliably to ITER-relevant regimes.
why: Wrong penetration predictions lead either to ineffective ELM control or to unacceptable confinement degradation — a direct risk for reactor-scale operation where both failure modes are intolerable.
key_works: Greenfield et al. (2023), *Report of the US ITER Research Program Research Needs Workshop*, arXiv:2303.12094.

title: Negative-triangularity burning-plasma compatibility
subfield: Pedestals, confinement transitions, and density limits
open: Can a negative-triangularity plasma maintain its confinement and edge benefits under genuine reactor conditions — self-heating from fusion products, reactor-level exhaust and fueling demands, and the required bootstrap current?
status: A 2024 pilot-plant design study by the MANTA Collaboration (Rutherford et al., 2024, *MANTA: A Negative-Triangularity NASEM-Compliant Fusion Pilot Plant*, arXiv:2405.20243) explores this route, but a design study does not constitute integrated burning-plasma evidence.
solved_when: Negative triangularity is shown, in an integrated burning-plasma experiment (not a design study), to retain its confinement and edge advantages while meeting reactor-level self-heating, exhaust, fueling, and bootstrap-current requirements.
why: Success would offer a reactor path that avoids reliance on conventional high-performance H-mode operation, with its attendant edge-localized-mode and pedestal-stability constraints.
key_works: Rutherford et al., MANTA Collaboration (2024), *MANTA: A Negative-Triangularity NASEM-Compliant Fusion Pilot Plant*, arXiv:2405.20243.

title: Mechanistic density-limit prediction
subfield: Pedestals, confinement transitions, and density limits
open: Can the density limit in tokamak plasmas be predicted from the underlying physics — coupled radiation, turbulence, neutral penetration, current-profile evolution, and detachment — rather than from a single empirical scaling? In other words, is there a first-principles criterion that determines when a plasma operating near its density limit undergoes collapse?
status: Several density-limit mechanisms and operating exceptions are known — including divertor detachment as characterized by Krasheninnikov et al. (2016), *Divertor plasma detachment*, *Physics of Plasmas* 23, 055602 — and ITER research-needs reports flag the gap, but a universal predictive reactor criterion is not established.
solved_when: A predictive, mechanistic criterion for the density limit is established that incorporates the coupled physics of radiation, turbulence, neutral penetration, current-profile evolution, and detachment, and holds universally as a reactor-relevant operating criterion rather than relying on empirical scaling.
why: Raising density is a powerful route to higher fusion power, but pushing beyond the density limit can trigger plasma collapse; a mechanistic prediction would let reactors operate safely near this boundary.
key_works: Krasheninnikov et al. (2016), *Divertor plasma detachment*, *Physics of Plasmas* 23, 055602; ITER research-needs reports.

title: Neutral–pedestal feedback
subfield: Pedestals, confinement transitions, and density limits
open: Can we predict, from first principles, how recycled and fueling neutrals shape the pedestal — its fueling, rotation, electric fields, and turbulence — under realistic reactor wall and pumping conditions?
status: Neutral effects are represented in edge modeling, but integrated predictive validation remains incomplete; see Loarte et al. (2025), *Required R&D in existing fusion facilities to support the new baseline ITER Research Plan*, ITR-25-005.
solved_when: An integrated edge model that self-consistently couples neutral transport to pedestal fueling, rotation, electric fields, and turbulence is validated against experiment under reactor-relevant wall and pumping conditions.
why: Fueling cannot be designed independently of the confinement barrier; without this coupling, reactor fueling specifications and pedestal performance predictions rest on unvalidated assumptions.
key_works: Loarte et al. (2025), *Required R&D in existing fusion facilities to support the new baseline ITER Research Plan*, ITR-25-005.

title: Low-torque quiescent high-confinement operation
subfield: Pedestals, confinement transitions, and density limits
open: Can quiescent high-confinement regimes be sustained using only the weak external torque and restricted actuators available in a reactor, rather than the strong rotation drive of present-day experiments?
status: Relevant regimes exist in present machines, but extrapolation to low-torque reactor conditions remains a distinct, unsolved step beyond demonstrating the regime itself; the US ITER Research Program Research Needs Workshop (Greenfield et al. 2023, arXiv:2303.12094) identifies this need.
solved_when: A quiescent high-confinement regime is demonstrated and maintained under reactor-relevant conditions — low external torque and a restricted actuator set — as distinct from mere demonstration of the regime in present machines.
why: It could provide continuous edge exhaust without large ELMs, a requirement for durable divertor and first-wall operation in a fusion power plant.
key_works: Greenfield et al. (2023), *Report of the US ITER Research Program Research Needs Workshop*, arXiv:2303.12094.

title: Sawtooth-trigger prediction
subfield: Magnetohydrodynamic stability, disruptions, and runaway electrons
open: Can the timing of a sawtooth crash, and the plasma profiles that follow it, be predicted from first principles in a burning plasma? A complete model would need to capture energetic-particle effects, two-fluid physics, and the reconnection dynamics that together govern the crash.
status: Sawteeth are longstanding observations in tokamak plasmas, but complete crash prediction remains beyond any universal validated model. Related background appears in Chen and Zonca (2016), *Physics of Alfvén waves and energetic particles in burning plasmas*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.88.015008.
solved_when: A validated model that predicts sawtooth crash timing and post-crash plasma profiles with energetic particles, two-fluid effects, and reconnection physics included.
why: Sawtooth crashes can seed more dangerous instabilities and redistribute fusion products, so reliable prediction is a prerequisite for assessing their impact on burning-plasma performance.
key_works: Chen and Zonca (2016), *Physics of Alfvén waves and energetic particles in burning plasmas*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.88.015008.

title: Locked-mode avoidance with imperfect fields
subfield: Magnetohydrodynamic stability, disruptions, and runaway electrons
open: How much field imperfection can a burning tokamak tolerate before error fields lock MHD modes and trigger disruptions, and how should correction coils compensate across the full operating cycle? A complete answer would specify robust tolerance spectra and correction strategies for startup, ramp-up, burn, and shutdown under uncertain plasma response.
status: Error-field correction is established, but a reactor-wide robust tolerance specification is not supplied by existing control demonstrations (see Ariola and Pironti, 2016, *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*, DOI: 10.1007/978-3-319-29890-0).
solved_when: A reactor-wide specification exists of tolerable error-field spectra, together with correction strategies valid across startup, ramp-up, burn, and shutdown, that remains robust to uncertain plasma response.
why: Small field errors can lock modes and precipitate disruptions, so without a robust tolerance specification reactor design cannot guarantee stable operation over the full pulse.
key_works: Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*, DOI: 10.1007/978-3-319-29890-0.

title: Resistive-wall-mode control at low rotation
subfield: Magnetohydrodynamic stability, disruptions, and runaway electrons
open: Can a resistive-wall-mode feedback system reliably stabilize a tokamak plasma under fully reactor-relevant conditions — with low plasma rotation, restricted sensor access, realistic conducting structures, and limited actuator authority — rather than in the more favorable geometry of present-day experiments?
status: Feedback control methods and experiments exist, but reactor implementation couples unresolved physics with hardware constraints; no demonstration under the full set of reactor-like conditions is in hand. Key references are Ariola and Pironti (2014), *Control of resistive wall modes in tokamak plasmas*, and Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*.
solved_when: Reliable resistive-wall-mode stabilization is experimentally demonstrated in a configuration reproducing reactor-like rotation, sensor access, conducting structures, and actuator limits.
why: It determines whether attractive high-pressure operating points — the regimes that make tokamak economics plausible — can be used safely, since unstabilized resistive-wall modes would otherwise exclude them.
key_works: Ariola and Pironti (2014), *Control of resistive wall modes in tokamak plasmas*; Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*.

title: Three-dimensional disruption-force prediction
subfield: Magnetohydrodynamic stability, disruptions, and runaway electrons
open: Can we predict the asymmetric electromagnetic forces that strike a tokamak during vertical displacement events and the current quench, when the current paths are uncertain and conducting structures reshape the loads? In formal terms, this asks for a validated calculation of three-dimensional asymmetric disruption loads that self-consistently includes eddy currents in nearby conducting structures and quantifies the uncertainty from unknown halo and plasma current distributions.
status: ITER disruption studies identify these asymmetric loads as major design drivers, and conservative margins remain substantial. Key works: Lehnen et al. (2015), *Disruptions in ITER and strategies for their control and mitigation*, DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2014.10.075.
solved_when: A predictive capability exists that computes asymmetric wall forces during vertical displacement and current quench in three dimensions, incorporating conducting structures and uncertain current paths, with accuracy sufficient to replace the conservative design margins currently used for ITER vessel and support design.
why: Underpredicting these forces can compromise vessel and support integrity, while overpredicting forces ITER studies must treat conservatively inflates the cost of the machine's structure.
key_works: Lehnen et al. (2015), *Disruptions in ITER and strategies for their control and mitigation*, DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2014.10.075.

title: Disruption-radiation asymmetry
subfield: Magnetohydrodynamic stability, disruptions, and runaway electrons
open: Can disruption-mitigation systems be designed so that the radiation they rely on deposits its energy nearly uniformly on the first wall? In formal terms, the question is to bound the localized radiative wall loading achievable during mitigation and to devise injection geometries that prevent damaging toroidal or poloidal concentration of that loading.
status: Radiation is intentionally used to spread disruption energy across the wall, but its nonuniformity remains a component-protection concern; Loarte et al. (2025), *Required R&D in existing fusion facilities to support the new baseline ITER Research Plan*, ITR-25-005, identifies this among required research areas.
solved_when: A quantified bound on localized radiative loading during mitigation is established, together with an injection geometry demonstrated to avoid damaging toroidal or poloidal concentration of radiation on wall components.
why: Converting a disruption's thermal energy into radiation does not by itself guarantee safe wall loading; without control of the asymmetry, the very mechanism used to protect components can concentrate destructive energy on them.
key_works: Loarte et al. (2025), *Required R&D in existing fusion facilities to support the new baseline ITER Research Plan*, ITR-25-005.

title: Avalanche multiplication under mitigation
subfield: Magnetohydrodynamic stability, disruptions, and runaway electrons
open: When does injected mitigation material actually suppress runaway-electron production during a tokamak disruption, and when do its combined effects — altered electric fields and enhanced collisions in the partially ionized plasma — instead increase avalanche multiplication?
status: Massive-material-injection effects were quantified in 2019 models (Hesslow et al. (2019), *Influence of massive material injection on avalanche runaway generation during tokamak disruptions*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/ab26c2), but robust reactor prescriptions remain unsettled.
solved_when: A criterion (analytic or validated model) is given that predicts, for given injection conditions, whether runaway avalanche multiplication is reduced or amplified, robust enough to serve as a reactor prescription.
why: An apparently protective intervention can worsen another disruption hazard, so without such a criterion mitigation strategies may amplify the runaway problem they aim to solve.
key_works: Hesslow et al. (2019), *Influence of massive material injection on avalanche runaway generation during tokamak disruptions*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/ab26c2.

title: Benign termination of a mature runaway beam
subfield: Magnetohydrodynamic stability, disruptions, and runaway electrons
open: Can a mature, high-current runaway electron beam in a tokamak disruption be terminated in a controlled way — avoiding concentrated wall damage, unacceptable electromagnetic loads on the machine, and the formation of a secondary runaway beam?
status: Runaway dynamics and mitigation strategies are extensively studied, including wall interaction effects (Breizman et al. 2019, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/ab1822; Ataeiseresht et al. 2023, DOI: 10.1038/s41598-023-48672-7), but a universally reliable reactor-scale termination method is not established.
solved_when: A reactor-scale termination method is demonstrated that dissipates a high-current runaway beam while keeping wall loads below damage thresholds, electromagnetic loads within acceptable limits, and suppressing secondary beam generation, reliably enough to qualify as a universal mitigation strategy.
why: Prevention of runaway beam formation alone does not constitute a credible protection strategy for a reactor; a controlled termination capability is required if a beam does form.
key_works: Breizman et al. (2019), *Physics of runaway electrons in tokamaks*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/ab1822; Ataeiseresht et al. (2023), *Runaway electrons and their interaction with tungsten wall*, DOI: 10.1038/s41598-023-48672-7.

title: Reactor divertor heat-flux width
open: How wide is the divertor heat-flux channel at reactor scale — a quantity today's machines cannot measure directly? The task is to determine this width, reconciling the empirical H-mode scaling with gyrokinetic simulations and assessing whether turbulence broadens the channel.
status: Eich's 2013 empirical scaling, extrapolated to ITER, gives roughly millimeter-scale widths; this remains an extrapolation rather than a reactor measurement. Gyrokinetic projections from present tokamaks to ITER (Chang et al., 2017) provide a simulation-based cross-check.
solved_when: The reactor-scale heat-flux width is established, with empirical extrapolations (such as the roughly millimeter-scale ITER prediction), kinetic simulation projections, and turbulence-broadening effects shown to agree within a defensible margin.
why: The width directly sets the peak divertor heat flux, which governs divertor survivability and exhaust design for a reactor.
key_works: Eich et al. (2013), *Scaling of the tokamak near the scrape-off layer H-mode power width and implications for ITER*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/53/9/093031; Chang et al. (2017), *Gyrokinetic projection of the divertor heat-flux width from present tokamaks to ITER*.

title: Stable detachment-front control
open: Can a tokamak sustain a fully detached divertor while keeping the radiation front pinned outside the confined plasma, even as heating power, fueling, and impurity sources vary? In control terms, this asks for a feedback scheme that stabilizes the detachment front's position within a narrow acceptable band despite these disturbances.
status: Detachment itself is experimentally established, but robust reactor-scale control of its operating window remains unresolved. Related formalisms include moving-boundary control and combustion-front stabilization; key references are Leonard (2018), *Plasma detachment in divertor tokamaks*, and Krasheninnikov et al. (2017), *Physics of ultimate detachment of a tokamak divertor plasma*.
solved_when: A demonstrated control strategy maintains detachment — with the radiation front excluded from the confined plasma — through realistic variations in power, fueling, and impurity influx, i.e., robust regulation of the front position across the divertor operating window under reactor-relevant conditions.
why: Both insufficient and excessive detachment terminate useful operation, so without robust control of the front's position the divertor cannot serve as a reliable exhaust solution for a power plant.
key_works: Leonard (2018), *Plasma detachment in divertor tokamaks*; Krasheninnikov et al. (2017), *Physics of ultimate detachment of a tokamak divertor plasma*.

title: Simultaneous reactor-grade confinement and detachment
open: Can a tokamak simultaneously maintain reactor-grade core confinement and a fully detached divertor exhaust under genuinely reactor-like conditions — heat loads, impurity concentrations, plasma density, and pulse duration all at once?
status: First coexistence has already been achieved: Wang et al. (2021), *Integration of full divertor detachment with improved core confinement for fusion energy*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-021-21645-y, demonstrated full detachment with improved core confinement in 2021. The open problem is integrating these capabilities under full reactor conditions, not achieving coexistence for the first time.
solved_when: An experiment demonstrates core performance and exhaust operating together at reactor heat loads, reactor-level impurity concentrations, reactor density, and reactor pulse durations.
why: Confinement and exhaust have each succeeded separately, but a power plant only works if both hold simultaneously; separate subsystem optima do not add up to a working reactor.
key_works: Wang et al. (2021), *Integration of full divertor detachment with improved core confinement for fusion energy*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-021-21645-y.

title: Filament-driven far-SOL loading
open: Can we predict the intermittent particle and heat transport that carries plasma to first-wall regions far from the nominal strike point, rather than only to the divertor? In formal terms, this asks for a theory of filament-driven transport that yields wall-load distributions in the far scrape-off layer.
status: Filament measurements and density-shoulder studies exist, notably work such as Kuang et al. (2019), *Plasma fluctuations in the scrape-off layer and at the divertor target in Alcator C-Mod and their relationship to divertor collisionality and density shoulder formation*, but reliable reactor wall-load distributions remain uncertain.
solved_when: A validated predictive capability exists for intermittent particle and heat fluxes — and the resulting wall-load distributions — on first-wall components far from the strike point, with reliability sufficient for reactor design.
why: Components outside the divertor may receive substantial unplanned plasma and heat exposure; without a prediction, first-wall sizing and lifetime estimates in that region are guesses.
key_works: Kuang et al. (2019), *Plasma fluctuations in the scrape-off layer and at the divertor target in Alcator C-Mod and their relationship to divertor collisionality and density shoulder formation*.

title: Molecular reaction closure in detached plasmas
open: Can we measure and model the molecular reactions of a detached plasma — molecular-assisted recombination and dissociation, charge exchange, and the vibrational state populations — well enough to predict when detachment will occur? In short, when does the full molecular chemistry of the divertor and scrape-off layer become quantitatively predictive of the detached state?
status: Atomic-only descriptions are known to be insufficient in important detached regimes, and reaction and state-population uncertainties remain unresolved. Krasheninnikov et al. (2016), *Divertor plasma detachment*, *Physics of Plasmas* 23, 055602.
solved_when: A validated set of molecular reaction rates and vibrational population models, benchmarked against experimental measurements, reproduces observed detachment behavior, replacing atomic-only descriptions with predictive accuracy in detached regimes.
why: Incorrect chemistry produces incorrect particle and power balances, so any reactor design relying on detached divertor operation would be built on the wrong exhaust physics.
key_works: Krasheninnikov et al. (2016), *Divertor plasma detachment*, *Physics of Plasmas* 23, 055602.

title: Inner–outer divertor asymmetry
open: Can we predict how heat and particle fluxes are divided between the inner and outer divertor legs as the magnetic-field direction, drifts, collisionality, and divertor geometry vary? A successful theory would give a general, reactor-relevant predictive capability for this asymmetry rather than case-by-case explanations.
status: Recent work has clarified the underlying mechanisms, including research reported by PPPL in 2026 (*Solving a mystery that could help fusion reactors survive decades of use*), but a general reactor predictive capability remains an open, broader goal.
solved_when: A validated predictive capability exists that quantitatively forecasts the inner–outer division of heat and particles across magnetic-field direction, drifts, collisionality, and geometry, applicable to general reactor conditions.
why: One divertor leg can fail while average exhaust performance appears acceptable, so without such prediction a seemingly healthy exhaust solution can conceal damaging localized loads.
key_works: PPPL (2026), *Solving a mystery that could help fusion reactors survive decades of use*.

title: Near-SOL heat-flux feature
open: Under what conditions does a narrow near-SOL heat-flux component form, and can it be predicted and suppressed without degrading useful confinement?
status: Impurity seeding was investigated as a suppression method by Nespoli et al. (2017), *Impurity seeding for suppression of the near Scrape-Off Layer heat flux feature in tokamaks* (arXiv:1712.00951); a general predictive criterion remains open.
solved_when: A general predictive criterion exists that specifies when the near-SOL heat-flux feature appears, together with a demonstrated suppression method that removes it while maintaining useful confinement.
why: A narrow additional component can dominate peak surface loading, so without prediction and control it directly threatens plasma-facing components.
key_works: Nespoli et al. (2017), *Impurity seeding for suppression of the near Scrape-Off Layer heat flux feature in tokamaks*, arXiv:1712.00951.

title: Tungsten-source feedback through the edge
open: Can we predict, and ultimately control, the coupled feedback loop in which tungsten sputtered from plasma-facing surfaces radiates impurity energy, cools the edge, and thereby drives further material release? Formally, this asks for a validated model of the closed tungsten–radiation–edge-temperature feedback system in reactor-relevant edge and divertor conditions.
status: Plasma–material interaction studies, e.g. Federici et al. (2001), *Plasma-material interactions in current tokamaks and their implications for next step fusion reactors*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/41/12/218, document the constituent mechanisms; their integration into a reactor-scale feedback picture remains difficult.
solved_when: A quantitative, predictive description of the full feedback loop — sputtering yield, impurity radiation, edge cooling, and re-entrant material release — exists and is validated against reactor-relevant conditions, sufficient to determine when an initial contamination event remains bounded and when it self-amplifies.
why: Without such a model, a small initial tungsten contamination event can become self-amplifying, threatening reactor operation through uncontrolled edge cooling and material loss.
key_works: Federici et al. (2001), *Plasma-material interactions in current tokamaks and their implications for next step fusion reactors*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/41/12/218.

title: Neutral residence and exhaust efficiency
open: How do divertor geometry, molecular kinetics, conductance, and pumping together determine the residence time of fuel particles and the removal of helium ash in an exhaust system? A predictive model is sought that couples these physical and engineering elements into a single quantitative framework.
status: Exhaust models and pumping technologies exist individually, but their simultaneous optimization with detachment and tritium inventory remains unresolved; related efforts include advanced exhaust pumping technology development for a DT fusion power plant (Day and Giegerich, 2014, DOI: 10.1109/TPS.2014.2307435) and work on rarefied-gas network transport and vacuum-system optimization.
solved_when: A validated predictive framework exists that quantitatively relates divertor geometry, molecular kinetics, conductance, and pumping to fuel residence time and helium removal rate, and can be optimized simultaneously with detachment control and tritium inventory constraints.
why: Poor exhaust performance inflates the fuel inventory and can destabilize the burning plasma, so a coupled solution directly limits tritium retention and burn control in a DT power plant.
key_works: Day and Giegerich (2014), *Development of Advanced Exhaust Pumping Technology for a DT Fusion Power Plant*, DOI: 10.1109/TPS.2014.2307435.

title: Exhaust control with finite actuator delays
open: Can a divertor exhaust controller be designed that tolerates the finite delays inherent to gas delivery, impurity transport, diagnostics, and magnetic actuators, while keeping the plasma safely clear of dangerous detachment excursions? Formally, this asks for a delay-robust feedback law for detachment control whose stability and constraint guarantees hold under the actual actuation and measurement lags of a reactor-relevant plant.
status: Detachment physics is considered mature enough to support control development, as surveyed in Leonard (2018), *Plasma detachment in divertor tokamaks*, and magnetic control techniques are established in Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*; however, control schemes meeting reactor delay and reliability requirements remain unproven. Related approaches include delay-robust control and constrained model-predictive control.
solved_when: A controller is demonstrated, analytically or experimentally, to regulate divertor detachment while explicitly accounting for gas-delivery, impurity-transport, diagnostic, and magnetic-actuator delays, without triggering detachment excursions, and meeting reactor-scale delay and reliability requirements.
why: Even if detachment is physically controllable in principle, slow hardware could make the regime operationally inaccessible; such a controller is what converts mature detachment physics into a usable reactor operating scenario.
key_works: Leonard (2018), *Plasma detachment in divertor tokamaks*; Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*.

title: Protective vapor shielding without plasma poisoning
open: Can a vapor layer released from a material surface reproducibly shield that surface against transient plasma loads, without poisoning the confined plasma? Formally, the question is whether vapor shielding can be achieved repeatedly in reactor-relevant conditions without triggering unacceptable contamination, radiative collapse, or accelerated erosion.
status: Vapor shielding is part of longstanding plasma–material interaction research, as surveyed in Federici et al. (2001), *Plasma-material interactions in current tokamaks and their implications for next step fusion reactors* (DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/41/12/218); however, useful repetitive reactor operation remains unestablished.
solved_when: A material-vapor shielding scheme is demonstrated that reproducibly protects surfaces across transient events while keeping plasma contamination, radiation losses, and erosion within acceptable limits — i.e., useful repetitive operation is established.
why: Successful vapor shielding would soften transient material loads on plasma-facing components, but if contamination cannot be controlled it introduces a new failure mechanism for the plasma itself.
key_works: Federici et al. (2001), *Plasma-material interactions in current tokamaks and their implications for next step fusion reactors*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/41/12/218.

title: Electron-cyclotron deposition accuracy
open: Can electron-cyclotron heating and current drive hold their deposition location and profile in a burning-plasma environment? The goal is deposition control that remains precise in the presence of density fluctuations, refraction through an evolving equilibrium, and diagnostic uncertainty.
status: Electron-cyclotron heating and current drive control is established, with real-time steering demonstrated for neoclassical tearing-mode control in DIII-D (Welander et al., 2013); reactor requirements tighten the tolerances on deposition location and reliability beyond what current systems deliver.
solved_when: A control scheme maintains the required deposition location and reliability under reactor-grade tolerances, robust to density fluctuations, refraction, evolving equilibrium, and diagnostic uncertainty.
why: Misaligned current drive can fail to suppress a magnetic island, so imprecise deposition directly undermines tearing-mode stabilization.
key_works: Prater (2004), *Heating and current drive by electron cyclotron waves*, DOI: 10.1063/1.1690762; Welander et al. (2013), *Advanced control of neoclassical tearing modes in DIII-D with real-time steering of the electron cyclotron current drive*.

title: Reactor-duty gyrotron systems
open: Can the full gyrotron chain — source, window, transmission line, and launcher — be qualified for the continuous duty and high availability a fusion power plant demands? Formally, the goal is to engineer and demonstrate efficient high-power electron-cyclotron systems that meet plant-relevant duty-cycle, lifetime, and availability targets end to end.
status: High-power electron-cyclotron systems exist today, but plant-wide efficiency and component lifetime remain separate, unresolved qualification problems. Key works: Prater (2004), *Heating and current drive by electron cyclotron waves*, DOI: 10.1063/1.1690762; Loarte et al. (2025), ITR-25-005.
solved_when: Efficient high-power gyrotrons, windows, transmission lines, and launchers are qualified for continuous, plant-grade duty with the availability a power plant requires.
why: Inefficiency in the heating system directly subtracts from the plant's net electricity output.
key_works: Prater (2004), *Heating and current drive by electron cyclotron waves*, DOI: 10.1063/1.1690762; Loarte et al. (2025), ITR-25-005.

title: High-density lower-hybrid current drive
open: Can lower-hybrid current drive sustain a plasma current efficiently at reactor-level density and temperature? The challenge is to do so while keeping edge losses, spectral evolution of the launched waves, and wave accessibility in the inhomogeneous plasma under control.
status: Current-drive theory and experiments are longstanding (Fisch 1987, *Theory of current drive in plasmas*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.59.175), but reactor-compatible efficiency is not established by general theory alone; the ITER research-needs workshop (2023, arXiv:2303.12094) frames this among open reactor research needs.
solved_when: A demonstration — experimental, given the problem type — of efficient lower-hybrid current drive at reactor density and temperature, with edge losses, spectral evolution, and accessibility controlled.
why: Efficient noninductive current drive is essential for many steady-state tokamak designs; without a reactor-compatible scheme, those operating scenarios cannot be realized.
key_works: Fisch (1987), *Theory of current drive in plasmas*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.59.175; ITER research-needs workshop (2023), arXiv:2303.12094.

title: Ion-cyclotron sheath and impurity control
open: Can radio-frequency sheath voltages that form around ion-cyclotron antennas in reactor-grade plasmas be predicted well enough to be actively suppressed, so that the antenna no longer drives impurity release into the core? The goal is a validated capability to predict and control sheath-driven impurity generation under reactor conditions.
status: Ion-cyclotron heating itself is established, but antenna–edge–wall coupling remains an open research requirement; see Loarte et al. (2025), *Required R&D in existing fusion facilities to support the new baseline ITER Research Plan*, ITR-25-005.
solved_when: RF sheath voltages near ion-cyclotron antennas under reactor conditions are predictable and can be suppressed to levels that prevent impurity contamination of the plasma.
why: An otherwise effective heating method becomes unusable if it contaminates the plasma it is meant to heat.
key_works: Loarte et al. (2025), *Required R&D in existing fusion facilities to support the new baseline ITER Research Plan*, ITR-25-005.

title: Reliable negative-ion neutral-beam sources
open: Can a negative-ion neutral-beam source run at reactor duty cycle while keeping cesium behavior controlled, beam optics stable, electron co-extraction low, and maintenance burden acceptable?
status: Negative-ion technology underpins advanced neutral beams, but reactor availability and long-duration control of the source surfaces remain unresolved qualification gaps (Greenfield et al. 2023, *Report of the US ITER Research Program Research Needs Workshop*, arXiv:2303.12094).
solved_when: A negative-ion source operates at reactor-relevant duty with stable cesium coverage and work function, sustained beam optics, low co-extracted electron current, and demonstrated maintenance intervals that do not dominate heating-system downtime.
why: Beam-source maintenance can dominate heating-system downtime, so a reliable source directly determines the availability of auxiliary heating and current drive in a fusion plant.
key_works: Greenfield et al. (2023), *Report of the US ITER Research Program Research Needs Workshop*, arXiv:2303.12094.

title: Efficient neutralization beyond gas cells
open: Can a neutralization architecture beyond the conventional gas cell — for example photoneutralization — be demonstrated with complete electrical efficiency and reliability that materially improve neutral beams on a reactor?
status: Alternative neutralization remains a development route rather than an established power-plant subsystem; related efforts concern high-finesse optical cavities under particle loading. (See NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991; Fisch (1987), *Theory of current drive in plasmas*.)
solved_when: A working alternative neutralization architecture is demonstrated whose overall electrical efficiency and reliability represent a material improvement over gas-cell neutralization for reactor-class neutral beams.
why: Neutralization losses can make otherwise useful beam heating too expensive energetically; a better architecture would make neutral-beam heating and current drive viable at reactor scale.
key_works: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991; Fisch (1987), *Theory of current drive in plasmas*.

title: Deep pellet fueling of hot plasmas
open: Can cryogenic pellets be driven deep into a reactor-grade hot plasma so that they deposit fuel near the core without provoking unacceptable disturbances at the edge?
status: Pellet fueling is established practice, but hotter plasmas and stringent tritium-efficiency requirements change the optimization problem; related directions include ablating projectiles and cryogenic multiphase injection (Abdou et al. 2021, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/abbf35).
solved_when: Pellet injection into reactor-temperature plasmas is both predicted and experimentally achieved with sufficient penetration and fuel deposition in the core while keeping edge disturbances within acceptable limits.
why: Gas fueling alone may not efficiently raise the core density, so deep pellet fueling is needed to sustain the desired plasma profile under stringent tritium-efficiency demands.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2021), *Physics and technology considerations for the deuterium–tritium fuel cycle and conditions for tritium fuel self sufficiency*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/abbf35.

title: High-availability tritium pellet production
open: Can a tritium pellet production and injection system be engineered to operate continuously at power-plant scale, holding only a low tritium inventory while keeping failure rates low and allowing remote maintenance? In other words, can the full chain — produce, accelerate, route, and inject tritium-bearing pellets — run as steady industrial equipment rather than a laboratory demonstration?
status: Experimental pellet systems exist, but power-plant throughput and lifecycle qualification remain open. A recent assessment is Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*, UKAEA-CCFE-PR(23)99.
solved_when: A pellet system demonstrates continuous production, acceleration, routing, and injection of tritium-bearing pellets at power-plant throughput with low tritium inventory, a low failure rate, and remote maintainability, and passes lifecycle qualification.
why: Without fuel delivery that works as industrial equipment rather than an experimental accessory, a fusion power plant cannot maintain the duty cycle and availability that its electricity production depends on.
key_works: Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*, UKAEA-CCFE-PR(23)99.

title: Noninductive current ramp to steady state
open: Can a tokamak ramp its plasma current from startup to full steady-state operation and hold the required current profile using only bootstrap current and externally driven current, without drawing on transformer flux that cannot be sustained?
status: Noninductive scenarios have substantial research history, but an integrated reactor ramp with acceptable power demand remains unproven.
solved_when: An integrated demonstration shows a noninductive current ramp to steady state with acceptable power demand for a reactor-scale device, maintaining the required current profile throughout.
why: Steady-state reactor operation depends on actually ramping and sustaining the current in practice, which demands more than a steady-state equilibrium calculation.
key_works: Fisch (1987), *Theory of current drive in plasmas*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.59.175; Greenfield et al. (2023), arXiv:2303.12094.

title: Exact global nonaxisymmetric quasisymmetry
open: Can a toroidal magnetic equilibrium be both nonaxisymmetric and exactly quasisymmetric everywhere, while remaining physically admissible? In formal terms: prove either an existence theorem or an appropriate impossibility theorem for global, nonaxisymmetric, physically admissible equilibria with exact quasisymmetry.
status: Extremely precise numerical quasisymmetry was demonstrated by Landreman and Paul (2022) (*Magnetic Fields with Precise Quasisymmetry for Plasma Confinement*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.128.035001), but this is numerical rather than an existence proof; work from September 2026 (Landreman, arXiv:2609.26742) still explicitly identifies exact nonaxisymmetric quasisymmetric equilibria as open.
solved_when: A rigorous proof establishes either that such an equilibrium exists or that no such equilibrium can exist; either resolution of the dichotomy closes the problem.
why: It would establish the mathematical limits of a central stellarator design principle, determining whether exact quasisymmetry is achievable in principle or only approximately.
key_works: Landreman and Paul (2022), *Magnetic Fields with Precise Quasisymmetry for Plasma Confinement*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.128.035001; Landreman (2026), arXiv:2609.26742.

title: Robustness of smooth three-dimensional equilibria
open: Which perturbations of pressure, boundary shape, or current preserve a smooth nested-surface three-dimensional equilibrium, and which destroy it by generating islands or singular structures?
status: September 2026 preprints report counterexamples to formulations of Grad's conjecture (Gómez-Serrano, Liehr, and Taylor (2026), *Counterexamples to Grad's conjecture*, arXiv:2609.24739); existence of such examples does not establish generic robustness.
solved_when: A characterization is given of the perturbations of pressure, boundary shape, or current under which smooth nested-surface equilibria persist, versus those producing islands or singular structures.
why: A mathematically exact but structurally fragile equilibrium may be unusable in an actual machine, so robustness determines which equilibria are physically viable.
key_works: Gómez-Serrano, Liehr, and Taylor (2026), *Counterexamples to Grad’s conjecture*, arXiv:2609.24739.

title: From local Boozer fields to global reactors
open: Which magnetic-field-strength functions that can be realized locally in Boozer coordinates can be extended to a complete toroidal configuration that satisfies force balance and can actually be produced by acceptable coils?
status: Klotz et al. (2026, arXiv:2609.09517, *All field strengths are possible locally in Boozer coordinates*) established a local realization result in September 2026; global topology, equilibrium, and coil realizability remain additional open conditions.
solved_when: A characterization (or constructive procedure) is given of the locally realizable field-strength functions that extend to globally toroidal, force-balanced fields generated by acceptable coils.
why: Without it, local freedom in choosing the field strength can be mistaken for unrestricted reactor-design freedom, misleading stellarator optimization.
key_works: Klotz et al. (2026), *All field strengths are possible locally in Boozer coordinates*, arXiv:2609.09517.

title: Analyticity versus omnigenity
open: How much confinement is actually lost when the idealized, exactly omnigenous field configurations of stellarator theory are replaced by smooth fields that real coils can produce?
status: Cary and Shasharina's 1997 analysis established subtle relationships among omnigenity, quasihelicity, and analyticity; practical approximation limits remain important (DOI: 10.1063/1.872473).
solved_when: A quantitative bound exists on the transport penalty (e.g., neoclassical transport degradation as a function of the approximation's smoothness or error budget) incurred by approximating an omnigenous construction with analytic fields; absent a stated target, a sharp such bound is the natural criterion for this theory problem.
why: Exact omnigenity guarantees perfect confinement of guiding centers, but the smoothing required for manufacturable coils may break that guarantee — without knowing the penalty, the theory cannot certify any practical design.
key_works: Cary and Shasharina (1997), *Omnigenity and quasihelicity in helical plasma confinement systems*, DOI: 10.1063/1.872473.

title: Near-axis expansion error bounds
open: How accurately do near-axis expansions describe actual stellarator fields and flux surfaces at finite distance from the magnetic axis? A theory is needed that supplies useful, computable error bounds on the finite-volume fields, surfaces, and confinement properties predicted by near-axis constructions.
status: Near-axis methods are powerful design tools, but finite-radius utility is not guaranteed by a local expansion alone. Key works include Garren and Boozer (1991), *Existence of quasihelically symmetric stellarators*, *Physics of Fluids B* 3, 2822, and Klotz et al. (2026), arXiv:2609.09517.
solved_when: Explicit, computable bounds are available that quantify the deviation between near-axis constructions and the corresponding finite-volume fields, surfaces, and confinement properties.
why: Certified error estimates would prevent optimization from converging on asymptotically attractive configurations that are impractical at realistic plasma size.
key_works: Garren and Boozer (1991), *Existence of quasihelically symmetric stellarators*, *Physics of Fluids B* 3, 2822; Klotz et al. (2026), arXiv:2609.09517.

title: Coil-complexity lower bounds
open: How expensive is it, in a fundamental sense, to realize a given stellarator plasma shape with electromagnetic coils? A formal answer would take the form of lower bounds or sharp tradeoffs among field accuracy, coil curvature, coil separation, conductor length, and access requirements.
status: Optimization methods currently produce good coil designs, including finite-element-aware work in 2026 (Kaptanoglu and Gil (2026), *A proof-of-concept for automated AI-driven stellarator coil optimization with in-the-loop finite-element calculations*, arXiv:2603.15240), but they do not establish any global limits.
solved_when: A proven lower bound (or tight tradeoff curve) exists relating field accuracy to coil curvature, coil separation, conductor length, and access requirements, so that no coil design can beat it.
why: Such bounds would identify when a proposed plasma shape is intrinsically expensive to realize, telling designers before optimization whether a target is achievable or must be relaxed.
key_works: Kaptanoglu and Gil (2026), *A proof-of-concept for automated AI-driven stellarator coil optimization with in-the-loop finite-element calculations*, arXiv:2603.15240.

title: Joint confinement–stability–engineering optimization
open: Can we find stellarator configurations that are simultaneously acceptable across every reactor-relevant criterion — transport, energetic-particle confinement, MHD stability, coil stresses, shielding, and maintenance — rather than good on some and infeasible on others? Formally, this asks for a validated exploration of the coupled Pareto frontier over these objectives rather than single-metric optimizations.
status: Individual objectives and some coupled optimizations exist, but a validated full reactor Pareto frontier does not. Relevant background includes Helander (2014), *Theory of plasma confinement in non-axisymmetric magnetic fields*, DOI: 10.1088/0034-4885/77/8/087001, and recent work by Kaptanoglu and Gil (2026), arXiv:2603.15240.
solved_when: A full multi-objective optimization over transport, energetic-particle, MHD, coil-stress, shielding, and maintenance constraints yields a validated Pareto frontier of stellarator configurations, with robustness of the solutions demonstrated.
why: Optimizing one metric can silently make another subsystem infeasible, so single-objective design work cannot be trusted to produce a buildable reactor; a joint frontier makes the trade-offs explicit and designable.
key_works: Helander (2014), *Theory of plasma confinement in non-axisymmetric magnetic fields*, DOI: 10.1088/0034-4885/77/8/087001; Kaptanoglu and Gil (2026), arXiv:2603.15240.

title: Symmetry-agnostic confinement design
open: Do stellarator design principles based on iso-action and related symmetry-free constructions actually confine heat and fast particles once realistic collisions and finite-coil geometry are included? In other words, can configurations designed without conventional quasisymmetry achieve reactor-grade thermal and energetic-particle confinement?
status: Sengupta, Bhattacharjee, and Buller proposed a general theory of symmetry-agnostic stellarators for collisionless confinement in August 2026 (Sengupta et al. (2026), *Symmetry-agnostic stellarators for collisionless confinement*, arXiv:2608.20042); validation under reactor-relevant conditions remains open.
solved_when: A validation — analytical or numerical — demonstrating robust thermal and energetic-particle confinement for an iso-action or related non-quasisymmetric design under realistic collision physics and realistic coil geometry, at reactor-relevant conditions.
why: Success would show that good confinement configurations exist outside the conventional symmetry-based design space, potentially revealing classes of viable stellarators that quasisymmetry constraints currently exclude.
key_works: Sengupta et al. (2026), *Symmetry-agnostic stellarators for collisionless confinement*, arXiv:2608.20042.

title: Experimental reactor-alpha confinement in optimized stellarators
open: Can an optimized stellarator confine energetic alpha particles well enough for a burning plasma under realistic high-pressure conditions? In other words, can the loss reductions predicted by orbit-optimization design tools be demonstrated experimentally with self-consistent pressure profiles?
status: Orbit optimization techniques can substantially reduce calculated energetic-particle losses in optimized stellarator designs, but burning-plasma experimental validation remains absent from those design results. Related work includes Landreman and Paul (2022), *Magnetic Fields with Precise Quasisymmetry for Plasma Confinement*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.128.035001, and IAEA energetic-particle optimization contributions (2021); a related thread is validation of long-time Hamiltonian orbit predictions.
solved_when: An optimized stellarator experiment demonstrates sufficiently low energetic-particle losses under self-consistent high-pressure conditions, validating in a burning-plasma-relevant regime the loss reductions predicted by orbit optimization.
why: Alpha confinement is required both for self-heating of the plasma and for survival of the first wall; without it, a stellarator reactor cannot sustain a burn or protect its hardware.
key_works: Landreman and Paul (2022), *Magnetic Fields with Precise Quasisymmetry for Plasma Confinement*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.128.035001; IAEA energetic-particle optimization contributions (2021).

title: Turbulence-optimized stellarators
open: Can a stellarator whose magnetic configuration is deliberately optimized to reduce turbulent transport actually show reproducible confinement improvement in experiment, without degrading its neoclassical or engineering performance?
status: Wendelstein 7-X demonstrated reduced neoclassical energy transport in 2021 (Beidler et al., DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-03687-w); turbulent transport remains a separate optimization frontier with no comparable experimental demonstration yet.
solved_when: A turbulence-optimized stellarator configuration is built and experimentally shown to yield reproducible confinement improvement attributable to reduced turbulent transport, while preserving the neoclassical and engineering performance of the design.
why: W7-X proved that neoclassical transport can be tamed by optimization, but neoclassical optimization alone does not guarantee reactor-grade confinement; turbulence is the remaining transport channel standing between optimized stellarators and a viable reactor.
key_works: Beidler et al. (2021), *Demonstration of reduced neoclassical energy transport in Wendelstein 7-X*, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-03687-w.

title: Stellarator impurity screening at high density
open: Can a stellarator sustain high-density operation without accumulating impurities, while preserving good confinement and manageable exhaust? Formally, the question is whether regimes exist at reactor-relevant density in which impurity transport is outward (screened) under the ambipolar electric field and collisionality conditions predicted by neoclassical theory.
status: Stellarator neoclassical theory identifies a strong dependence of impurity transport on the electric field and collisionality (Helander 2014, *Theory of plasma confinement in non-axisymmetric magnetic fields*, DOI: 10.1088/0034-4885/77/8/087001), but the reactor operating window for impurity screening remains unresolved.
solved_when: An experimentally demonstrated high-density operating regime is shown to avoid impurity accumulation while simultaneously maintaining good confinement and manageable exhaust.
why: Accumulation of high-charge impurities destroys core plasma performance through radiative losses, negating the advantages of steady-state stellarator confinement.
key_works: Helander (2014), *Theory of plasma confinement in non-axisymmetric magnetic fields*, DOI: 10.1088/0034-4885/77/8/087001.

title: High-beta stellarator stability margins
open: What pressure can a stellarator plasma actually sustain before losing confinement? An experimentally reliable determination of the beta limit must account for nonlinear MHD activity, equilibrium changes, magnetic islands, and energetic-particle effects together rather than in isolation.
status: Stellarator stability and equilibrium theory are mature research areas, but reactor-pressure margins remain configuration-dependent; a comprehensive overview is given in Helander (2014), *Theory of plasma confinement in non-axisymmetric magnetic fields*, DOI: 10.1088/0034-4885/77/8/087001.
solved_when: A validated, configuration-specific experimental pressure limit is established that incorporates nonlinear MHD activity, equilibrium changes, islands, and energetic particles, and that can be used to predict reactor-pressure margins.
why: The achievable pressure limit directly sets reactor size and magnet requirements, so reliable margins determine the economic feasibility of stellarator reactor designs.
key_works: Helander (2014), *Theory of plasma confinement in non-axisymmetric magnetic fields*, DOI: 10.1088/0034-4885/77/8/087001.

title: Bootstrap-current and transform robustness
open: Can a stellarator maintain its rotational transform and island topology within acceptable limits as the bootstrap current evolves during startup, fueling, heating, and burn? Formally, the question is whether operating scenarios or configuration design can hold the equilibrium's transform profile and island structure robust against the time-varying plasma-generated current.
status: Optimized configurations can reduce sensitivity to the bootstrap current, but operating trajectories still couple transport to equilibrium. Beidler et al. (2021), *Demonstration of reduced neoclassical energy transport in Wendelstein 7-X*, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-03687-w; Helander (2014).
solved_when: Rotational transform and island topology remain within acceptable limits throughout the full operating trajectory — startup, fueling, heating, and burn — as the bootstrap current varies.
why: A nominally current-free concept like the stellarator can still develop consequential plasma-generated currents, so without this robustness the device's carefully optimized equilibrium can be degraded in operation.
key_works: Beidler et al. (2021), *Demonstration of reduced neoclassical energy transport in Wendelstein 7-X*, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-03687-w; Helander (2014).

title: Reactor island-divertor exhaust
open: Can a stellarator reactor be equipped with an island divertor that tames its exhaust at full reactor power? Formally, the goal is to demonstrate an island-divertor configuration with adequate heat spreading, pumping, and impurity control that also tolerates equilibrium changes at reactor-relevant power levels.
status: Island divertors are implemented experimentally today, but their integration into a reactor-level exhaust system remains open.
solved_when: An island-divertor configuration is demonstrated that simultaneously provides adequate heat spreading, pumping, and impurity control, while remaining robust to equilibrium changes, at reactor power.
why: Stellarators exchange the tokamak's specific exhaust and stability challenges for a different, three-dimensional exhaust problem; solving it is what makes a stellarator power plant's heat and particle handling viable.
key_works: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991; Helander (2014), DOI: 10.1088/0034-4885/77/8/087001.

title: As-built coil-error certification
open: Can the accumulated realities of coil construction—manufacturing metrology, assembly tolerances, thermal deformation, and electromagnetic loading under operation—be converted into rigorous, certified bounds on how much plasma confinement degrades relative to the design? Formally, this asks for an end-to-end pipeline from as-built coil data to a quantified confinement-loss certificate.
status: Accurate coil designs and mechanical optimization methods exist, but end-to-end uncertainty certification of the as-built machine remains a separate, unsolved problem.
solved_when: A method exists that takes measured coil geometry, assembly tolerance data, thermal and electromagnetic load deformation as inputs and outputs certified bounds on confinement degradation for the as-built machine.
why: The plasma responds to the loaded, assembled coils as they actually exist—not to the ideal CAD model—so without this certification the connection between design optimization and real machine performance is unverified.
key_works: Kaptanoglu and Gil (2026), *A proof-of-concept for automated AI-driven stellarator coil optimization with in-the-loop finite-element calculations*, arXiv:2603.15240.

title: Maintainable stellarator coil and blanket geometry
open: Can a stellarator be designed so that its blanket and divertor can be replaced on a practical timescale without unacceptably degrading magnetic performance? In other words, can maintenance access be treated as a first-class constraint in coil and plasma optimization rather than retrofitted afterward?
status: Coil optimization has advanced substantially, but reactor maintenance access remains an independent integration constraint that has not been jointly solved with magnetic design. Key works: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991; Crofts and Harman (2014), arXiv:1412.4008.
solved_when: A stellarator coil-and-blanket architecture is demonstrated in which timely blanket and divertor replacement is possible while magnetic performance remains within acceptable bounds.
why: Excellent confinement alone is commercially insufficient if activated components cannot be replaced efficiently; maintainability is what turns a high-performance physics design into a serviceable power plant.
key_works: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991; Crofts and Harman (2014), arXiv:1412.4008.

title: Spherical-tokamak center-column lifetime
subfield: Spherical tokamaks, reversed-field pinches, spheromaks, and mirrors
open: Can the center column of a spherical tokamak be designed to last long enough to make a pilot plant viable, while simultaneously meeting neutron shielding, structural, cooling, and magnetic-field requirements? Formally, the problem is to find an integrated center-column architecture in which these competing constraints are simultaneously satisfied at an acceptable component lifetime.
status: The shielding-versus-lifetime tradeoff is explicit in spherical-tokamak pilot studies, e.g. Menard et al. (2016), *Fusion nuclear science facilities and pilot plants based on the tokamak* (DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/56/10/106023), but integrated lifetime qualification of the center column remains open.
solved_when: An integrated center-column design is qualified for lifetime under simultaneous neutron shielding, structural-load, cooling, and magnetic-field requirements, at a level acceptable to spherical-tokamak pilot-plant economics.
why: If the center column must be replaced frequently, that maintenance burden can erase the economic advantages that compactness is supposed to deliver.
key_works: Menard et al. (2016), *Fusion nuclear science facilities and pilot plants based on the spherical tokamak*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/56/10/106023.

title: Burning-plasma single-helical-axis RFP operation
subfield: Spherical tokamaks, reversed-field pinches, spheromaks, and mirrors
open: Can the single-helical-axis state of a reversed-field pinch — a self-organized helical equilibrium with favorable confinement — be sustained under fusion-relevant conditions? Formally, this asks for steady SHAx operation at fusion-relevant temperature, density, and self-heating.
