status: Self-organized helical equilibria were demonstrated by 2009 (Lorenzini et al., *Self-organized helical equilibria as a new paradigm for ohmically heated fusion plasmas*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys1308), but reactor-grade confinement remains a separate, unresolved target.
solved_when: A single-helical-axis RFP equilibrium is maintained at fusion-relevant temperature, density, and level of self-heating, with confinement adequate for a reactor extrapolation.
why: Success would establish a lower-magnetic-field route to confinement, reducing the field requirements of a fusion reactor.
key_works: Lorenzini et al. (2009), *Self-organized helical equilibria as a new paradigm for ohmically heated fusion plasmas*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys1308.

title: Low-loss RFP sustainment
subfield: Spherical tokamaks, reversed-field pinches, spheromaks, and mirrors
open: Can a reversed-field-pinch plasma's current and magnetic configuration be sustained indefinitely with only a modest recirculating power budget, while its inherently stochastic transport stays controlled? In other words, can RFP sustainment be made efficient enough to be an economical fusion operating mode?
status: RFP self-organization and boundary structure have been studied experimentally, notably the plasma boundary in Single Helical Axis RFP plasmas (Martines et al., 2009, arXiv:0909.3011; Lorenzini et al., 2009, DOI: 10.1038/nphys1308), but economical sustained fusion operation has not been established.
solved_when: A sustained RFP configuration is demonstrated in which the current and magnetic structure are maintained with acceptable recirculating power and controlled stochastic transport at the plasma boundary.
why: The RFP's appeal is its low magnet requirements, but that advantage evaporates if driving and sustaining the plasma consumes excessive power, so efficient sustainment is the gate to any economical RFP reactor.
key_works: Martines et al. (2009), *The plasma boundary in Single Helical Axis RFP plasmas*, arXiv:0909.3011; Lorenzini et al. (2009), DOI: 10.1038/nphys1308.

title: Spheromak helicity injection without confinement loss
subfield: Spherical tokamaks, reversed-field pinches, spheromaks, and mirrors
open: Can a spheromak be actively sustained by magnetic helicity injection while still maintaining confinement good enough for fusion gain? Formally, is there an injection scheme that drives helicity into the plasma without the accompanying transport enhancement or impurity influx that degrades energy confinement?
status: Relaxation theory and helicity-driven configurations are longstanding (Taylor, 1986, *Relaxation and magnetic reconnection in plasmas*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.58.741), and recent work has explored particle confinement in helical force-free plasmas (Light et al., 2025, *Counterintuitive Particle Confinement In A Helical Force-Free Plasma*, DOI: 10.3390/plasma8020020); nevertheless, sustainment and good confinement remain difficult to combine.
solved_when: A spheromak is experimentally sustained via helicity injection and simultaneously exhibits confinement (transport and impurity levels) compatible with fusion gain, rather than injection that trades sustainment against confinement.
why: It tests whether simple coil geometry can coexist with adequate plasma performance, which would validate the spheromak as a low-complexity path to fusion-relevant plasma.
key_works: Taylor (1986), *Relaxation and magnetic reconnection in plasmas*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.58.741; Light et al. (2025), *Counterintuitive Particle Confinement In A Helical Force-Free Plasma*, DOI: 10.3390/plasma8020020.

title: Predictive reconnection heating in compact tori
subfield: Spherical tokamaks, reversed-field pinches, spheromaks, and mirrors
open: During the formation or merging of a compact torus, where does the released magnetic reconnection energy go — into ions, electrons, bulk plasma motion, or particles that escape? A predictive theory would specify the energy partition among these channels from the plasma parameters and formation conditions.
status: Reconnection-based heating has been investigated experimentally, but a transferable reactor-design closure for the energy partition remains unavailable.
solved_when: A transferable closure exists that predicts the partition of reconnection energy among ions, electrons, bulk motion, and escaping particles during compact-torus formation or merging, usable in reactor design.
why: The energy invested in formation is only useful if it ends up as heat in the confined fuel rather than in exhausted channels.
key_works: Taylor (1986), *Relaxation and magnetic reconnection in plasmas*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.58.741; Steinhauer (2011), *Review of field-reversed configurations*, DOI: 10.1063/1.3613680.

title: Gas-dynamic-trap end-loss reduction
subfield: Spherical tokamaks, reversed-field pinches, spheromaks, and mirrors
open: Can the axial energy escaping along open field lines in a gas-dynamic trap be reduced far enough to make a useful fusion system, while the mirror retains stable and accessible operation?
status: Gas-dynamic-trap experiments and models were comprehensively reviewed in 2013 (Ivanov and Prikhodko, *Gas-dynamic trap: an overview of the concept and experimental results*, *Plasma Physics and Controlled Fusion* 55, 063001); power-plant energy balance remains unresolved.
solved_when: A gas-dynamic-trap configuration demonstrates an energy balance compatible with a power plant — i.e., end losses suppressed sufficiently that net-energy-relevant confinement is achieved without loss of stability or accessibility.
why: Open field lines create an end-loss channel absent from closed toroidal confinement, so axial losses directly set the viability of mirror-based fusion.
key_works: Ivanov and Prikhodko (2013), *Gas-dynamic trap: an overview of the concept and experimental results*, *Plasma Physics and Controlled Fusion* 55, 063001.

title: Economical tandem-mirror barriers
subfield: Spherical tokamaks, reversed-field pinches, spheromaks, and mirrors
open: Can the end-plug or thermal-barrier potentials of a tandem mirror be sustained by an auxiliary-power scheme whose total electrical cost is compatible with net fusion electricity production? In other words, the barrier's full creation and maintenance budget must be accounted for, not just its confinement benefit.
status: Mirror confinement concepts are longstanding, but useful barriers must be assessed together with their creation and maintenance costs, which has not been done in a way compatible with net electricity. Key works include Ivanov and Prikhodko (2013), *Gas-dynamic trap: an overview of the concept and experimental results*, and Wurzel and Hsu (2022), DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990.
solved_when: A tandem-mirror barrier concept is demonstrated (in design or experiment) to sustain the required plug/thermal-barrier potentials with a complete auxiliary-power requirement that permits net electricity from the fusion plant.
why: A barrier that reduces plasma energy loss but consumes more electrical energy than it saves does not solve the plant problem; the accounting must close for the reactor as a whole.
key_works: Ivanov and Prikhodko (2013), *Gas-dynamic trap: an overview of the concept and experimental results*; Wurzel and Hsu (2022), DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990.

title: Mirror end-loss energy recovery
subfield: Spherical tokamaks, reversed-field pinches, spheromaks, and mirrors
open: Can a mirror machine recover a useful fraction of the energy carried by charged particles escaping through its ends, in a system that tolerates broad particle distributions, secondary electrons, impurities, and neutron exposure?
status: Direct-conversion concepts exist, but no integrated system qualified for reactor duty has been demonstrated; related work includes Wurzel and Hsu (2025), *Continuing progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criteria*, arXiv:2505.03834.
solved_when: An integrated end-loss energy recovery system, operating under reactor-relevant conditions (broad distribution functions, secondary electrons, impurities, and neutron flux), demonstrates recovery of a useful fraction of escaping charged-particle energy at reactor duty.
why: Turning the mirror machine's inherent end-loss weakness into a partially useful energy stream improves its overall power balance and strengthens its case as a reactor concept.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2025), *Continuing progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criteria*, arXiv:2505.03834.

title: FRC electron-energy confinement
subfield: Field-reversed configurations, Z pinches, cusps, and dipoles
open: Can field-reversed configurations confine electron energy well enough at reactor-relevant temperatures and sizes to support net gain — that is, what is the electron heat-confinement scaling in an FRC under reactor conditions?
status: The 2011 review by Steinhauer (*Review of field-reversed configurations*, DOI: 10.1063/1.3613680) identifies transport as a central issue for FRCs; subsequent progress on formation and sustainment has not independently settled reactor-relevant electron losses.
solved_when: A demonstrated electron-energy confinement scaling law is established for FRC plasmas at reactor-relevant temperatures and device size, such that electron losses are quantified at those conditions.
why: Rapid electron losses can prevent net gain even when ion behavior is favorable, so this scaling determines whether FRC reactor designs are viable.
key_works: Steinhauer (2011), *Review of field-reversed configurations*, DOI: 10.1063/1.3613680.

title: FRC merging and compression efficiency
subfield: Field-reversed configurations, Z pinches, cusps, and dipoles
open: Can a field-reversed configuration be carried through formation, translation, merging, and compression while retaining enough flux, particle inventory, and thermal energy to make the full reactor cycle net-positive? In formal terms, what is the cumulative retention efficiency of these staged processes, and how can it be optimized?
status: These processes are established research techniques, but their cumulative reactor-cycle efficiency remains unresolved. Key works: Steinhauer (2011), *Review of field-reversed configurations*, DOI: 10.1063/1.3613680; Ellison et al. (2024), arXiv:2408.15206.
solved_when: Quantitative measurements and optimization demonstrate retained flux, particle inventory, and thermal energy through the complete formation–translation–merging–compression sequence at levels sufficient to preserve total-cycle gain.
why: Modest losses at each stage can compound to eliminate total-cycle gain, so the viability of the reactor concept hinges on closing this efficiency budget.
key_works: Steinhauer (2011), *Review of field-reversed configurations*, DOI: 10.1063/1.3613680; Ellison et al. (2024), arXiv:2408.15206.

title: Unambiguous Z-pinch fusion-source attribution
subfield: Field-reversed configurations, Z pinches, cusps, and dipoles
open: How can experiments on Z pinches reliably tell whether the neutrons they measure come from a hot, bulk thermonuclear plasma or from fast beam–target interactions, rather than relying on yield alone?
status: Mitrani et al. (2021), *Thermonuclear neutron emission from a sheared-flow stabilized Z-pinch* (DOI: 10.1063/5.0066257), demonstrated relevant discrimination, but extending it across devices and higher-performance regimes remains necessary.
solved_when: Discrimination techniques of the kind demonstrated in 2021 are established and validated across multiple devices and extended into higher-performance regimes over the course of scaling campaigns, so that beam–target and thermonuclear contributions are separated robustly throughout.
why: Neutron yield alone can misrepresent fuel temperature and hence the prospects for achieving gain, so attribution errors could steer scaling campaigns toward false conclusions.
key_works: Mitrani et al. (2021), *Thermonuclear neutron emission from a sheared-flow stabilized Z-pinch*, DOI: 10.1063/5.0066257.

title: Repetitive dense-plasma-focus operation
subfield: Field-reversed configurations, Z pinches, cusps, and dipoles
open: Can dense-plasma-focus systems deliver useful fusion performance shot after shot, with electrode erosion, impurity influx, and shot-to-shot variability held under control?
status: Pinch fusion has a long experimental history, but qualification of repetitive energy-system operation remains unresolved (Shumlak (2020), *Z-pinch fusion*, *Journal of Applied Physics* 127, 200901; Wurzel and Hsu (2022), DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990).
solved_when: A dense-plasma-focus device demonstrates reproducible, useful fusion performance over repeated shots while keeping electrode erosion, impurities, and shot-to-shot variability controlled — a qualification standard for repetitive energy-system operation.
why: A high-yield isolated shot is not a repeatable industrial process; without repetition under control, the configuration cannot serve as a practical fusion energy source.
key_works: Shumlak (2020), *Z-pinch fusion*, *Journal of Applied Physics* 127, 200901; Wurzel and Hsu (2022), DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990.

title: High-beta cusp confinement with full power balance
subfield: Field-reversed configurations, Z pinches, cusps, and dipoles
open: Can a high-beta cusp system simultaneously confine electrons and ions well enough to sustain useful fusion reactivity without excessive injection losses? In formal terms, the goal is a demonstration of full power balance — confinement, reactivity, and loss rates all acceptable at once.
status: Enhanced high-energy-electron confinement was demonstrated in 2015 (Park et al., *High-Energy Electron Confinement in a Magnetic Cusp Configuration*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevX.5.021024), but complete fusion gain was not achieved. Related directions include ambipolar confinement and kinetic boundary losses.
solved_when: A high-beta cusp device demonstrates simultaneous electron and ion confinement, useful fusion reactivity, and acceptable injection losses — i.e., full fusion power balance — experimentally.
why: Electron confinement alone does not yield net fusion in a cusp; without ion confinement and acceptable losses, cusp-based fusion cannot work.
key_works: Park et al. (2015), *High-Energy Electron Confinement in a Magnetic Cusp Configuration*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevX.5.021024.

title: Fusion-relevant levitated-dipole confinement
subfield: Field-reversed configurations, Z pinches, cusps, and dipoles
open: Can a levitated dipole magnet confine plasma at fusion-relevant ion temperatures while maintaining fueling, stability, and coil survivability? In formal terms, this asks whether the levitated-dipole topology can sustain high-temperature ion confinement under the operating conditions useful for fusion.
status: Turbulent inward particle pinch in a levitated-dipole-confined plasma was demonstrated in 2010 (Boxer et al., *Turbulent inward pinch of plasma confined by a levitated dipole magnet*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys1510; related work by Kobayashi et al., 2009, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.103.055003), but reactor-level energy confinement and the required engineering remain open.
solved_when: A levitated dipole experiment demonstrates high-temperature ion confinement together with fueling, stability, and coil survivability at useful fusion conditions; reactor-level energy confinement and the associated engineering are thereby demonstrated.
why: Dipoles offer a qualitatively different confinement topology from mainstream magnetic-confinement approaches, potentially unlocking an alternative route to fusion if these basic feasibility questions are settled.
key_works: Boxer et al. (2010), *Turbulent inward pinch of plasma confined by a levitated dipole magnet*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys1510; Kobayashi et al. (2009), DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.103.055003.

title: Generalized IEC power-balance bounds
subfield: Field-reversed configurations, Z pinches, cusps, and dipoles
open: Can we establish rigorous power-balance limits for precisely defined inertial-electrostatic-confinement architectures, including proposed mechanisms that depart from standard assumptions?
status: Important restricted loss arguments already exist, notably Rider (1995), *A general critique of inertial-electrostatic confinement fusion systems*, DOI: 10.1063/1.871273, and Rider (1997), DOI: 10.1063/1.872556; simply restating them is not an open problem.
solved_when: A rigorous power-balance bound (or impossibility result) is proven for a precisely specified IEC architecture, covering mechanisms that depart from the standard assumptions underlying existing restricted loss arguments — not a restatement of those arguments.
why: Strong bounds can eliminate unproductive designs or identify genuinely different regimes.
key_works: Rider (1995), *A general critique of inertial-electrostatic confinement fusion systems*, DOI: 10.1063/1.871273; Rider (1997), DOI: 10.1063/1.872556.

title: High-gain magnetized-liner fusion
subfield: Magnetized inertial fusion and pulsed power
open: Can a magnetized-liner fusion target actually reach the gain needed for a complete power-plant system to balance, rather than just showing favorable pressure–confinement products in isolation?
status: Magnetized pulsed approaches have seen substantial experimental progress; the 2024 opportunities paper (Ellison et al., *Opportunities in Pulsed Magnetic Fusion Energy*, arXiv:2408.15206) advocates further development rather than reporting a power plant.
solved_when: A magnetized-liner target demonstrates gain sufficient for a credible complete-system power balance, with the full system (not merely the physics figure of merit) closing.
why: Target gain at this level is the central performance discriminator deciding whether this fusion family can become a practical energy source.
key_works: Ellison et al. (2024), *Opportunities in Pulsed Magnetic Fusion Energy*, arXiv:2408.15206.

title: Nonlinear magneto-Rayleigh–Taylor control
subfield: Magnetized inertial fusion and pulsed power
open: Can the magneto-Rayleigh–Taylor instability of an imploding fusion liner be predicted, and ultimately suppressed, through its fully nonlinear evolution — including mode coupling, evolving material strength, and stagnation?
status: Instability physics is extensively studied, but acceptable perturbation growth at high-gain conditions remains a limiting issue. See Hurricane et al. (2023), *Physics principles of inertial confinement fusion and U.S. program overview*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.95.025005.
solved_when: A theory or model quantitatively predicts nonlinear perturbation growth under high-gain conditions and identifies a control strategy that keeps growth within acceptable limits through stagnation.
why: Small liner imperfections can grow into fuel contamination or asymmetric compression, degrading target performance.
key_works: Hurricane et al. (2023), *Physics principles of inertial confinement fusion and U.S. program overview*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.95.025005.

title: Magnetic-flux retention during compression
subfield: Magnetized inertial fusion and pulsed power
open: Can we predict, and ultimately control, how much magnetic flux survives the violent compression of a magnetized implosion? A complete answer would account simultaneously for flux loss from resistive diffusion, Nernst thermomagnetic transport, magnetic reconnection, and multidimensional plasma motion.
status: Magnetized-target models include resistivity, Nernst transport, reconnection, and multidimensional motion, but their combined quantitative validation remains incomplete (Ellison et al. (2024), *Opportunities in Pulsed Magnetic Fusion Energy*, arXiv:2408.15206).
solved_when: A quantitative model incorporating resistivity, Nernst transport, reconnection, and multidimensional motion is validated against experimental data from magnetized implosions, accurately predicting the retained magnetic flux in the compressed fuel.
why: Compressed magnetic fields are only useful for confinement if they remain coupled to the hot fuel; unexplained flux loss directly degrades the insulation and heating that magnetized inertial fusion depends on.
key_works: Ellison et al. (2024), *Opportunities in Pulsed Magnetic Fusion Energy*, arXiv:2408.15206.

title: Uniform magnetized-fuel preheat
subfield: Magnetized inertial fusion and pulsed power
open: Can preheat energy be deposited in magnetized fusion fuel uniformly enough that it heats the fuel without disturbing the liner walls or introducing impurities? Formally, the goal is an energy-deposition scheme whose spatial nonuniformity, wall interaction, and impurity production all stay below the levels compatible with high-gain target designs.
status: Preheat is a demonstrated ingredient of magnetized-liner inertial fusion approaches, but its efficient integration into a high-gain design remains open. See Hurricane et al. (2023), *Physics principles of inertial confinement fusion and U.S. program overview*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.95.025005.
solved_when: A preheat scheme deposits the required energy in the fuel with sufficiently low nonuniformity, wall interaction, and impurity production, integrated efficiently into a high-gain magnetized-liner target.
why: Poor preheat forces higher compression of the target or seeds destructive asymmetry, either of which can prevent ignition and gain.
key_works: Hurricane et al. (2023), *Physics principles of inertial confinement fusion and U.S. program overview*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.95.025005.

title: Axial end-loss closure in magnetized targets
subfield: Magnetized inertial fusion and pulsed power
open: How can particle and energy losses through the ends of a magnetized fusion target be quantified and suppressed, without introducing unacceptable preheat, fuel-injection, or manufacturing penalties? Formally, the goal is an end-loss closure scheme whose axial particle and thermal fluxes are reduced to tolerable levels while preserving target integrity and manufacturability.
status: End losses are included as a consideration in magnetized-target design studies, but a robust end-loss solution for reactor targets remains unresolved; see Ellison et al. (2024), *Opportunities in Pulsed Magnetic Fusion Energy*, arXiv:2408.15206.
solved_when: A reactor-relevant target design demonstrates suppressed axial particle and thermal end losses without incurring unacceptable preheat, injection, or manufacturing penalties.
why: Radial magnetic insulation confines transport perpendicular to the field but does nothing to stop losses streaming along open field lines through the target ends, so this channel can dominate the energy budget of a magnetized target.
key_works: Ellison et al. (2024), *Opportunities in Pulsed Magnetic Fusion Energy*, arXiv:2408.15206.

title: Liner-material mix prediction
subfield: Magnetized inertial fusion and pulsed power
open: Can we predict, from first principles, how much liner material contaminates the fusion fuel during compression, and what manufacturing tolerances on the liner–fuel interfaces suffice to keep the resulting radiation losses acceptable? A quantitative, multiscale treatment of this instability-driven mixing is the goal.
status: Mixing is recognized as an issue across inertial-fusion approaches, but a predictive multiscale treatment remains difficult; see Zhou, Sadler, and Hurricane (2025), *Instabilities and Mixing in Inertial Confinement Fusion*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-fluid-022824-110008.
solved_when: A validated predictive model quantifies fuel contamination from liner interfaces and yields concrete manufacturing tolerances that keep radiation losses within acceptable bounds.
why: Even a small mass of high-charge-number material mixed into the compressed fuel can strongly cool it through radiation, threatening ignition.
key_works: Zhou, Sadler, and Hurricane (2025), *Instabilities and Mixing in Inertial Confinement Fusion*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-fluid-022824-110008.

title: Pulsed-power current delivery at scale
subfield: Magnetized inertial fusion and pulsed power
open: Can a pulsed-power driver deliver the intended current waveform to an imploding load at reactor scale while simultaneously controlling plasma formation, insulation breakdown, current loss, and electrode damage?
status: Large pulsed-power facilities demonstrate substantial capability, but reactor repetition and efficient scaling remain unresolved; see Ellison et al. (2024), *Opportunities in Pulsed Magnetic Fusion Energy*, arXiv:2408.15206.
solved_when: The full intended current waveform reaches the imploding load at reactor-relevant repetition rate and efficient scaling, with plasma formation, insulation breakdown, current loss, and electrode damage controlled.
why: Stored electrical energy is irrelevant if it does not reach the target in the required waveform — power delivery, not energy storage, sets the viability of the scheme.
key_works: Ellison et al. (2024), *Opportunities in Pulsed Magnetic Fusion Energy*, arXiv:2408.15206.

title: Repetitive pulser energy recovery
subfield: Magnetized inertial fusion and pulsed power
open: Can a repetitive pulsed fusion system recapture the magnetic and electrical energy left over after each shot and feed it back into subsequent cycles, without degrading pulse quality or shortening component lifetime?
status: Energy recovery is regarded as an attractive systems objective, but integrated validation under repetitive fusion-duty conditions has not been established.
solved_when: An energy-recovery scheme is demonstrated over repeated fusion-duty cycles that maintains pulse quality and component lifetime while returning the unused magnetic and electrical energy to the system.
why: Whether such recovery works decides whether a pulsed fusion concept has an acceptable level of recirculating power, and hence whether it is viable as a power plant.
key_works: Ellison et al. (2024), *Opportunities in Pulsed Magnetic Fusion Energy*, arXiv:2408.15206; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Symmetric liquid-piston compression
subfield: Magnetized inertial fusion and pulsed power
open: Can a magnetized plasma be compressed to high gain by a liquid or mechanically driven liner, with the imperfections of real hardware — synchronization errors, jets, shocks, and plasma contamination — held within tolerable bounds? More precisely, what level of driver synchronization and liner uniformity still permits repeatable high-gain compression?
status: Magneto-inertial architectures are included in gain surveys (Wurzel and Hsu (2025), *Continuing progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criteria*, arXiv:2505.03834), but repeatable high-gain compression remains an experimental discriminator for the field.
solved_when: A liquid or mechanically driven liner compresses magnetized plasma to high gain in repeatable experiments, with synchronization errors, jet formation, shocks, and plasma contamination characterized and shown not to break the compression.
why: Mechanical drivers could substantially reduce the cost of a fusion scheme, but they introduce hydrodynamic tolerances that are difficult to meet; demonstrating that these tolerances are achievable would validate a lower-cost path to gain.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2025), *Continuing progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criteria*, arXiv:2505.03834.

title: Robust high target gain
open: Can an inertial-confinement fusion target achieve high gain not just once, but reliably — with a broad tolerance margin against realistic variations in the driver and the target itself?
status: LLNL reported 8.6 ± 0.45 MJ from 2.08 MJ laser input in 2025, and still cited 8.6 MJ in May 2026; this establishes gain, not industrial robustness. Key works: Abu-Shawareb et al. (2024), *Achievement of Target Gain Larger than Unity in an Inertial Fusion Experiment*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.132.065102; LLNL reports, 2025–2026.
solved_when: High target gain is demonstrated with a broad tolerance margin under realistic driver and target variations, establishing repeatable gain rather than exceptional single shots.
why: A power plant needs repeatable gain, not occasional exceptional shots; without robustness, high-gain results remain laboratory milestones rather than a path to fusion energy.
key_works: Abu-Shawareb et al. (2024), *Achievement of Target Gain Larger than Unity in an Inertial Fusion Experiment*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.132.065102; LLNL reports, 2025–2026.

title: Low-mode implosion asymmetry prediction
open: Can we predict, from first principles, how low-order shape and drive asymmetries shape the final outcome of an inertial-confinement implosion — its stagnation, residual motion, and burn — with uncertainties validated against experiment? In other words, is there a predictive theory whose error bars hold across target designs?
status: Asymmetry control has already helped enable ignition at current facilities, but predictive tolerance for low-mode asymmetries across target families remains open. Key works include Betti and Hurricane (2016), *Inertial-confinement fusion with lasers*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3736, and Hurricane et al. (2023), DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.95.025005.
solved_when: A predictive model of low-mode asymmetry effects on stagnation, residual motion, and burn is demonstrated with experimentally validated uncertainty across target families.
why: A small global asymmetry can prevent an otherwise adequate compression from achieving ignition-relevant performance, so credible tolerances are essential to target design.
key_works: Betti and Hurricane (2016), *Inertial-confinement fusion with lasers*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3736; Hurricane et al. (2023), DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.95.025005.

title: Ablative Rayleigh–Taylor prediction across scales
open: Can we predict how an ablative Rayleigh–Taylor instability grows from manufacturing-scale perturbations all the way through nonlinear saturation into burn-relevant turbulent mixing? The goal is a single predictive framework carrying the instability cascade across those scales in an inertial-confinement target.
status: Linear and nonlinear models of the instability are well developed, as surveyed by Zhou, Sadler, and Hurricane (2025), *Instabilities and Mixing in Inertial Confinement Fusion*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-fluid-022824-110008, but a complete predictive multiscale closure remains difficult.
solved_when: A validated multiscale closure exists that predicts instability growth from initial target-roughness perturbations through nonlinear saturation and mixing at burn-relevant scales, with no scale regime left to empirical fitting.
why: The allowable roughness specification for a manufactured ICF target depends on the entire instability cascade; without end-to-end prediction, targets cannot be confidently qualified for ignition.
key_works: Zhou, Sadler, and Hurricane (2025), *Instabilities and Mixing in Inertial Confinement Fusion*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-fluid-022824-110008.

title: Defect-induced mix tolerance
open: How large can capsule defects, support structures, fill-tube perturbations, and inclusions be before they unacceptably degrade an inertial-confinement implosion? The goal is a quantified, validated tolerance specification grounded in three-dimensional burn predictions.
status: Defect control has materially improved implosions, but a broad industrial tolerance specification remains unresolved. See Zhou et al. (2025), *Instabilities and Mixing in Inertial Confinement Fusion*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-fluid-022824-110008.
solved_when: Acceptable size and configuration limits for capsule defects, supports, fill-tube perturbations, and inclusions are quantitatively specified and validated by three-dimensional burn predictions.
why: Target manufacturing cost depends strongly on what imperfections can be tolerated, so a validated tolerance specification directly controls the economics of producing implosion targets at scale.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2025), *Instabilities and Mixing in Inertial Confinement Fusion*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-fluid-022824-110008.

title: Rapid, uniform cryogenic fuel layering
open: Can deuterium–tritium ice layers of the required thickness and roughness be formed at industrial throughput, and preserved intact until implosion? In other words, a layering process is sought that meets target uniformity specifications while scaling far beyond single-shot laboratory practice.
status: Precision cryogenic layering exists for experimental use; high-throughput, inexpensive production remains a stated IFE need (Ma 2023, *Priority Research Opportunities from the 2022 DOE Basic Research Needs for Inertial Fusion Energy*).
solved_when: DT fuel layers meeting the required thickness and roughness are produced at industrial (high-throughput, inexpensive) rates and remain sufficiently uniform until implosion.
why: Existing precision cryogenic layering methods suit individual experiments but are likely incompatible with the millions of targets an inertial fusion energy plant would consume.
key_works: Ma (2023), *Priority Research Opportunities from the 2022 DOE Basic Research Needs for Inertial Fusion Energy*.

title: Multispecies kinetic effects in hot spots
open: How do species separation and non-Maxwellian ion distributions during ignition-scale implosions change the kinetic transport of energy and particles in the hot spot? More precisely, can we quantify these multispecies kinetic effects well enough to predict the fusion burn of an imploding capsule?
status: Hydrodynamic models explain much of the observed performance, but kinetic corrections can alter inferred temperature and reactivity; see Betti and Hurricane (2016), *Inertial-confinement fusion with lasers*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3736.
solved_when: A quantitative description of species separation, non-Maxwellian distributions, and kinetic transport is available for ignition-scale implosions, sufficient to determine how far a single-fluid temperature mispredicts hot-spot burn and reactivity.
why: A single-fluid temperature may not correctly determine fusion burn; kinetic corrections can alter inferred temperature and reactivity, and thus the interpretation and design of implosion performance.
key_works: Betti and Hurricane (2016), *Inertial-confinement fusion with lasers*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3736.

title: Nonlocal electron heat flow in implosions
open: Can a computationally practical reduced model of electron heat transport be built that stays accurate in implosions, where temperature gradients are steep, collisionality varies, and magnetic fields may alter the flow? Formally, this asks for a closure of the electron kinetic equation that recovers the correct heat flux in the nonlocal, transitional, and magnetized regimes at a cost compatible with full-scale hydrodynamic simulation.
status: Present practice combines flux-limited diffusion with kinetic calculations, but no universally reliable reduced closure is available; see Craxton et al. (2015), *Direct-drive inertial confinement fusion: A review*, DOI: 10.1063/1.4934714.
solved_when: A reduced electron-transport model exists that is computationally practical, remains accurate across steep gradients, changing collisionality, and magnetization, and is validated as reliable in regimes where flux limits and kinetic calculations are currently used.
why: Electron heat flow governs ablation, shock timing, and hot-spot formation, so an unreliable closure directly corrupts ignition predictions for inertial-confinement targets.
key_works: Craxton et al. (2015), *Direct-drive inertial confinement fusion: A review*, DOI: 10.1063/1.4934714.

title: Alpha stopping in burning dense plasma
open: Can we directly measure how alpha particles deposit their energy in a burning dense plasma, under the coupled density, temperature, degeneracy, and nonequilibrium conditions of an igniting target?
status: Ignition has been achieved and demonstrates effective self-heating, but it does not uniquely validate every stopping model over the relevant state space.
solved_when: An experimental measurement (or validated inference) of alpha-energy deposition is obtained under igniting-target conditions that discriminates among competing stopping models across the relevant state space.
why: Small differences in stopping can shift ignition thresholds and inferred margins, so the fidelity of model predictions of self-heating depends on this validation.
key_works: Hurricane et al. (2023), *Physics principles of inertial confinement fusion and U.S. program overview*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.95.025005.

title: Equation-of-state and opacity uncertainty
open: How accurately do we know the equations of state and opacities of the fuel, ablators, and mixed materials traversed during an inertial-confinement implosion, and how do those uncertainties propagate along the implosion trajectory? A satisfactory answer would deliver reduced, experimentally constrained material models with quantified uncertainty propagated through full implosion simulations.
status: First-principles deuterium and polystyrene tables improved modeling in 2011–2015 (Hu et al. 2011, *First-principles equation-of-state table of deuterium for inertial confinement fusion applications*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevB.84.224109; Hu 2015, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevE.92.043104), but complete experimentally constrained coverage remains open.
solved_when: Complete experimentally constrained equation-of-state and opacity coverage exists for fuel, ablators, and mixed materials over implosion trajectories, with uncertainties quantified and propagated.
why: Errors in material models can masquerade as errors in drive or hydrodynamic instability, corrupting the diagnosis and design of implosions.
key_works: Hu et al. (2011), *First-principles equation-of-state table of deuterium for inertial confinement fusion applications*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevB.84.224109; Hu (2015), DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevE.92.043104.

title: Shock-ignition coupling
open: Can an intense laser pulse delivered late in the implosion launch the ignition shock while keeping hot-electron preheat and laser–plasma interaction losses within acceptable bounds? Formally, this asks for an integrated experimental demonstration that shock-ignition coupling achieves the required strong-shock generation without degrading target compression.
status: Shock ignition is a studied alternative target scheme in inertial-confinement fusion, but integrated high-gain experimental validation remains open. Key works include Craxton et al. (2015), *Direct-drive inertial confinement fusion: A review* (DOI: 10.1063/1.4934714) and Tikhonchuk (2020), *Progress and opportunities for inertial fusion energy in Europe*.
solved_when: An integrated high-gain experimental validation of shock ignition is achieved, showing the late-time intense drive launches the required ignition shock with hot-electron preheat and laser–plasma losses at acceptable levels.
why: Favorable shock-ignition coupling could relax the requirements on the main compression driver, easing the path to inertial fusion energy targets.
key_works: Craxton et al. (2015), *Direct-drive inertial confinement fusion: A review*, DOI: 10.1063/1.4934714; Tikhonchuk (2020), *Progress and opportunities for inertial fusion energy in Europe*.

title: Fast-ignition energy deposition
open: Can a relativistic electron or ion beam deposit its energy into compressed fusion fuel at the intensity and precision needed to ignite it? More formally, can energy be delivered to the hot spot with simultaneously acceptable conversion, transport, and pointing efficiency?
status: Fast ignition has a substantial research literature (e.g., Betti and Hurricane 2016, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3736; Tikhonchuk 2020), but integrated target gain remains unresolved.
solved_when: An integrated fast-ignition target demonstrates ignition and gain, with the delivered energy pulse concentrated in the compressed fuel at acceptable conversion, transport, and pointing efficiency.
why: Separating the compression driver from the ignition pulse would enlarge the space of viable target designs and relax requirements on uniform implosion.
key_works: Betti and Hurricane (2016), *Inertial-confinement fusion with lasers*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3736; Tikhonchuk (2020), *Progress and opportunities for inertial fusion energy in Europe*.

title: Two-plasmon-decay hot-electron control
open: Can hot-electron production from two-plasmon decay be bounded and suppressed under ignition-scale direct-drive conditions? Formally, this means establishing drive configurations — beam geometry, wavelength, and target parameters — for which the hot-electron fraction and preheat stay below levels compatible with ignition.
status: The instability and mitigation approaches are longstanding; acceptable reactor-target performance remains configuration-dependent. Key reference: Craxton et al. (2015), *Direct-drive inertial confinement fusion: A review*, DOI: 10.1063/1.4934714.
solved_when: An ignition-scale direct-drive configuration demonstrates suppression of two-plasmon-decay hot-electron generation to levels yielding acceptable reactor-target performance, with the result holding beyond a single configuration-dependent regime.
why: Hot electrons from two-plasmon decay preheat the fuel, and premature fuel heating can prevent adequate compression, blocking ignition.
key_works: Craxton et al. (2015), *Direct-drive inertial confinement fusion: A review*, DOI: 10.1063/1.4934714.

title: Raman and Brillouin backscatter prediction
open: Can we predict the level of stimulated Raman and Brillouin backscatter — and how it saturates — in realistic fusion plasmas with laser speckles, finite bandwidth, and evolving hydrodynamics? A complete theory would take the driver and plasma conditions as input and yield quantitative backscatter without fitting to full-scale experiments.
status: Detailed models of stimulated scattering exist, but full-scale quantitative prediction remains difficult because multiple kinetic and optical effects interact; see Tikhonchuk (2020), *Progress and opportunities for inertial fusion energy in Europe*.
solved_when: A first-principles predictive model matches observed backscatter levels and saturation behavior in realistic speckled, broadband, evolving fusion plasmas at full scale, accounting for the interacting kinetic and optical effects.
why: Backscatter diverts driver energy away from the target and can damage optics, so reliable prediction is needed to design fusion drivers that stay within acceptable energy-loss and damage budgets.
key_works: Tikhonchuk (2020), *Progress and opportunities for inertial fusion energy in Europe*.

title: Self-generated magnetic fields in laser targets
open: Can we predict how magnetic fields that generate themselves inside a laser-driven target — through Biermann battery effects, thermomagnetic transport, and magnetic reconnection — reshape the heat flow and implosion symmetry over the course of an inertial confinement fusion implosion? More formally, the goal is an integrated, predictive account of these self-generated fields and their feedback on energy transport throughout the implosion.
status: These effects are represented in advanced models, but their validated integrated impact remains uncertain. Key work: Hurricane et al. (2023), *Physics principles of inertial confinement fusion and U.S. program overview*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.95.025005.
solved_when: A validated, integrated prediction of how Biermann generation, thermomagnetic transport, and reconnection modify heat flow and symmetry across a full implosion, demonstrated against experimental data rather than model representation alone.
why: Unplanned magnetization can change transport even in nominally unmagnetized targets, so without such a prediction, implosion performance and symmetry cannot be reliably controlled.
key_works: Hurricane et al. (2023), *Physics principles of inertial confinement fusion and U.S. program overview*, DOI: 10.1103/RevModPhys.95.025005.

title: Broadband-driver instability suppression
open: Can realistic laser bandwidth and beam-smoothing architectures suppress the damaging laser–plasma instabilities of an inertial-fusion driver without paying an unacceptable price in efficiency or optical complexity?
status: Broadband and smoothing strategies are active design approaches, but the benefits for integrated high-gain performance still require experimental validation (Tikhonchuk 2020, *Progress and opportunities for inertial fusion energy in Europe*; Craxton et al. 2015, DOI: 10.1063/1.4934714).
solved_when: An integrated experimental demonstration shows broadband/smoothed drive suppressing the target instabilities while keeping efficiency and optical penalties within design tolerance; no numerical targets were specified in the record, so the natural criterion is a validated experimental demonstration of instability suppression under realistic driver conditions.
why: It determines whether driver design and plasma-instability control can be optimized together rather than traded off against each other, which directly constrains viable inertial-fusion-energy driver architectures.
key_works: Tikhonchuk (2020), *Progress and opportunities for inertial fusion energy in Europe*; Craxton et al. (2015), DOI: 10.1063/1.4934714.

title: Efficient repetitive megajoule-class laser systems
open: Can a single laser driver simultaneously deliver fusion-relevant pulse energy, the required waveform and wavelength, high repetition rate, high efficiency, and long operational lifetime — rather than achieving each of these in separate, smaller-scale demonstrations?
status: Diode-pumped systems have demonstrated important smaller-scale capabilities, but no integrated system exists; IFE workshops identify roughly 10–20% driver efficiency as a development objective rather than a completed achievement (Ma 2023, *Priority Research Opportunities from the 2022 DOE Basic Research Needs for Inertial Fusion Energy*; Gorman et al. 2024, DOI: 10.1063/5.0201702).
solved_when: One complete driver system demonstrates megajoule-class fusion-relevant pulse energy together with the required waveform, wavelength, repetition rate, and lifetime at roughly 10–20% driver efficiency.
why: Single-shot high-energy lasers and high-repetition low-energy systems excel on different axes; the field lacks a driver that integrates both, which is what an inertial fusion energy power plant actually requires.
key_works: Ma (2023), *Priority Research Opportunities from the 2022 DOE Basic Research Needs for Inertial Fusion Energy*; Gorman et al. (2024), DOI: 10.1063/5.0201702.

title: Long-lived ultraviolet final optics
open: Can final optics for an inertial fusion power plant survive the combined assault of cumulative laser damage, contamination, neutron flux, debris, and thermal distortion — and be repaired or replaced on a schedule compatible with plant operation? In formal terms, this asks for optics qualified against all degradation mechanisms simultaneously over a power-plant repetition-rate lifetime, including a demonstrated repair pathway.
status: NIF operates with sophisticated optics inspection and maintenance (e.g., its Optics Inspector), but at power-plant repetition rates the lifetime requirement changes dramatically; IFE research opportunities (Ma, 2023) and LLNL's work on optics inspection machinery (LLNL, 2026, *Meet the Machines That Matter: The Optics Inspector*) frame the gap between present-day practice and power-plant needs.
solved_when: A final-optics design demonstrates, under power-plant conditions, acceptable throughput degradation from cumulative laser damage, contamination, neutron irradiation, debris, and thermal distortion, together with a repair or replacement scheme that keeps optics cost and downtime from dominating driver availability.
why: Optics replacement can dominate driver availability and operating cost, so without qualified long-lived final optics a fusion power plant cannot run economically.
key_works: LLNL (2026), *Meet the Machines That Matter: The Optics Inspector*; Ma (2023), IFE research opportunities.

title: Heavy-ion driver compression and focusing
open: Can an intense heavy-ion pulse be compressed in time and focused to the required spot size while transported through a realistic fusion chamber environment? Formally, the goal is an integrated demonstration of beam compression and focusing at driver-relevant intensity through a chamber, not merely of the components separately.
status: Heavy-ion fusion remains a studied driver alternative; an integrated high-gain driver–target demonstration is not established. Related context appears in Wurzel and Hsu (2022), *Progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criterion*, DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990, and NASEM (2021), DOI: 10.17226/25991.
solved_when: An intense heavy-ion beam achieves the required temporal compression and focal spot size after transport through a realistic fusion chamber, as part of an integrated high-gain driver–target demonstration.
why: Accelerator drivers could offer attractive efficiency and high repetition rates for inertial fusion, but only if beam transport through the chamber is solved; without it, heavy-ion fusion cannot advance beyond a studied alternative.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2022), *Progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criterion*, DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990; NASEM (2021), DOI: 10.17226/25991.

title: Low-cost precision target manufacturing
open: Can ignition-capable inertial-fusion targets be manufactured at industrial throughput, with a verified delivered cost per target that is compatible with power-plant economics?
status: The 2023 IFE workshop presentation (Ma (2023), *Priority Research Opportunities from the 2022 DOE Basic Research Needs for Inertial Fusion Energy*) cites approximately million-per-day production and sub-dollar targets as objectives; these are not demonstrated production records.
solved_when: Targets are produced at approximately million-per-day rates with sub-dollar cost per target, demonstrated as production records rather than objectives.
why: A plant consumes targets several times per second, so a consumable at that rate cannot carry laboratory-production economics and still yield an economically viable plant.
key_works: Ma (2023), *Priority Research Opportunities from the 2022 DOE Basic Research Needs for Inertial Fusion Energy*.

title: Inline target qualification
open: Can every performance-relevant defect in an inertial-fusion target be detected inline, fast enough to keep pace with production, while keeping false-accept and false-reject rates at validated, acceptable levels?
status: Experimental target metrology is sophisticated, but production-speed predictive acceptance remains an unresolved industrial step.
solved_when: A production-speed inspection method exists that detects all performance-relevant target defects with measured and validated false-accept and false-reject rates meeting production requirements.
why: Manufacturing throughput is useless if bad targets cannot be identified economically — without qualified inline acceptance, defective targets would enter shots or require costly offline rejection.
key_works: Ma (2023), IFE research opportunities; Zhou et al. (2025), *Instabilities and Mixing in Inertial Confinement Fusion*.

title: Cryogenic target injection
open: Can cryogenic fusion targets be injected into a reactor chamber at flight speed and still arrive at the shot point with their fuel layer, orientation, and dimensions intact?
status: IFE studies specify demanding injection speeds and precision, but integrated reactor-chamber qualification remains open; key context is Ma (2023), *Priority Research Opportunities from the 2022 DOE Basic Research Needs for Inertial Fusion Energy*.
solved_when: An integrated injection system demonstrably delivers cryogenic targets through the chamber preserving layer quality, orientation, and dimensional tolerances at the speeds and precision specified in IFE studies, with reactor-chamber qualification achieved.
why: Even a perfectly formed stationary target can be damaged in transit before it reaches the shot point, so target survival in flight is a prerequisite for any repetitively pulsed inertial fusion power plant.
key_works: Ma (2023), *Priority Research Opportunities from the 2022 DOE Basic Research Needs for Inertial Fusion Energy*.

title: Real-time target tracking and beam interception
open: Can a moving target inside an inertial-fusion chamber be tracked in real time and intercepted by all driver beams with sufficiently low error, despite chamber light, debris, vibration, and thermal distortion?
status: Tracking requirements are identified in IFE development plans (Ma, 2023; Tikhonchuk, 2020, *Progress and opportunities for inertial fusion energy in Europe*), but a complete power-plant environment remains unqualified.
solved_when: A tracking and beam-steering system demonstrates the required interception accuracy for every driver beam under a complete power-plant environment, including chamber light, debris, vibration, and thermal distortion.
why: Small positioning errors translate directly into failed or asymmetric implosions.
key_works: Ma (2023), IFE research opportunities; Tikhonchuk (2020), *Progress and opportunities for inertial fusion energy in Europe*.

title: Chamber clearing between shots
open: How can the vapor, ions, aerosols, and debris left in a fusion chamber after a shot be removed or redistributed fast enough that the next target and driver pulse meet acceptable conditions?
status: Chamber concepts exist, but high-yield repetitive clearing remains a distinct and unproven systems requirement (Tikhonchuk 2020, *Progress and opportunities for inertial fusion energy in Europe*; Ellison et al. 2024, arXiv:2408.15206).
solved_when: A chamber-clearing scheme is demonstrated under high-yield, repetitive operation and shown to restore acceptable conditions before each subsequent shot.
why: Residual chamber material can ruin coupling and target survival, so without rapid clearing a repetitive inertial-fusion plant cannot run at all.
key_works: Tikhonchuk (2020), *Progress and opportunities for inertial fusion energy in Europe*; Ellison et al. (2024), arXiv:2408.15206.

title: Stable protective liquid-wall jets
open: Can a protective liquid-wall jet hold its required geometry through the repeated insults of a fusion chamber — neutron and photon fluxes, shock waves, and vapor loading — while still leaving beam and target paths clear?
status: Liquid protection has long been studied as a chamber approach, but no integrated qualification under repetitive fusion conditions has been achieved; that remains open. Relevant context appears in NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991, and Ellison et al. (2024), *Opportunities in Pulsed Magnetic Fusion Energy*.
solved_when: The jet maintains the specified geometry under cyclic neutron, photon, shock, and vapor loading for the full set of required repetitions, with beam and target access preserved throughout; a qualification demonstrating this in an integrated, repetitively pulsed fusion environment closes the problem.
why: A durable liquid wall would cut damage to solid chamber components and slash how often they must be replaced, directly improving the availability and economics of an inertial-fusion power plant.
key_works: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991; Ellison et al. (2024), *Opportunities in Pulsed Magnetic Fusion Energy*.

title: Dry-wall cyclic survival
open: Can dry chamber-wall surfaces be qualified to survive the full combination of cyclic thermal shock, implantation, sputtering, and neutron damage expected under a specified inertial-fusion energy (IFE) plant design? That is, can a wall material be certified not merely against each load individually but against their simultaneous, repeated action at shot-by-shot time scales?
status: Existing materials research characterizes the individual loading mechanisms — thermal shock, implantation, sputtering, and neutron damage — in isolation, but complete repetitive exposure combining all of them remains unqualified (Knaster, Moeslang, and Muroga, 2016, *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735).
solved_when: A dry chamber-wall material or coating demonstrates survival under the combined repetitive exposure — thermal shock, implantation, sputtering, and neutron damage simultaneously — at the pulse count and conditions specified by the target IFE design, with qualification established for the design's full load spectrum rather than single-load tests.
why: Average heat flux can conceal destructive pulse-by-pulse fatigue, so a wall qualified only on averaged loads can fail in service; reliable qualification is what makes a dry-wall IFE chamber licensable.
key_works: Knaster, Moeslang, and Muroga (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735.

title: Low-inventory IFE target fuel cycle
open: Can an industrial inertial-fusion-energy plant hold its working tritium inventory — spanning target filling, layering, storage, injection, failed shots, and chamber recovery — small enough to be both safe and self-sufficient? Formally, the question is whether a complete consumable-target fuel cycle can be designed whose steady-state tritium inventory and loss rates stay within safety and fuel-self-sufficiency limits.
status: General tritium technology for fusion devices exists, as surveyed in Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*, UKAEA-CCFE-PR(23)99, and Ma (2023), but the logistics of consumable targets introduce distinct inventory and recovery problems not addressed by that base technology.
solved_when: A target fuel-cycle design exists in which tritium inventory and losses through each stage (filling, layering, storage, injection, failed-shot handling, and chamber recovery) are quantified and shown to remain within acceptable safety and fuel-self-sufficiency bounds.
why: Even a high-gain target system can fail fuel-self-sufficiency or violate safety requirements if its tritium inventory and losses are not controlled, so this gap stands between a working target and a deployable power plant.
key_works: Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*, UKAEA-CCFE-PR(23)99; Ma (2023).

title: High-gain repetitive campaign reliability
open: Can an inertial-fusion system sustain a statistically meaningful campaign of high-gain shots at industrially relevant repetition rate — including how it fails, how long recovery takes, and how components degrade over the sequence?
status: Repeated ignition shots have been reported, but this is not equivalent to an industrial-duty campaign. Key works: LLNL (2026), *Meet the Machines That Matter: The Optics Inspector*; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.
solved_when: A high-gain shot campaign is demonstrated with a sample size large enough to yield meaningful statistics on success rate, failure modes, recovery time, and component degradation at relevant repetition.
why: Plant economics depend on successful shots per operating hour, not the best single shot; without demonstrated campaign reliability, no fusion plant cost model is credible.
key_works: LLNL (2026), *Meet the Machines That Matter: The Optics Inspector*; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Target-debris recycling
open: Can the activated, tritium-contaminated debris from inertial-fusion targets and chambers be reprocessed so that useful target and chamber materials are recovered rather than discarded? Formally, the goal is an integrated recycling process whose waste volume, tritium loss, and processing cost all fall within acceptable plant-level limits.
status: IFE development work identifies chamber and fuel-cycle needs (Ma, 2023), and tritium technology status and R&D needs have been surveyed (Glugla et al., 2023 report, *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*), but integrated industrial recycling remains unresolved.
solved_when: A demonstrated processing route exists that recovers target and chamber materials from activated mixed debris with acceptable waste volume, tritium loss, and processing cost.
why: Consumable targets generate continuous material flows, and without a recycling route these flows must be carried as liabilities in the plant economics; including them makes the fuel cycle and cost model complete.
key_works: Ma (2023), IFE research opportunities; Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*.

title: Positive complete-system proton–boron power balance
open: Can a proton–boron-11 fusion system produce more energy than it consumes, once every loss and sustainment cost is counted within a transparently defined boundary?
status: Magnetically confined p–¹¹B reactions were measured in 2023 (Magee et al., *First measurements of p11B fusion in a magnetically confined plasma*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-023-36655-1); this did not establish net energy.
solved_when: A p–¹¹B system is shown to have fusion output exceeding all losses and sustainment costs under a transparently defined complete-system boundary, i.e. positive net energy.
why: It is the decisive test for a widely discussed low-neutron fusion route: without positive complete-system power balance, p–¹¹B remains a laboratory reaction rather than an energy source.
key_works: Magee et al. (2023), *First measurements of p11B fusion in a magnetically confined plasma*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-023-36655-1.

title: Proton–boron reactivity uncertainty
open: Can the divergent measurements of the proton–boron-11 fusion reaction be reconciled into a single dataset with quantified uncertainties, and what do those uncertainties imply for realistic particle distribution functions and reactor energy balance?
status: A 2026 reassessment (Wang et al. (2026), *Revisiting p-11B Fusion: Updated Cross-sections, Reactivity, and Energy Balance*, arXiv:2601.00241) revisits cross-sections, reactivity, and energy balance; uncertainty-sensitive design conclusions remain active.
solved_when: A reconciled, uncertainty-quantified p–¹¹B reaction dataset exists, and its consequences for realistic distribution functions and energy balance have been determined.
why: Small changes in a difficult fuel's reactivity can materially alter feasibility claims for p–¹¹B fusion, so design conclusions built on unquantified data are unreliable.
key_works: Wang et al. (2026), *Revisiting p-11B Fusion: Updated Cross-sections, Reactivity, and Energy Balance*, arXiv:2601.00241.

title: Proton–boron alpha-ash management
open: In a proton–boron-11 fusion scheme, how can the three alpha particles produced by the reaction be removed or put to beneficial use, without degrading the proton and boron fuel distributions on which favorable p–¹¹B performance depends?
status: Alpha-channeling schemes improve modeled balances, but experimentally validated ash handling remains open (Ochs et al. 2022, *Improving the Feasibility of Economical Proton-Boron 11 Fusion via Alpha Channeling with a Hybrid Fast and Thermal Proton Scheme*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevE.106.055215).
solved_when: An experiment demonstrates alpha-ash handling — removal or productive channeling of the three-alpha reaction products — while preserving the fuel distributions required for favorable p–¹¹B performance.
why: Accumulation and thermalization of the reaction products can undermine the proposed nonequilibrium advantages of proton–boron fusion, so ash management is a gate on any credible reactor concept.
key_works: Ochs et al. (2022), *Improving the Feasibility of Economical Proton-Boron 11 Fusion via Alpha Channeling with a Hybrid Fast and Thermal Proton Scheme*, DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevE.106.055215.

title: Nonequilibrium fusion maintenance bounds
open: How much power is genuinely required to sustain a useful non-Maxwellian ion distribution in a fusion plasma, once all proposed exceptions — wave-driven schemes, selective heating — are included? Establish sharp upper and lower bounds on this maintenance power.
status: Rider (1997) established important limitations on nonequilibrium fusion systems under stated assumptions (*Fundamental limitations on plasma fusion systems not in thermodynamic equilibrium*, DOI: 10.1063/1.872556); proposed new architectures must be assessed without ignoring those assumptions.
solved_when: Tight bounds on the power needed to maintain non-Maxwellian distributions are proven, covering the known wave-driven and selective-heating architectures, so that any claimed reactivity advantage can be checked against its true maintenance cost.
why: Apparent reactivity advantages of nonequilibrium fusion schemes can vanish entirely once the power required to maintain the distribution is properly counted, deciding which architectures are physically viable.
key_works: Rider (1997), *Fundamental limitations on plasma fusion systems not in thermodynamic equilibrium*, DOI: 10.1063/1.872556.

title: Practical catalyzed deuterium–deuterium cycles
open: Can a deuterium–deuterium fusion cycle be made practical by productively burning or managing its tritium and helium-3 intermediates, rather than treating them as waste? Formally, this means demonstrating such a cycle with confinement and fuel-processing requirements that are acceptable for an operating plant.
status: The relevant reaction pathways are known, but whether a complete catalyzed D–D cycle can achieve practical gain remains unresolved (Wurzel and Hsu, 2022, *Progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criterion*, DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990).
solved_when: A D–D-based cycle is demonstrated in which the tritium and helium-3 intermediates are productively burned or managed, with confinement and processing requirements shown to be acceptable.
why: Success would free fusion designs from dependence on externally supplied tritium, at the cost of confronting substantially harder plasma conditions.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2022), *Progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criterion*, DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990.

title: Sustainable helium-3 fuel supply
open: Can a credible terrestrial pathway be established for supplying, producing, or recovering helium-3 at a specified deployment scale for D–³He fusion, together with a full accounting of the energy and cost involved?
status: D–³He remains an alternative-fuel concept in fusion research, and fuel availability is treated as a separate, unresolved deployment constraint; no credible supply pathway with energy and cost accounting has been established.
solved_when: A specified D–³He deployment scale has an identified terrestrial supply, production, or recovery pathway whose energy and cost accounting shows it to be viable for that scale.
why: Even a favorable D–³He plasma design cannot be deployed without a realistic fuel supply; helium-3 availability is a distinct and unresolved deployment constraint beyond plasma performance.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2025), *Continuing progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criteria*, arXiv:2505.03834.

title: Polarization survival in fusion fuel
open: Can nuclear-spin polarization of fusion fuel survive the full journey from production through storage, injection, ionization, and confinement in an operating fusion system? Formally, the question is whether useful polarization can be preserved across every stage of fuel handling rather than only in isolated laboratory conditions.
status: Ab initio calculations predict polarized D–T benefits, as in Hupin, Quaglioni, and Navrátil (2019), *Ab initio predictions for polarized deuterium-tritium thermonuclear fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-018-08052-6; however, maintaining the polarization in an operating fusion system remains a distinct, unsolved challenge.
solved_when: A working fusion system demonstrates that fuel retains useful nuclear-spin polarization from production through confinement at the operating conditions where polarized-fusion benefits are predicted.
why: Ab initio calculations predict enhanced cross sections for polarized D–T fuel, but those gains are irrelevant if the polarization is rapidly lost in practice.
key_works: Hupin, Quaglioni, and Navrátil (2019), *Ab initio predictions for polarized deuterium-tritium thermonuclear fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-018-08052-6.

title: Polarized-fusion reaction validation
open: Can we experimentally measure how the reactivity and angular distributions of fusion reactions depend on the spin polarization of the reactants, at the precision needed to validate reactor-relevant nuclear calculations? A definitive answer would supply the polarization-dependent cross sections and product-direction data that current predictive theory provides but experiments have not fully constrained.
status: Predictive calculations exist — including ab initio predictions for polarized deuterium-tritium thermonuclear fusion (Hupin et al., 2019, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-018-08052-6) — but complete experimentally constrained reactor inputs remain open.
solved_when: Polarization-dependent reactivities and angular distributions are measured with precision sufficient to serve as complete, experimentally constrained inputs for reactor-relevant nuclear calculations.
why: If spin polarization enhances reactivity and directs fusion products anisotropically, reactor performance and shielding requirements could both shift materially; without validated data, these effects cannot be reliably designed for.
key_works: Hupin et al. (2019), *Ab initio predictions for polarized deuterium-tritium thermonuclear fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-018-08052-6.

title: Economical muon production
open: Can muons be produced and delivered to a stopping target cheaply enough, in energy terms, that a complete muon-catalyzed fusion cycle yields positive net output?
status: Muon-catalyzed fusion itself is established physics, but production efficiency remains the central obstacle. Yin, Kou, and Chen (2026), *Muon-Catalyzed Nuclear Fusion: Physical Mechanism, Bottleneck Breakthroughs, and an Engineering Pathway* (arXiv:2605.26432), discuss the mechanism and a proposed engineering route.
solved_when: A demonstrated scheme produces and delivers useful stopped muons at an energy cost below what the resulting muon-catalyzed fusion reactions return, giving the full cycle positive net output.
why: Catalysis cannot yield useful power if making the catalyst consumes too much energy; the production step is the energy-system bottleneck for the entire pathway.
key_works: Yin, Kou, and Chen (2026), *Muon-Catalyzed Nuclear Fusion: Physical Mechanism, Bottleneck Breakthroughs, and an Engineering Pathway*, arXiv:2605.26432.

title: Muon sticking and reactivation control
open: Can a muon be made to catalyze substantially more fusion cycles than currently achieved, by experimentally controlling the loss channels — sticking, reactivation, molecular formation, and decay? Formally, the goal is to raise the useful number of fusion cycles per muon through validated experimental control of these processes.
status: The relevant molecular and catalytic processes have been studied directly in experiments, but proposed large improvements in cycle counts should not be treated as achieved records. Key works include Yin et al. (2026), *Muon-Catalyzed Nuclear Fusion: Physical Mechanism, Bottleneck Breakthroughs, and an Engineering Pathway*, arXiv:2605.26432, and Toyama et al. (2026), DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aed3321.
solved_when: A demonstrated, experimentally validated increase in fusion cycles per muon is achieved via control of sticking, reactivation, molecular formation, and decay losses.
why: The muon's finite lifetime caps the number of fusion cycles it can catalyze, so catalyst lifetime is a fundamental determinant of whether muon-catalyzed fusion could work as a complete system.
key_works: Yin et al. (2026), *Muon-Catalyzed Nuclear Fusion: Physical Mechanism, Bottleneck Breakthroughs, and an Engineering Pathway*, arXiv:2605.26432; Toyama et al. (2026), DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aed3321.

title: REBCO performance under fusion irradiation
open: Can REBCO conductors retain their critical current, mechanical integrity, and thermal behavior after sustained exposure to a fusion-reactor neutron spectrum? The question is qualification of these conductors under the relevant neutron spectrum and accumulated dose.
status: The SPARC model-coil program (Hartwig et al., 2024, *The SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil Program*, DOI: 10.1109/TASC.2023.3332613; Knaster et al., 2016, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735) demonstrated high-field engineering, but it did not establish a full fusion-irradiation lifetime for the conductor.
solved_when: REBCO conductor performance — critical current, mechanical integrity, and thermal behavior — is measured and qualified under the relevant neutron spectrum and accumulated fusion-relevant dose.
why: Magnet compactness, the core advantage of high-field REBCO tokamaks, is useful only if the conductor survives the neutron environment.
key_works: Hartwig et al. (2024), *The SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil Program*, DOI: 10.1109/TASC.2023.3332613; Knaster et al. (2016), DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735.

title: REBCO strain and fatigue lifetime
open: Can we predict how REBCO conductors degrade in service, when cyclic strain, transverse stress, thermal cycling, and irradiation act together over a magnet's lifetime? A validated model is sought that forecasts conductor performance loss under these coupled loads rather than treating each mechanism in isolation.
status: Large high-field coils, including the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil (Vieira et al., 2024, *Design, Fabrication, and Assembly of the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil*), have been built and tested, but long-term lifetime under coupled loads remains unaddressed as a separate question.
solved_when: A predictive framework exists that quantifies REBCO conductor degradation under the combined action of cyclic strain, transverse stress, thermal cycling, and irradiation, sufficient to estimate long-term coupled-load lifetime of conductors in operating high-field coils.
why: Local damage in a single conductor segment can compromise or limit the entire magnet system, so reliable lifetime prediction is what stands between demonstrated short-baseline coil performance and confident long-term magnet operation.
key_works: Vieira et al. (2024), *Design, Fabrication, and Assembly of the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil*.

title: Early HTS quench detection
open: Can damaging local disturbances in high-temperature superconducting magnets be detected before hot spots become irreversible, given slow normal-zone propagation and large electromagnetic backgrounds?
status: Quench studies of the SPARC toroidal field model coil (SPARC TFMC collaboration, 2024, *Quench Response of the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil*) provide important evidence, but reactor-wide detection guarantees remain unresolved.
solved_when: A detection method is demonstrated with reactor-wide guarantees of catching local disturbances before they become irreversible hot spots, robust to slow normal-zone propagation and electromagnetic backgrounds.
why: A small undetected defect can destroy expensive stored-energy hardware.
key_works: SPARC TFMC collaboration (2024), *Quench Response of the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil*.

title: Safe HTS energy extraction
open: How can the stored energy of a reactor-scale superconducting magnet be discharged safely, without excessive voltage, hot-spot temperature, mechanical shock, or damage to neighboring coils?
status: Model-coil tests, including the SPARC toroidal field model coil quench response work (Hartwig et al., 2024, DOI: 10.1109/TASC.2023.3332613), address quench response, but complete reactor protection remains a larger unsolved systems problem.
solved_when: A protection scheme is demonstrated that extracts a reactor magnet's full stored energy while keeping voltage, hot-spot temperature, and mechanical loads within acceptable limits and leaving neighboring coils undamaged.
why: High magnetic energy makes the consequences of a protection failure severe, so safe extraction is a prerequisite for reactor-scale magnet operation.
key_works: *Quench Response of the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil* (2024); Hartwig et al. (2024), DOI: 10.1109/TASC.2023.3332613.

title: Low-loss reactor magnet joints
open: Can superconducting magnet joints be engineered so their resistance and thermal behavior stay predictable under production spread, mechanical loading, and irradiation over a reactor's life?
status: High-field coil fabrication, including practical joints, has been demonstrated, e.g. Vieira et al. (2024), *Design, Fabrication, and Assembly of the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil*; however, reactor-lifetime behavior and population-level reliability of such joints remain open.
solved_when: Joint resistance and thermal stability are demonstrably predictable across production variability, mechanical loading, and irradiation on a population and reactor-lifetime scale, not just in individual coil demonstrations.
why: Even small resistive losses at cryogenic temperature carry large electrical penalties, so unpredictable joints directly erode reactor efficiency and reliability.
key_works: Vieira et al. (2024), *Design, Fabrication, and Assembly of the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil*.

title: Radiation-resistant magnet insulation
open: Can an electrical insulation system for superconducting fusion magnets be qualified to survive the full combination of radiation exposure, cryogenic cycling, mechanical stress, and high-voltage transients that a reactor imposes — and if so, what material system and qualification protocol achieve it?
status: Fusion materials research, notably Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735, identifies combined-environment testing as essential, but a universal reactor-qualified insulation system does not follow from current work.
solved_when: An insulating system demonstrates performance under simultaneous radiation, cryogenic cycling, mechanical stress, and high-voltage events, with a documented qualification protocol suitable for reactor magnets.
why: Insulation failure can disable a magnet even when the superconductor itself remains functional, so magnet availability hinges on the insulation, not just the conductor.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735.

title: Acceptable HTS alternating-current losses
open: Can high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets be driven through reactor-relevant ramps, control transients, and pulsed operation while keeping conductor and structural alternating-current losses low enough for practical use, without sacrificing current capacity or quench protection?
status: High-field demonstrations, including the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil Program (Hartwig et al., 2024, DOI: 10.1109/TASC.2023.3332613), establish feasibility of components, but not of every reactor waveform and duty cycle.
solved_when: A conductor and structural design demonstrates acceptable losses across ramps, control transients, and pulsed operation — for every reactor waveform and duty cycle, not just demonstration components — while preserving current capacity and protection.
