why: Dynamic losses during ramping and transients increase required cryogenic power and may constrain the speed and range of plasma control, directly affecting plant efficiency and operability.
key_works: Hartwig et al. (2024), *The SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil Program*, DOI: 10.1109/TASC.2023.3332613.

title: Industrial REBCO quality and scale
open: Can industry supply rare-earth-barium-copper-oxide (REBCO) tape in the very long lengths a fusion power fleet demands, with uniformity, traceability, and repairability verified under reactor-relevant acceptance testing?
status: The SPARC model coil used hundreds of kilometers of tape (Vieira et al. 2024, *Design, Fabrication, and Assembly of the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil*), but scaling that achievement into a reliable fleet supply chain remains a distinct problem.
solved_when: Long conductor lengths can be delivered at fleet scale with verified uniformity, traceability, repairability, and reactor-relevant acceptance testing.
why: Rare local defects that are tolerable in a single magnet become consequential in very long conductor inventories, threatening magnet reliability across a fleet.
key_works: Vieira et al. (2024), *Design, Fabrication, and Assembly of the SPARC Toroidal Field Model Coil*.

title: Fusion-plant cryogenic availability
open: Can a fusion plant's cryogenic system be engineered so that a small cold-system fault no longer forces the shutdown of a much larger generating asset? Concretely, this means demonstrating cryogenic systems whose efficiency, redundancy, maintenance, and recovery times together meet complete-plant availability requirements.
status: Large cryogenic systems exist today, but fusion-specific integrated availability remains a development objective (DOE 2026, *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*; NASEM 2021, *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*).
solved_when: An integrated fusion cryogenic system is demonstrated whose efficiency, redundancy, maintenance, and recovery times satisfy complete-plant availability requirements.
why: Cryogenic faults propagate: a minor failure in the cold system can interrupt a much larger generating asset, so plant availability — and thus economic viability — hinges on this engineering frontier.
key_works: DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*; NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*.

title: Ductile tungsten operating window
open: Can tungsten-based plasma-facing materials be engineered to stay adequately tough through the full life of a fusion device — from fabrication and startup through operation, irradiation, and shutdown? Formally, the goal is a material and processing route whose ductile-to-brittle transition temperature and fracture toughness remain compatible with reactor-relevant thermal and neutron loads over all these phases.
status: Tungsten brittleness and processing were major issues already identified in the 2013 European review (Rieth et al., 2013, *Recent progress in research on tungsten materials for nuclear fusion applications in Europe*, DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2012.08.018); coupled reactor qualification remains open.
solved_when: A tungsten-based plasma-facing material is developed and demonstrated to retain adequate toughness across fabrication, startup, operation, irradiation, and shutdown, and passes coupled reactor qualification.
why: A material can withstand intense heat flux yet still fail by cracking, so toughness — not just thermal capability — is what gates whether tungsten components survive in a reactor.
key_works: Rieth et al. (2013), *Recent progress in research on tungsten materials for nuclear fusion applications in Europe*, DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2012.08.018.

title: Predictive tungsten erosion lifetime
open: Can we predict, from first principles, the net erosion rate and lifetime of tungsten plasma-facing components under realistic reactor conditions? The challenge is to couple mixed-species plasma exposure, transient events, and evolving surface morphology into a single predictive model of erosion and redeposition.
status: Sputtering and redeposition have been studied extensively, notably in Federici et al. (2001), *Plasma-material interactions in current tokamaks and their implications for next step fusion reactors* (DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/41/12/218), but lifetime prediction under combined reactor conditions remains uncertain.
solved_when: A validated predictive capability exists that quantitatively forecasts net tungsten erosion and redeposition — hence component lifetime — under combined realistic conditions of mixed-species plasma exposure, transients, and evolving surface morphology.
why: Erosion determines how long plasma-facing components survive and how much tungsten contaminates the burning plasma, so without reliable prediction neither component design nor core plasma performance can be certified for a reactor.
key_works: Federici et al. (2001), *Plasma-material interactions in current tokamaks and their implications for next step fusion reactors*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/41/12/218.

title: Helium-induced tungsten morphology
open: Under what reactor-relevant exposure conditions do helium bubbles, surface roughening, and tungsten fuzz nucleate and grow in plasma-facing tungsten, and how do these morphologies in turn govern erosion, thermal response, and dust production?
status: Helium-ion-implantation experiments have established the major formation mechanisms, but extrapolation to simultaneous neutron and mixed-plasma loading remains open. Key works include Hofmann et al. (2017), *Helium-Ion-Implantation in Tungsten: Progress towards a…* (full title to be verified), and Rieth et al. (2013), DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2012.08.018.
solved_when: A predictive determination exists of the conditions (temperature, helium flux and fluence, and loading environment) under which bubbles, roughening, and fuzz form, together with a quantitative account of their effect on erosion, thermal response, and dust, validated under simultaneous neutron and mixed-plasma loading.
why: Surface morphology can evolve faster than bulk material properties, so morphology — not bulk degradation — may set the lifetime limits of plasma-facing tungsten components.
key_works: Hofmann et al. (2017), *Helium-Ion-Implantation in Tungsten: Progress towards a…* (full title verify); Rieth et al. (2013), DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2012.08.018.

title: Tritium trapping in damaged tungsten
open: Can we predict how much tritium a tungsten plasma-facing component will actually retain once it carries the full suite of operating damage — neutron-created defects, helium, impurities, temperature cycles, and plasma exposure — rather than idealized material? Formally, the goal is a validated predictive capability, backed by measurement, for tritium inventory in tungsten under realistically coupled conditions.
status: The individual retention mechanisms are established, but predicting tritium inventory under coupled realistic conditions remains uncertain. Key works: Federici et al. (2001), DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/41/12/218; Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*.
solved_when: Tritium retention in tungsten with neutron-induced defects, helium, impurities, temperature cycling, and plasma exposure can be predicted quantitatively and confirmed by measurement under those coupled conditions.
why: Tritium retained in the walls directly reduces fuel availability and creates safety and disposal liabilities for components, so an unpredictable inventory is a reactor-level problem, not a materials detail.
key_works: Federici et al. (2001), DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/41/12/218; Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*.

title: Tungsten recrystallization under service loads
open: Can tungsten plasma-facing components be engineered so that their microstructure — and hence their strength — survives the long, hot, irradiating environment of a working fusion reactor? Formally, the goal is to control recrystallization and grain growth under coupled high-temperature and irradiation service loads over reactor lifetime.
status: Recrystallization is a longstanding concern in tungsten development, and reactor lifetime is understood to depend on the coupled thermal and irradiation history of the material. Key works: Rieth et al. (2013), *Recent progress in research on tungsten materials for nuclear fusion applications in Europe*, DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2012.08.018.
solved_when: A tungsten material and component design is demonstrated to retain acceptable strength throughout reactor lifetime, i.e., recrystallization and grain growth are controlled (slowed, suppressed, or otherwise managed) under the coupled thermal and irradiation history of prolonged service.
why: Initial properties of tungsten components may not survive prolonged operation, so a reactor built with otherwise acceptable materials would lose strength as service progresses.
key_works: Rieth et al. (2013), *Recent progress in research on tungsten materials for nuclear fusion applications in Europe*, DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2012.08.018.

title: Tungsten transmutation effects
open: How do neutron-driven transmutation products reshape the properties of tungsten as a plasma-facing material over a reactor lifetime? A predictive account is needed of how evolving composition alters thermal conductivity, toughness, swelling, and hydrogen retention.
status: Fusion materials research identifies transmutation as a distinctive challenge for tungsten, but full lifetime property evolution remains incompletely validated (Knaster et al. 2016, *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735; Zinkle and Snead 2014, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627).
solved_when: A validated predictive model exists for the evolution of tungsten thermal conductivity, toughness, swelling, and hydrogen retention under neutron-driven composition changes, covering full reactor-lifetime property evolution.
why: Tungsten's composition changes while the reactor operates, so properties measured on the starting material cannot be assumed to hold; without such prediction, component lifetime in fusion devices cannot be reliably assessed.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735; Zinkle and Snead (2014), DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627.

title: Durable tungsten-to-heat-sink joints
open: Can a tungsten-to-heat-sink joint be qualified to survive full reactor duty, where thermal-expansion mismatch, high heat flux, irradiation, cyclic loading, and manufacturing defects all act on the interface at once?
status: Plasma-facing joining technology has advanced, but complete reactor-duty qualification of tungsten-to-heat-sink joints remains unresolved; see Rieth et al. (2013), *Recent progress in research on tungsten materials for nuclear fusion applications in Europe*, DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2012.08.018.
solved_when: A joint design is qualified against all of the listed degradation drivers — thermal-expansion mismatch, high heat flux, irradiation, cyclic loading, and manufacturing defects — under complete reactor-duty conditions.
why: The joint may fail before either bulk material reaches its limit, making interface durability the governing bottleneck for plasma-facing component lifetime.
key_works: Rieth et al. (2013), *Recent progress in research on tungsten materials for nuclear fusion applications in Europe*, DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2012.08.018.

title: Melt-layer motion and resolidification
open: Can we predict how a molten plasma-facing surface moves and deforms under an extreme plasma transient — including melt flow, droplet ejection, electromagnetic body forces, and the final frozen geometry? Formally, this asks for a validated model of the coupled free-surface magnetohydrodynamics and rapid resolidification of metallic plasma-facing components during disruptions and edge-localized modes.
status: Melting and material redistribution are recognized damage mechanisms in plasma-facing components, but validated reactor-scale predictions of these processes remain difficult; see Federici et al. (2001), *Plasma-material interactions in current tokamaks and their implications for next step fusion reactors*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/41/12/218.
solved_when: A model predicts molten surface motion, ejected material, electrical-force effects, and post-event resolidified geometry at reactor scale, with validation against experimental observation.
why: A brief melt event can permanently change the surface geometry of a plasma-facing component, and that defect worsens subsequent heating, degrading the component over repeated transients.
key_works: Federici et al. (2001), *Plasma-material interactions in current tokamaks and their implications for next step fusion reactors*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/41/12/218.

title: Liquid-metal surface contamination control
open: Can a liquid-metal plasma-facing surface be operated in a fusion device without releasing vapor, droplets, or impurities at levels that poison the confined plasma? Formally, the goal is to demonstrate sustained operation of a flowing liquid-metal first wall or divertor surface under reactor-relevant heat and particle fluxes with impurity transport into the plasma held below acceptable limits.
status: Liquid surfaces are recognized as self-renewing, but plasma compatibility remains an independent qualification issue that has not been settled (Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021).
solved_when: A liquid-metal plasma-facing surface is maintained under reactor-relevant conditions with no unacceptable vapor release, droplet ejection, or impurity transport into the confined plasma, as judged by plasma performance remaining within acceptable limits.
why: Liquid surfaces offer self-renewal that could solve solid-wall erosion, but if vapor and droplet fluxes contaminate the plasma, the cure becomes worse than the disease — erosion is traded for a more severe plasma-contamination problem.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Liquid-metal wetting and replenishment
open: Can a liquid-metal plasma-facing surface keep itself uniformly wetted and self-replenished while exposed to magnetic fields, thermal gradients, plasma pressure, and evolving substrate chemistry? Formally, this asks for engineering solutions sustaining a stable, complete liquid film under simultaneous magnetohydrodynamic, thermal, and surface-chemical loads.
status: Liquid-metal engineering studies identify strong coupling among flow, materials, and magnetohydrodynamics, as surveyed by Smolentsev and Abdou (2015), *Dual-Coolant Lead-Lithium blanket: status and R&D in the area of MHD thermofluids and fluid materials interaction*.
solved_when: A liquid-metal wall concept demonstrates uniform wetting and continuous replenishment of dry spots under concurrent magnetic fields, thermal gradients, plasma pressure, and substrate-chemistry evolution.
why: Any local dry spot defeats the protection a nominally liquid-covered wall is supposed to provide, exposing the solid substrate directly to plasma heat and particle flux.
key_works: Smolentsev and Abdou (2015), *Dual-Coolant Lead-Lithium blanket: status and R&D in the area of MHD thermofluids and fluid materials interaction*.

title: Low-temperature RAFM embrittlement
open: Can reduced-activation ferritic–martensitic steels be qualified against neutron-induced hardening and embrittlement at the lower end of their service-temperature range? More precisely, this asks for experimental qualification data establishing how the embrittlement and hardening response of RAFM steels behaves under neutron irradiation at low service temperatures.
status: Radiation-resistant alloy development is mature research, but complete fusion-spectrum qualification remains incomplete (Zinkle and Snead 2014, *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627).
solved_when: RAFM steels are experimentally qualified against neutron-induced hardening and embrittlement across the lower end of their service-temperature range, closing the gap in complete fusion-spectrum qualification.
why: The usable temperature window of these steels constrains reactor cooling design and thermal efficiency, so an unqualified low-temperature limit directly restricts plant design choices.
key_works: Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627.

title: High-temperature RAFM creep strength
open: Can reduced-activation ferritic-martensitic (RAFM) steels be qualified to operate reliably at higher temperatures than currently permitted, without succumbing to excessive creep, microstructural instability, or irradiation-induced degradation?
status: Existing RAFM steels are caught between competing constraints: low-temperature embrittlement caps how far down the window can extend, while high-temperature strength limits cap how far up it can go.
solved_when: A RAFM steel (or extension of an existing grade) demonstrates acceptable creep strength, microstructural stability, and irradiation tolerance throughout an extended upper-temperature operating window, as verified by qualification testing.
why: Raising the coolant temperature improves power-conversion efficiency, but every increment pushes structural materials closer to their creep and stability limits — unlocking the higher window directly enables more economical fusion power plants.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735.

title: Large-scale ODS fabrication and joining
open: Can oxide-dispersion-strengthened (ODS) structural components be manufactured and joined at industrial scale while preserving the dispersoid nanostructure that gives them their radiation tolerance?
status: ODS materials show promising radiation tolerance at the level of small-scale studies (e.g., Lu et al. (2017), PMCID: PMC5228121), and radiation-resistant material design is well surveyed (Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627), but component-scale processing remains a separate, unsolved barrier.
solved_when: A component-scale ODS part is fabricated and joined (e.g., welded) such that the nanostructure and irradiation performance demonstrated at coupon level are retained in the processed regions.
why: Coupon-level properties do not automatically survive welding and industrial fabrication; without joining-compatible processing, ODS alloys cannot become real fusion structural components.
key_works: Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627; Lu et al. (2017), ODS irradiation study, PMCID: PMC5228121.

title: Irradiation-tolerant SiC composite joints
open: Can SiC/SiC composite joints and seals be qualified to survive the full demands of a reactor environment — holding mechanical integrity and hermeticity through thermal cycling and neutron exposure?
status: SiC composites have a substantial nuclear-materials research history (e.g., Katoh et al., 2007; Ozawa et al., 2007), but qualification of joints and components remains the limiting gap.
solved_when: SiC/SiC joints and seals demonstrate, under qualification testing, mechanical integrity, hermeticity, resistance to thermal cycling, and tolerance to neutron exposure.
why: A strong composite is insufficient if its joints leak or fail; the joint, not the base material, is the limiting link for component qualification.
key_works: Katoh et al. (2007), *Assessment of Silicon Carbide Composites for Advanced Salt-Cooled Reactors*; Ozawa et al. (2007), *Mechanical properties of advanced SiC/SiC composites…* (full title verify).

title: Irradiated SiC thermal conductivity
open: Can we predict — and by design preserve — the thermal conductivity of silicon carbide composites as fusion-neutron irradiation accumulates defects, evolves interfaces, and produces transmutation gases?
status: Irradiation effects on SiC have been measured only in selected conditions; full thermal qualification of fusion components remains open.
solved_when: A validated model, confirmed by measurement across the relevant irradiation conditions, predicts heat conduction in SiC composites throughout component lifetime, completing the thermal qualification of fusion components.
why: Loss of thermal conductivity can cause overheating of components even when their mechanical strength remains acceptable.
key_works: Katoh et al. (2007), *Assessment of Silicon Carbide Composites for Advanced Salt-Cooled Reactors*; Knaster et al. (2016), DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735.

title: Vanadium-alloy impurity tolerance
open: What levels of oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, and corrosion products can vanadium alloys tolerate without degrading, under realistic fabrication and service conditions?
status: Alternative low-activation alloys remain research candidates; environmental sensitivity complicates practical qualification (Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735).
solved_when: Quantitative acceptance limits for oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen, and corrosion-product content are established and shown to hold under realistic fabrication and service conditions for vanadium alloys.
why: Vanadium alloys have attractive intrinsic properties that can be lost through trace contamination, so without defined impurity tolerances they cannot be practically qualified for fusion service.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735.

title: Helium–hydrogen–displacement synergy
open: How does simultaneous exposure to helium implantation, hydrogen implantation, and displacement damage produce material degradation that differs from what single-effect or sequentially applied exposures would predict — and can the coupled response be quantified and extrapolated to fusion service conditions?
status: Radiation-resistant design principles are established, as summarized by Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy* (DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627), but reproducing and extrapolating coupled fusion damage remains a central qualification issue.
solved_when: A quantitative characterization of the coupled helium–hydrogen–displacement damage response exists that reproduces fusion-relevant damage under experimental conditions and supports extrapolation to service behavior, demonstrating where and by how much it deviates from the sum of separate exposures.
why: Single-effect tests can systematically mispredict service behavior, so qualification of fusion structural materials without accounting for the coupling risks unsafe or overly conservative design margins.
key_works: Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627.

title: Microstructure-to-component lifetime prediction
open: Can we predict the lifetime of a fusion component from first knowledge of its microstructure — tracing how defect production and microstructural evolution under irradiation determine engineering properties and, ultimately, failure, with uncertainties quantified at every step? Formally, this asks for a validated predictive chain linking defect kinetics to component-scale failure with quantified uncertainty.
status: Multiscale methods exist, but the complete predictive chain remains incompletely validated.
solved_when: A complete, validated predictive chain exists from defect production and microstructural evolution through engineering properties to component failure, with uncertainty quantified end-to-end.
why: Without this connection, atomistic insight cannot reliably reduce qualification time for fusion materials.
key_works: Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627.

title: Irradiation creep–fatigue–fracture interaction
open: Can we predict how long a fusion structural component survives when irradiation damage, cyclic thermal stress, creep, and crack growth act on it at the same time? The goal is a validated lifetime rule that captures the genuine coupling of these mechanisms rather than their separate contributions.
status: Individual mechanisms have each been studied separately, but fusion components require combined-load extrapolation beyond simple damage summation, and no validated interaction rule yet exists. Key works include Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735, and Rieth et al. (2013), DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2012.08.018.
solved_when: A lifetime rule is developed and validated for structures under simultaneous irradiation, cyclic thermal stress, creep, and crack growth, going beyond simple damage summation and usable for combined-load extrapolation to fusion components.
why: Maintenance intervals for fusion devices can only be set safely if they reflect how these failure mechanisms actually interact, rather than how each behaves in isolation.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735; Rieth et al. (2013), DOI: 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2012.08.018.

title: Corrosion under simultaneous irradiation
open: How does simultaneous irradiation alter corrosion, mass transfer, and cracking in blanket structural materials exposed to flowing liquid coolant? In other words, what happens when radiation damage and flowing-corrosive-chemistry attack the same material at the same time?
status: Flowing-liquid and radiation studies exist separately; their coupling remains difficult to reproduce (Smolentsev and Abdou, 2015; Abdou et al., 2015, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021).
solved_when: Experiments successfully reproduce the coupled condition — structural materials under simultaneous irradiation and flowing coolant — with measurements of corrosion, mass transfer, and cracking attributable to the coupling.
why: Radiation can change both the material and the chemistry attacking it, so results from separate flowing-liquid and radiation studies cannot simply be combined; fusion blanket design depends on knowing the coupled behavior.
key_works: Smolentsev and Abdou (2015), *Dual-Coolant Lead-Lithium blanket: status and R&D in the area of MHD thermofluids and fluid materials interaction*; Abdou et al. (2015), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Reliable fusion-spectrum irradiation sources
open: How can we build an irradiation source that reproduces the fusion neutron spectrum at sustained high flux, with enough test volume and dependable temperature control for materials qualification?
status: Materials reviews identify this infrastructure gap (Knaster et al. 2016, *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735; DOE 2026, *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*); accelerator-driven source concepts address it but do not eliminate all qualification needs.
solved_when: A facility exists that delivers sustained high-flux irradiation with a fusion-representative spectrum, adequate usable test volume, and reliable specimen temperature control.
why: Without a representative source, structural-component lifetime in fusion reactors cannot be established from irradiation data alone.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Surrogate-irradiation equivalence
open: When can irradiation by ions, fission neutrons, or accelerators stand in for fusion-neutron exposure? The problem is to establish equivalence conditions with explicit error bounds and the regimes where each surrogate fails.
status: Surrogates are used to accelerate research, but differences in spectrum, dose rate, gas production, and damage geometry remain consequential, per Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627.
solved_when: A framework exists that states, with explicit error bounds, under which conditions ion, fission-neutron, and accelerator exposures predict fusion-neutron behavior, and identifies the failure conditions of each surrogate.
why: Reliable equivalence would greatly accelerate materials qualification for fusion; unjustified equivalence could invalidate qualification altogether.
key_works: Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627.

title: Small-specimen-to-component transfer
open: Can we infer the toughness, fatigue, and failure distributions of a full reactor component from the tiny specimens that fit inside high-flux irradiation volumes? A formal answer would give a statistically validated scaling rule mapping small-specimen measurements to component-scale property distributions.
status: The limited irradiation volume available in high-flux facilities makes small-specimen testing attractive, but scale transfer remains an open qualification problem; see Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735.
solved_when: A transfer methodology exists whose predicted component-scale toughness, fatigue, and failure distributions are validated against full-scale component behavior, accounting for size effects in fracture and statistical weakest-link scaling.
why: Reactor components cannot all be irradiated at full scale before deployment, so qualification of fusion materials hinges on the ability to extrapolate reliably from small specimens.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735.

title: Fusion gas-production nuclear data
open: How accurately can we know the helium- and hydrogen-production cross-sections of the structural and functional materials that matter for fusion? The goal is to reduce the residual discrepancies and uncertainties in these gas-production data, which current evaluations still leave unresolved.
status: The 2024 FENDL paper (Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*, DOI: 10.1016/j.nds.2024.01.001; arXiv:2311.10063) identifies remaining gas-production differences and the associated validation needs.
solved_when: The helium- and hydrogen-production cross-sections for important structural and functional materials are re-evaluated or re-measured such that the discrepancies among evaluations and the quoted uncertainties are reduced to a level that satisfies fusion validation needs, as identified in the 2024 FENDL assessment.
why: Gas production drives helium embrittlement, swelling, and the establishment of irradiation equivalence, so uncertain cross-sections propagate directly into unreliable predictions of material degradation and component qualification.
key_works: Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*, DOI: 10.1016/j.nds.2024.01.001; arXiv:2311.10063.

title: Activation and decay-data uncertainty
open: Can we produce activation and decay nuclear-data libraries whose uncertainties — including full covariance information — are validated well enough to be trusted inputs for fusion facility safety assessments?
status: FENDL and associated activation-data efforts exist, but validation and covariance gaps are explicitly documented as remaining open (Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*, DOI: 10.1016/j.nds.2024.01.001; WANDA nuclear-data workshop (2024)).
solved_when: A validated activation and decay dataset with covariances exists that is sufficient for waste classification, maintenance dose estimation, and accident analysis.
why: Data uncertainty propagates directly into safety, maintenance, and disposal decisions, so unquantified gaps today translate into unquantified margins in real facility operation.
key_works: Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*, DOI: 10.1016/j.nds.2024.01.001; WANDA nuclear-data workshop (2024).

title: Streaming through realistic penetrations
open: Can we experimentally validate neutron and gamma transport through the complex penetrations of a real fusion facility — ports, ducts, gaps, joints, and evolving maintenance configurations — rather than idealized geometries? In formal terms, the question is whether current transport predictions hold up against measurements in realistic three-dimensional streaming paths.
status: Transport codes and libraries are established, notably including FENDL (Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*, DOI: 10.1016/j.nds.2024.01.001), but realistic three-dimensional benchmark coverage remains incomplete.
solved_when: Predicted neutron and gamma dose and damage rates along realistic penetration geometries are confirmed by experimental benchmarks covering complex, fully three-dimensional configurations, closing the gap left by incomplete existing coverage.
why: Small penetrations can dominate local dose and magnet damage, so unvalidated streaming predictions translate directly into uncertainty in worker safety and component lifetimes.
key_works: Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*, DOI: 10.1016/j.nds.2024.01.001.

title: Better-than-dpa damage metrics
open: Can we construct a practical irradiation exposure descriptor that predicts changes in engineering properties more reliably than total displacements per atom alone? Formally, the aim is a damage metric — incorporating physics beyond scalar dpa, such as defect survival, gas production, and microstructural response — that demonstrably outperforms dpa as a predictor of material property degradation.
status: The radiation-resistant materials community, as summarized by Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627, recognizes that defect survival, gas production, and microstructure matter beyond a scalar exposure measure; no such improved metric is established.
solved_when: A quantitative descriptor (or set of descriptors) computable for realistic irradiation environments is shown, across experiments and materials, to correlate with engineering property changes more accurately than dpa totals, enabling improved cross-experiment comparison and lifetime extrapolation.
why: Without it, experiment comparison and component lifetime extrapolation rest on a scalar measure known to miss key physics; a better metric would make qualification of fusion materials more predictive and transferable.
key_works: Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*, DOI: 10.1146/annurev-matsci-070813-113627.

title: Joint irradiation-property benchmark database
open: Can we assemble a single traceable database that links composition, processing, irradiation history, microstructure, and measured engineering properties — including negative results? The goal is comprehensive, interoperable linkage with reproducible uncertainty quantification across the fusion materials community.
status: Materials databases already exist; the gap is not the absence of all data but the lack of comprehensive interoperable linkage and reproducible uncertainty across records.
solved_when: A publicly available benchmark database exists that records composition, processing, irradiation history, microstructure, and measured engineering properties for a substantial body of irradiated materials, includes negative results, and supports interoperable querying and reproducible uncertainty statements.
why: Fragmented records obstruct materials qualification for fusion devices and prevent machine-learning models from generalizing across datasets; a linked benchmark database would make both feasible.
key_works: Hosemann et al. (2018), *Materials selection for nuclear applications*; Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*.

title: Uncertainty-qualified tritium breeding margin
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Can an as-built fusion plant, with all of its real-world imperfections, actually produce enough recoverable tritium to fuel itself? Formally, demonstrate complete fuel self-sufficiency for a fully configured plant after accounting for ports, structures, losses, decay, reserve requirements, and uncertainty.
status: Fuel-self-sufficiency analyses (Abdou et al., 2021, *Physics and technology considerations for the deuterium–tritium fuel cycle and conditions for tritium fuel self sufficiency*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/abbf35) show why a nominal breeding ratio above one is insufficient.
solved_when: A complete plant design — including ports, internal structures, and all tritium losses, decay, and reserve inventory requirements — is shown to achieve a recoverable tritium breeding margin above one, robust under quantified uncertainties.
why: A plant can consume its fuel supply despite an attractive idealized neutronics result, so only an uncertainty-qualified, as-built accounting establishes true operational viability.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2021), *Physics and technology considerations for the deuterium–tritium fuel cycle and conditions for tritium fuel self sufficiency*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/abbf35.

title: Integral blanket breeding validation
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Can a full breeding blanket be validated experimentally under realistic, coupled reactor conditions — neutron multiplication, tritium breeding, heat removal, tritium extraction, and structural response acting together rather than in isolation?
status: Blanket concepts and component-level studies are extensive, but integrated validation in a reactor-relevant environment remains a major gap; Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021, documents this R&D shortfall.
solved_when: An integral experiment demonstrates blanket performance with neutron multiplication, breeding, heat removal, extraction, and structural effects simultaneously coupled, and its measurements confirm (or correct) complete-blanket breeding predictions.
why: Separate subsystem tests can miss coupling interactions that reduce recoverable tritium breeding, so integrated validation is needed before blanket designs can be trusted for a reactor.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Three-dimensional liquid-metal MHD pressure drop
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Can pressure loss and flow maldistribution in liquid-metal breeding blankets be predicted from first principles through realistic three-dimensional geometries — manifolds, bends, field gradients, and electrically coupled channels — rather than extrapolated from prototypical tests? In formal terms, the goal is a validated theory-scale predictive capability for 3D magnetohydrodynamic duct flow with full electrical coupling.
status: Prototypical experiments and modeling exist, notably Rhodes et al. (2021) (*Pressure drop in a prototypical 3D magnetohydrodynamic…*, OSTI:1773976) and the review by Smolentsev et al. (2017) (*Review of recent MHD activities for liquid metal blankets in the US*), but general reactor-scale predictive accuracy remains incomplete.
solved_when: A predictive model reproduces measured pressure drop and flow distribution in prototypical 3D MHD experiments (e.g., Rhodes et al. 2021) and extends with reactor-scale accuracy to coupled-channel blanket configurations.
why: Excessive pressure drop drives up pumping power and structural loads, so without reliable prediction the blanket design cannot be optimized or qualified with confidence.
key_works: Rhodes et al. (2021), *Pressure drop in a prototypical 3D magnetohydrodynamic…* (full title verify), OSTI:1773976; Smolentsev et al. (2017), *Review of recent MHD activities for liquid metal blankets in the US*.

title: Flow-channel-insert lifetime
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Can an electrically insulating insert survive the full coupled environment of a liquid-metal breeding blanket channel — irradiation, steep thermal gradients, and contact with flowing coolant — without cracking or admitting leakage currents? In other words, does there exist an insert design that remains electrically and mechanically intact over a blanket-relevant lifetime?
status: Inserts are a proposed route to reduce liquid-metal MHD losses, but their coupled-environment lifetime remains unresolved; see Smolentsev and Abdou (2015), *Dual-Coolant Lead-Lithium blanket: status and R&D in the area of MHD thermofluids and fluid materials interaction*.
solved_when: An insulating insert design is qualified against all of the identified degradation mechanisms — cracking, irradiation damage, thermal-gradient stress, leakage currents, and coolant infiltration — with demonstrated retention of its insulating function under coupled conditions.
why: A single small insulation failure can change the entire hydraulic behavior of a blanket channel, so insert reliability gates the viability of this route to reducing liquid-metal MHD losses.
key_works: Smolentsev and Abdou (2015), *Dual-Coolant Lead-Lithium blanket: status and R&D in the area of MHD thermofluids and fluid materials interaction*.

title: Lead–lithium corrosion and mass transfer
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Can we predict how flowing lead–lithium corrodes and redistributes material over the lifetime of a reactor — specifically the coupled dissolution, deposition, plugging, and composition changes under strong magnetic and thermal gradients?
status: Dedicated MHD and corrosion facilities exist and support study of these effects, including numerical work such as Saeidi and Smolentsev (2014) on magnetic-field effects on corrosion of ferritic/martensitic steel in turbulent PbLi flow; however, extrapolation to reactor-duration exposures remains uncertain.
solved_when: A validated predictive capability exists whose extrapolations to reactor-relevant exposure durations, under combined magnetic and thermal gradients, are quantitatively confirmed by dedicated MHD and corrosion facility experiments.
why: Corrosion can thin load-bearing structures to failure while dissolved material deposits elsewhere and blocks remote parts of the loop, so uncertainty here directly constrains blanket design lifetimes.
key_works: Saeidi and Smolentsev (2014), *Numerical study of the effect of a magnetic field on corrosion of ferritic/martensitic steel in a turbulent PbLi flow*.

title: FLiBe redox and impurity control
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Can the chemistry of a molten FLiBe breeding blanket be actively controlled so that corrosion stays within acceptable limits while tritium extraction remains effective, even as the salt is continuously irradiated and exchanges material with its surroundings? Formally, this asks for a control scheme (with sensing and actuation) that holds the salt's redox state and impurity inventory inside a window compatible with structural materials and tritium removal over blanket-relevant timescales.
status: Salt blanket concepts are established design options, but their complete chemistry-control envelope remains unresolved. Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021, frame this among the key blanket R&D needs; related directions include molten-salt electrochemistry and online chemical-state estimation.
solved_when: A demonstrated chemistry-control strategy — measurement plus active redox/impurity management — maintains a salt state that simultaneously limits corrosion of structural materials and sustains tritium extraction under sustained irradiation and material exchange.
why: Breeding performance, corrosion rate, tritium removal, and maintenance burden all depend on the same, continuously evolving salt chemistry, so without such control the entire liquid-blanket concept degrades in service.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Tritium transport in molten-salt blankets
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: How does tritium actually move through a molten-salt breeding blanket under realistic conditions? A predictive treatment is needed for tritium speciation, solubility, diffusion, trapping, and interfacial transfer across realistic salt chemistry and irradiation environments.
status: Tritium transport models exist, but outer-cycle extraction and inventory predictions remain sensitive to uncertain properties (Humrickhouse et al. (2017), *Tritium aspects of the fusion nuclear science facility*; Yang et al. (2026), arXiv:2604.19647).
solved_when: Measured values and validated models of tritium speciation, solubility, diffusion, trapping, and interfacial transfer exist over realistic salt chemistry and irradiation conditions, sufficient to make outer-cycle extraction and inventory predictions insensitive to the remaining property uncertainties.
why: Slow tritium recovery can leave an otherwise adequate breeder fuel-starved, so reliable transport data directly bounds the viability of a molten-salt blanket concept.
key_works: Humrickhouse et al. (2017), *Tritium aspects of the fusion nuclear science facility*; Yang et al. (2026), arXiv:2604.19647.

title: Ceramic-breeder tritium-release kinetics
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Can we predict how much tritium escapes from a ceramic breeder as its microstructure evolves under irradiation, thermal gradients, and purge-gas chemistry? In other words, what quantitative model links release kinetics to the changing structure of the material itself?
status: Solid-breeder concepts have extensive development history, and it is established that recoverable breeding depends on release kinetics rather than neutron production alone (Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021).
solved_when: A predictive model reproduces measured tritium release from ceramic breeders under realistic irradiation, temperature-gradient, and purge-gas conditions, accounting for microstructural evolution.
why: Tritium trapped in the breeder material cannot fuel the plasma, so unmodeled retention directly erodes the tritium breeding balance of a reactor.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Breeder-pebble bed evolution
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Can we predict how an irradiated ceramic breeder pebble bed evolves over its lifetime — how the pebbles crush, rearrange, and sinter, and how contact conductance and purge-gas flow change as a result? Formally, this asks for a coupled mechanical–thermal model of long-term bed evolution under irradiation and thermal cycling.
status: Pebble-bed designs are established blanket candidates, but the coupled long-term mechanical and thermal evolution of the beds remains uncertain. Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021, frame this among the key blanket/first-wall R&D needs on the path to DEMO.
solved_when: A predictive model reproduces the coupled evolution of crushing, rearrangement, sintering, contact conductance, and purge-flow changes in an irradiated breeder bed over blanket-relevant lifetimes.
why: A bed can silently lose cooling or tritium release performance without any obvious bulk structural failure, so lifetime predictions of blanket behavior depend on resolving this evolution.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Neutron-multiplier material lifetime
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Can neutron-multiplier materials for breeding blankets be qualified to survive the full range of operating threats they will face — swelling, gas generation, chemical reactivity, and thermal cycling — while meeting end-of-life recovery or disposal requirements?
status: Current multiplier choices improve breeding performance but each introduces material-specific lifetime and safety tradeoffs that remain unresolved (Abdou et al. (2015), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021; Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*).
solved_when: A multiplier material is demonstrated to remain serviceable under blanket-relevant irradiation and thermal-cycling conditions, with acceptable swelling and gas-generation behavior, manageable chemical reactivity, and a defined recovery or disposal pathway.
why: Multipliers improve tritium breeding, but that benefit only counts if the material stays serviceable and safe over its lifetime; otherwise blanket designs built on them fail in practice.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021; Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*.

title: Low-parasitic-power helium cooling
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Can a helium-cooled fusion blanket reject the full blanket heat load without its own pumping power, pressure-boundary stress, leakage, and heat-transfer margins becoming unacceptable?
status: Helium-cooled blanket concepts exist, but the full efficiency–materials–pressure tradeoff remains design-limiting, as surveyed in Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.
solved_when: A helium cooling design is demonstrated that removes the blanket heat load while keeping pumping power, pressure-boundary stress, leakage, and heat-transfer margins all within acceptable limits.
why: High pumping power in helium loops can consume a substantial share of the plant's generated electricity, directly eroding net output.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Blanket transient survivability
subfield: Breeding blankets, liquid metals, and molten salts
open: Can a fusion breeding blanket survive its transients — loss of flow, pressure excursions, plasma transients, and electromagnetic forcing — without a cascading failure of the blanket system?
status: A 2025 study by Smolentsev explicitly examines transient-plasma effects on liquid-metal blanket flows, but integrated accident qualification for the blanket remains broader and unaddressed.
solved_when: A blanket concept is shown, through integrated transient analysis or experiment, to respond acceptably to loss-of-flow, pressure excursions, plasma transients, and electromagnetic forcing, with no cascading blanket failure — in effect, achieving integrated accident qualification beyond steady-state thermal adequacy.
why: Demonstrating steady-state thermal adequacy does not establish safe transient behavior; without transient survivability, a single upset could cascade into blanket failure.
key_works: Smolentsev (2025), *A model and assessments of the effect of transient plasma on liquid metal flows in a fusion blanket*.

title: Startup tritium for a growing fleet
open: Can a credible, timed supply of startup tritium be established for multiple simultaneous fusion plants, once competing demand, radioactive decay, existing reserves, and breeding ramp-up are all accounted for?
status: The supply problem was analyzed explicitly by Pearson, Antoniazzi, and Nuttall (2018) in *Tritium supply and use: a key issue for the development of nuclear fusion energy* (DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2018.04.090), who showed that individual plant self-sufficiency does not automatically imply fleet growth.
solved_when: A supply schedule exists that specifies, with timing, how multiple plants' startup tritium demands can be met from reserves and breeding ramp-up under decay and competing demand.
why: Fusion plants could be technically ready to operate yet never receive their initial fuel inventory, blocking deployment regardless of engineering success.
key_works: Pearson, Antoniazzi, and Nuttall (2018), *Tritium supply and use: a key issue for the development of nuclear fusion energy*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2018.04.090.

title: High effective tritium burn fraction
open: Can a fusion power plant be made to burn a substantially larger fraction of the tritium it injects, without degrading plasma performance or making recycling of unburned fuel unmanageable?
status: Fuel-cycle analyses, including Abdou et al. (2021), *Physics and technology considerations for the deuterium–tritium fuel cycle and conditions for tritium fuel self sufficiency* (DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/abbf35), show that low burn fraction drives throughput and inventory requirements.
solved_when: A fuel-cycle design demonstrates increased effective tritium burn fraction while plasma performance is maintained and recycling stays manageable; no specific quantitative targets beyond this are stated in the record.
why: Low burn fraction forces high tritium throughput and large inventories, so improving burn efficiency relaxes multiple downstream fuel-cycle systems simultaneously.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2021), *Physics and technology considerations for the deuterium–tritium fuel cycle and conditions for tritium fuel self sufficiency*, DOI: 10.1088/1741-4326/abbf35.

title: Fast, low-inventory isotope separation
open: Can hydrogen isotopes be separated at the throughput a fusion power plant requires while keeping the tritium held up in the separation system small? Formally, the goal is a separation process that meets required throughput under tight constraints on inventory holdup, energy use, contamination sensitivity, and recovery time.
status: Separation technologies exist today, but the inventory and availability requirements of a power plant remain demanding. Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*, UKAEA-CCFE-PR(23)99, surveys the current state and outstanding R&D needs.
solved_when: An isotope separation technology is demonstrated that achieves required power-plant throughput while simultaneously minimizing tritium holdup inventory, energy consumption, contamination sensitivity, and recovery time to levels compatible with plant availability requirements.
why: Tritium tied up in the separation system is inventory that can neither power the plant nor seed new plants, so slow or inventory-heavy separation directly erodes fuel-cycle economics and fleet growth.
key_works: Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*, UKAEA-CCFE-PR(23)99.

title: Durable tritium permeation barriers
open: Can tritium permeation barriers be qualified to survive the full range of fusion-relevant service conditions — radiation, corrosion, thermal cycling, and mechanical defects — while keeping tritium permeation low enough for practical operation, and can damaged barriers be repaired or their function restored?
status: Barrier and membrane approaches exist, but their durability under coupled environments remains unresolved; see Humrickhouse et al. (2017), *Tritium aspects of the fusion nuclear science facility*, and Glugla et al. (2023 report). Related work concerns selective membranes under damage.
solved_when: A barrier material or coating is demonstrated to maintain sufficiently low tritium permeation under coupled radiation, corrosion, thermal-cycling, and defect conditions, with a credible repair or mitigation path.
why: Excessive permeation directly drives tritium fuel loss, increases worker exposure, and contaminates power-conversion systems, so unqualified barriers are a blocking issue for practical tritium fuel cycles.
key_works: Humrickhouse et al. (2017), *Tritium aspects of the fusion nuclear science facility*; Glugla et al. (2023 report).

title: Tritium-isotopologue property database
open: Establish experimentally constrained thermophysical and transport properties for tritium-bearing mixtures over fuel-cycle operating conditions. A second sentence may sharpen it: the target is a validated property database covering mixtures, not just pure isotopologues, with quantified uncertainties across the relevant operating range.
status: A 2023 study (Lee et al., *Thermodynamic property calculation for pure component hydrogen isotopologues considering tritium processing technologies in fusion fuel cycle*, *Fusion Engineering and Design* 197, 114059) calculates pure-isotopologue thermodynamic properties; broader mixtures and uncertainty validation remain open.
solved_when: Thermophysical and transport properties of tritium-bearing mixtures are available for fuel-cycle operating conditions, anchored to experimental data and accompanied by validated uncertainty bounds.
why: Process designs can be sensitive to extrapolated hydrogen-isotope properties, so fuel-cycle equipment designed on unvalidated data risks off-spec performance or failure.
key_works: Lee et al. (2023), *Thermodynamic property calculation for pure component hydrogen isotopologues considering tritium processing technologies in fusion fuel cycle*, *Fusion Engineering and Design* 197, 114059.

title: Real-time whole-plant tritium accounting
open: Can a fusion plant continuously locate and quantify its tritium inventory — including material held in walls and other inaccessible reservoirs — with uncertainty small enough to support fuel management, leak detection, and safety decisions in real time?
status: Accounting methods exist, but distributed retention and inaccessible inventories complicate achieving a closed real-time balance.
solved_when: A method exists that closes the whole-plant tritium balance in real time, with quantified uncertainty on distributed retention and otherwise inaccessible inventories sufficient for fuel management, leak detection, and safety decisions.
why: An unexplained inventory deficit is ambiguous: it may indicate fuel loss, hidden retention, or leakage, and without resolved accounting these cases cannot be distinguished in time for operational or safety response.
key_works: Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*; Yang et al. (2026), arXiv:2604.19647.

title: Rapid accident detritiation
open: Can a detritiation system reliably clean up a realistic accidental tritium release spanning all the forms it actually takes — water, contaminated surfaces, airborne aerosols, and equipment that cannot be reached? Formally, this asks for demonstrated, reproducible cleanup performance under representative accident transients rather than idealized single-phase releases.
status: Detritiation technology itself exists, but its transient performance under plant-specific accident conditions and post-accident recovery remain open qualification problems. Key context: Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*, UKAEA-CCFE-PR(23)99.
solved_when: Reliable detritiation is demonstrated after representative releases covering water, surfaces, aerosols, and inaccessible equipment, with plant-specific transient performance and recovery qualified for the plant in question.
why: The radiological consequences of a release and how quickly a plant can restart both hinge directly on how fast and completely cleanup proceeds.
key_works: Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*, UKAEA-CCFE-PR(23)99.

title: Long-life tritium storage and getters
open: Can tritium storage materials and systems be qualified to remain safe and effective over a full plant lifetime despite cycling, contamination, aging, helium-3 buildup from radioactive decay, and abnormal thermal conditions?
status: Tritium storage itself is established technology, but plant-scale lifecycle and inventory optimization remain unresolved; see Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*, and Pearson et al. (2018), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2018.04.090.
solved_when: Storage materials and systems are qualified against all of the listed degradation mechanisms — cycling, contamination, aging, helium-3 buildup, and abnormal thermal conditions — at plant-relevant scale and lifecycle duration.
why: Storage serves both as the operational buffer that smooths fuel supply in the tritium fuel cycle and as a concentrated tritium hazard, so unqualified long-life storage limits both plant availability and safety.
key_works: Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*; Pearson et al. (2018), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2018.04.090.

title: Continuous fusion exhaust pumping
open: Can fusion exhaust — fuel, helium ash, impurities, and reactive species — be pumped continuously at reactor-scale throughput while keeping the tritium inventory low and avoiding frequent regeneration shutdowns? Formally, the goal is an exhaust pumping system that sustains DT power-plant flow conditions with high availability and minimal trapped inventory.
status: Advanced DT exhaust pumping was reviewed in 2014 (Day and Giegerich, *Development of Advanced Exhaust Pumping Technology for a DT Fusion Power Plant*, DOI: 10.1109/TPS.2014.2307435); continuous, high-availability integration of such pumping remains an open development problem.
solved_when: A pumping system demonstrates reactor-throughput removal of fuel, helium, impurities, and reactive species with low inventory and little interruption for regeneration, integrated with continuous high-availability plant operation.
why: Pumping limits propagate directly into confinement performance, fuel inventory, and plant uptime, so exhaust pumping is a bottleneck on the whole reactor system.
key_works: Day and Giegerich (2014), *Development of Advanced Exhaust Pumping Technology for a DT Fusion Power Plant*, DOI: 10.1109/TPS.2014.2307435.

title: Minimum diagnostic set for safe burn control
open: Which measurements are necessary and sufficient to control a burning plasma safely when diagnostic access is strongly restricted? Formally, this asks for an observability characterization of the burning-plasma state under reactor-relevant shielding and lifetime constraints.
status: Research machines rely on extensive diagnostics, but observability of a reactor plasma under shielding and lifetime constraints remains unresolved; related threads include observability bounds and sensor-selection complexity (Loarte et al. (2025), ITR-25-005; Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*).
solved_when: A characterization exists of the minimal diagnostic set that renders all dangerous plasma states observable, along with an argument that removing any element of that set destroys observability, under reactor-relevant access constraints.
why: A controller cannot compensate for fundamentally unobservable dangerous states, so without such a set the safety case for burn control rests on unverified assumptions.
key_works: Loarte et al. (2025), ITR-25-005; Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*.

title: Three-dimensional neutron-source reconstruction
open: Can the three-dimensional shape and motion of a fusion neutron source be reconstructed from sparse neutron measurements and complementary diagnostics, with a rigorous quantification of the uncertainty in the result? Formally, this asks for an inverse-problem method whose output is a calibrated posterior over source geometry and flow rather than a single point estimate.
status: Three-dimensional multimodal reconstruction has advanced in inertial confinement fusion, including 2024–2025 studies (Kunimune et al. 2024, DOI: 10.1063/5.0205656; Churnetski et al. 2025, DOI: 10.1063/5.0268312), but ambiguity from sparse viewing angles remains unresolved.
solved_when: A reconstruction method exists that recovers the 3D source shape and motion from sparse views, resolves the remaining sparse-view ambiguity, and delivers uncertainty estimates that are validated as calibrated against ground truth or independent diagnostics.
why: Without it, apparent changes in inferred temperature or yield may in fact be artifacts of source geometry or bulk flow, corrupting the interpretation of implosion and plasma measurements.
key_works: Kunimune et al. (2024), *3D reconstruction of an inertial-confinement fusion implosion with neural networks using multiple heterogeneous data sources*, DOI: 10.1063/5.0205656; Churnetski et al. (2025), DOI: 10.1063/5.0268312.

title: Radiation-hard optical diagnostics
open: Can optical diagnostic systems — their transmission, calibration, alignment, and detector performance — be maintained through reactor-level neutron exposure and contamination over a power-plant lifetime? Formally, the goal is an engineering design that preserves diagnostic fidelity under neutron fluences and contamination levels representative of operating reactors rather than laboratory conditions.
status: ITER research plans still retain diagnostic development as an open need; power-plant lifetime requirements are more demanding than what laboratory access can provide, so the problem remains unresolved at reactor scale (Loarte et al. (2025), *Required R&D in existing fusion facilities to support the new baseline ITER Research Plan*, ITR-25-005).
solved_when: An optical diagnostic architecture demonstrates sustained transmission, calibration, alignment, and detector performance under reactor-relevant neutron exposure and contamination, meeting power-plant lifetime requirements rather than the shorter-duration access typical of laboratory facilities.
why: Gradual diagnostic drift can silently corrupt control and safety decisions, so without hardened, self-calibrating optics a reactor's protection and control systems may act on corrupted data without any visible failure.
key_works: Loarte et al. (2025), *Required R&D in existing fusion facilities to support the new baseline ITER Research Plan*, ITR-25-005.

title: Long-duration microwave diagnostic calibration
open: Can a microwave diagnostic maintain accurate density and magnetic-field inference over long-duration reactor operation without manual recalibration, even as wall conditions, reflections, vibration, and inaccessible calibration paths degrade the measurement? Formally, this asks for an autonomous self-calibration scheme robust to the evolving in-vessel environment.
status: Microwave diagnostics are established; autonomous long-duration calibration remains an operational qualification problem (Loarte et al., 2025, ITR-25-005; Imbeaux et al., 2015, *Design and first applications of the ITER integrated modelling & analysis suite*).
solved_when: Density and magnetic-field inference accuracy is preserved throughout long-duration operation — with changing wall conditions, reflections, vibration, and inaccessible calibration paths — without frequent manual recalibration; this must be demonstrated as an operational qualification.
why: Reactor operation cannot rely on frequent manual recalibration, so without autonomous long-duration calibration microwave diagnostics cannot remain qualified instruments in a power plant.
key_works: Loarte et al. (2025), ITR-25-005; Imbeaux et al. (2015), *Design and first applications of the ITER integrated modelling & analysis suite*.

title: Real-time current-profile inference
open: Can the internal current density and safety-factor profiles of a tokamak plasma be inferred in real time, accurately enough to support feedback control, using only a diagnostic set that would be feasible on a reactor? A formal version asks whether the associated inverse problem can be solved, perhaps via constrained state estimation, to the accuracy required by control despite being underdetermined by external magnetic measurements alone.
status: Magnetic control and integrated analysis frameworks exist, but internal-profile ambiguity remains a limiting inverse problem; the problem connects to ill-posed inverse problems and constrained state estimation. Key framework: Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*, DOI: 10.1007/978-3-319-29890-0.
solved_when: A method is demonstrated that reconstructs the internal current and safety-factor profiles, in real time, to the accuracy required for plasma control, using only reactor-feasible diagnostics.
why: Many dangerous instabilities depend on quantities that external sensors do not directly measure, so without such inference these profiles remain a limiting ambiguity for control and integrated plasma analysis.
key_works: Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*, DOI: 10.1007/978-3-319-29890-0.

title: Certified safe learned plasma control
open: Can a learned plasma controller be equipped with safety guarantees that hold up in actual experiments, not just in simulation? In particular, can such guarantees be established under model error, distribution shift, sensor failure, and actuator saturation?
status: Reinforcement learning has controlled TCV plasmas (Degrave et al., 2022, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-04301-9) and has been used to avoid tearing instability (Seo et al., 2024, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-07024-9), but certification under reactor conditions remains open.
solved_when: A learned plasma controller is demonstrated experimentally with safety guarantees that provably account for model error, distribution shift, sensor failure, and actuator saturation.
why: A high-consequence control system cannot rely on good average performance; a single unsafe episode can damage the device or terminate the discharge.

title: Counterfactual disruption-control benchmarks
open: Can we construct benchmark datasets and evaluation protocols for machine-learning disruption controllers that measure whether a system actually prevents disruptions, rather than merely predicting them? Such benchmarks must handle intervention and selection bias defensibly, since the controller's own actions alter the data it is judged on.
status: Prediction and avoidance demonstrations exist, but observational labels alone cannot establish a controller's causal benefit. Relevant work includes Kates-Harbeck et al. (2019), DOI: 10.1038/s41586-019-1116-4, and Seo et al. (2024), DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-07024-9.
solved_when: A benchmark exists in which the causal benefit of a disruption controller — its effect on disruption outcomes under intervention, not just predictive accuracy on observational labels — can be measured and compared in a way that is robust to intervention and selection bias.
why: Successful interventions remove the very events a naive benchmark expects to observe, so observational labels alone systematically misjudge controllers; a valid benchmark would make claims of prevention trustworthy and comparable across systems.

title: Diagnostic-degradation-aware control
open: Can a plasma control system detect and safely accommodate sensors whose measurements are biased, drifting, intermittently missing, or damaged by radiation — rather than treating them as either fully healthy or fully dead? Formally, the goal is a control architecture that maintains safe operation under such degraded diagnostics without producing unsafe control actions.
status: Learned plasma control has demonstrated experimental success (e.g., Degrave et al. 2022, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-04301-9; Loarte et al. 2025, ITR-25-005), but systematic handling of diagnostic degradation remains a separate reactor requirement rather than an integrated capability.
solved_when: A control scheme exists that detects biased, drifting, intermittently missing, and radiation-damaged measurements and accommodates them while guaranteeing no unsafe control actions — moving degradation handling from a separate requirement into the learned control system itself.
why: Sensor failure need not look like an obvious outage; a controller that cannot distinguish subtle degradation from good data can act on corrupted measurements and drive unsafe control actions.
key_works: Degrave et al. (2022), *Magnetic control of tokamak plasmas through deep reinforcement learning*, DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-04301-9; Loarte et al. (2025), ITR-25-005.

title: Integrated multi-actuator planning
open: Can a single control architecture coordinate all major tokamak actuators — heating, current drive, fueling, impurity injection, plasma shape, and exhaust — in real time, despite their conflicting objectives and widely different response times?
status: Individual control capabilities are established, but complete reactor-wide constrained control remains unresolved; relevant groundwork includes Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*, and Degrave et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-04301-9.
solved_when: A reactor-wide controller demonstrably coordinates all listed actuator groups simultaneously, respecting their conflicting objectives and differing timescales without issuing mutually incompatible commands.
why: Independent controllers optimized for individual subsystems can issue mutually incompatible actions, so a reactor cannot be reliably operated by simply stacking them; integrated control is required for consistent machine behavior.
key_works: Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*; Degrave et al. (2022), DOI: 10.1038/s41586-021-04301-9.

title: Verifiable cyber-resilient fusion control
open: How can networked controllers for plasma, fuel-cycle, and plant systems in a fusion device be made resilient to cyber faults, so that security is built into the control architecture rather than bolted on afterwards? Formally, the goal is to establish a threat model, an isolation architecture, and testable recovery guarantees spanning these interacting control layers.
status: This is a proposed fusion-specific qualification problem built on existing industrial-control and emerging learned-control architectures.
solved_when: A fusion-specific qualification framework exists that specifies the threat model, isolation architecture, and testable recovery guarantees for networked plasma, fuel-cycle, and plant controllers.
why: Cyber faults must not defeat physical protection or create unsafe coordinated actions across the coupled control systems of a fusion plant.
key_works: Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Predictive whole-plasma multiscale simulation
open: Can a single simulation predictively capture the whole plasma — coupled core, pedestal, scrape-off layer, neutrals, impurities, and evolving equilibrium — at a computational cost practical for design and operation?
status: Specialized models of individual regions and physics are powerful, but no single validated calculation today resolves every relevant scale and regime; integrated modelling efforts include Garbet et al. (2010), *Gyrokinetic simulations of turbulent transport*, and Imbeaux et al. (2015), *Design and first applications of the ITER integrated modelling & analysis suite*.
solved_when: A validated whole-plasma calculation resolving every relevant scale and regime is demonstrated at practical computational cost.
why: Reactor performance depends on interactions across model boundaries, so predictions that omit any region or coupling can misestimate it.
key_works: Garbet et al. (2010), *Gyrokinetic simulations of turbulent transport*; Imbeaux et al. (2015), *Design and first applications of the ITER integrated modelling & analysis suite*.

title: Conservative kinetic–fluid interfaces
open: How can kinetic and fluid descriptions be joined at a moving interface where collisionality varies, so that the coupling itself introduces no spurious transport? Formally, the goal is a coupling scheme that conserves particle, momentum, and energy budgets and produces no artificial entropy across the kinetic–fluid transition.
status: Both model classes — kinetic and fluid — are individually established, but trustworthy interfaces between them remain a general unresolved numerical challenge. Related work includes asymptotic-preserving numerical schemes; see Garbet et al. (2010), DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/50/4/043002, and Giacomin and Ricci (2020), *Investigation of turbulent transport regimes in the tokamak edge by using two-fluid simulations*.
solved_when: A coupling method exists for which exact conservation of particles, momentum, and energy is verifiable across the interface, and entropy behavior is consistent with the underlying physics — i.e., the scheme demonstrably introduces no spurious source or sink of any of these quantities under changing collisionality.
why: Errors introduced at the interface can masquerade as physical transport, contaminating simulation results in ways that are difficult to distinguish from real plasma dynamics.
key_works: Garbet et al. (2010), DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/50/4/043002; Giacomin and Ricci (2020), *Investigation of turbulent transport regimes in the tokamak edge by using two-fluid simulations*.

title: Whole-device uncertainty propagation
open: Can the many correlated uncertainties in a fusion plant — from nuclear data and material properties to transport models, controls, and manufacturing tolerances — be propagated end-to-end into predictions of plant performance and safety? The goal is a rigorous whole-device framework that traces how these input uncertainties combine and propagate through coupled physics to plant-level outputs.
status: Integrated modeling frameworks exist, but a calibrated end-to-end uncertainty budget remains unavailable for most proposed plants. Key works include Imbeaux et al. (2015), DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/55/12/123006, and Schnabel et al. (2024), DOI: 10.1016/j.nds.2024.01.001.
solved_when: A calibrated end-to-end uncertainty budget is available for a proposed plant, quantifying the propagated, correlated contribution of nuclear data, material property, transport model, control, and manufacturing uncertainties to plant performance and safety metrics.
why: Independent conservative margins stack wastefully and drive cost up, while ignored correlations among uncertainty sources can hide genuine safety risk; a defensible end-to-end budget replaces both failure modes.

title: Cross-code verification with analytic three-dimensional equilibria
open: Can we build benchmark suites of analytically known three-dimensional MHD equilibria that expose errors in equilibrium codes — including nonaxisymmetric, sheared-transform, and nonstandard-symmetry configurations? Such suites would give exact reference solutions against which individual codes, not just pairs of codes, can be tested.
status: Landreman (2026), *Analytic toroidal 3D MHD equilibria and steady Euler flows with invariant surfaces* (arXiv:2609.26742), provides new exact analytic equilibria usable as tests; however, benchmark adoption and systematic code comparison remain open.
