solved_when: A benchmark suite based on analytic equilibria exists and is adopted for systematic, community-wide comparison of equilibrium codes in nonaxisymmetric, sheared-transform, and nonstandard-symmetry cases.
why: Agreement between two numerical codes is weaker evidence when they share assumptions or bugs; exact analytic solutions break this circularity.
key_works: Landreman (2026), *Analytic toroidal 3D MHD equilibria and steady Euler flows with invariant surfaces*, arXiv:2609.26742.

title: Open negative-result fusion datasets
open: Can the fusion community build and sustain a shared data infrastructure that systematically publishes failed shots, unsuccessful materials, and rejected operating regimes alongside the successes, with metadata rich enough for reproducible analysis?
status: Existing public data systems, such as the ITER integrated modelling & analysis suite (Imbeaux et al., 2015) and LHD analyzed data (Ida, 2023, DOI: 10.57451/lhd.analyzed-data), are valuable but do not guarantee unbiased coverage of failures; this remains a proposed infrastructure target rather than an existing resource.
solved_when: A public dataset exists containing representative negative results — failed shots, unsuccessful materials, rejected regimes — with sufficient metadata for reproducible analysis and not obviously biased toward successful outcomes.
why: Success-biased datasets distort model training and feasibility assessment; without negative data, models and design decisions learn from a censored view of what actually works.
key_works: Imbeaux et al. (2015), *Design and first applications of the ITER integrated modelling & analysis suite*; Ida (2023), associated LHD data DOI: 10.57451/lhd.analyzed-data.

title: Cross-device data semantics and provenance
open: Can experimental and simulated fusion data be made genuinely interoperable across devices, carrying explicit units, calibration, uncertainty, geometry, processing history, and access rights as first-class metadata?
status: IMAS already supplies a machine-generic framework (Imbeaux et al. (2015), *Design and first applications of the ITER integrated modelling & Analysis suite*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/55/12/123006); the open problem is complete adoption and semantic fidelity, not inventing the first schema.
solved_when: Data from different devices can be exchanged and reinterpreted without loss of physical meaning — every dataset carries explicit units, calibration, uncertainty, geometry, processing history, and access rights, and the fusion community has adopted such a framework completely, with full semantic fidelity.
why: Superficially compatible files can still encode incompatible physical meanings, so cross-device analysis and machine learning on pooled data silently fails without faithful semantics and provenance.
key_works: Imbeaux et al. (2015), *Design and first applications of the ITER integrated modelling & analysis suite*, DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/55/12/123006.

title: Comparable cross-concept performance reporting
open: Can the fusion community adopt a reporting standard that makes performance claims from different confinement concepts genuinely comparable, by separating target gain, plasma gain, engineering gain, pulse energy, duty factor, uncertainty, and externally maintained distributions in an auditable way?
status: Lawson-based surveys improve cross-concept comparison, but complete-system reporting remains less standardized than isolated plasma metrics; see Wurzel and Hsu (2022), DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990, and Wurzel and Hsu (2025), arXiv:2505.03834.
solved_when: A reporting framework exists that is auditable and explicitly distinguishes target gain, plasma gain, engineering gain, pulse energy, duty factor, uncertainty, and externally maintained distributions, and is adopted for complete-system (not just isolated plasma) performance reporting across concepts.
why: Inconsistent reporting boundaries can make incomparable experiments look directly competitive, misleading comparisons across confinement concepts.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2022), DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990; Wurzel and Hsu (2025), arXiv:2505.03834.

title: Out-of-distribution materials benchmarks
open: Do predictive materials models hold up when tested outside their training distribution — on irradiation conditions, alloy families, processing routes, or laboratories they have never seen — rather than on random splits of similar samples? A benchmark is needed that systematically evaluates generalization under such distribution shifts.
status: Materials-informatics opportunities exist (Hosemann et al., 2018, *Materials selection for nuclear applications*), but reactor-relevant generalization requires more demanding validation; related efforts include distribution-shift benchmarks and scientific machine learning, with foundational context from Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*.
solved_when: A benchmark exists that evaluates predictive materials models across held-out irradiation conditions, alloy families, processing routes, and laboratories (i.e., out-of-distribution splits rather than random ones), and reports performance under these shifts.
why: Interpolation accuracy can badly overstate a model's usefulness for qualification, so decisions about reactor materials could rest on misleadingly optimistic numbers.
key_works: Hosemann et al. (2018), *Materials selection for nuclear applications*; Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*.

title: Identifiable multimodal ICF reconstruction
open: Which physical properties of an inertial-confinement-fusion hot spot are uniquely recoverable from the diagnostics we actually have? A formal answer would characterize the identifiable subset of hot-spot properties and, for the remainder, quantify and report the calibrated ambiguity left by the data.
status: Neural and multimodal reconstruction methods advanced in 2024–2025, notably Kunimune et al. (2024), DOI: 10.1063/5.0205656, and Churnetski et al. (2025), DOI: 10.1063/5.0268312, but visual plausibility of a reconstruction does not establish identifiability, and no such identifiability characterization currently exists.
solved_when: A stated set of hot-spot properties is proven uniquely recoverable from the available diagnostics, and for each non-identifiable property a calibrated ambiguity (uncertainty) quantification is produced.
why: Reconstructions that look plausible but carry hidden non-uniqueness can misdirect target-design optimization with false certainty; identifiability results make reconstruction trustworthy input to that optimization.

title: Hundredfold faster validated fusion prediction
open: Can we make validated fusion prediction a hundred times cheaper end-to-end without giving up correctness? Specifically, can end-to-end prediction cost be reduced by 100× while still meeting specified error bounds and reliably detecting out-of-domain inputs?
status: Surrogates and integrated models exist (e.g., Imbeaux et al. (2015), DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/55/12/123006; Yang et al. (2026), *Multiscale Assessment of Tritium Behavior…Using Surrogate Models in TMAP8*, arXiv:2604.19647), but the 100× target requires validating complete decision quality, not only inference speed.
solved_when: A demonstrated prediction pipeline achieves a 100× reduction in end-to-end cost, satisfies the specified error bounds, and detects out-of-domain inputs — i.e., validation of complete decision quality, not inference speed alone.
why: It would make uncertainty-aware reactor optimization and real-time planning practical.
key_works: Imbeaux et al. (2015), DOI: 10.1088/0029-5515/55/12/123006; Yang et al. (2026), *Multiscale Assessment of Tritium Behavior…Using Surrogate Models in TMAP8*, arXiv:2604.19647.

title: Hot-cell throughput
open: Can activated components removed from a fusion plant be processed — through receipt, inspection, repair, detritiation, storage, and disposal — at a rate that keeps pace with maintenance operations, so that the hot cell itself never becomes the bottleneck of the plant? Formally, the question is whether the full hot-cell logistics chain can be sized and scheduled to match the throughput demanded by scheduled component replacement.
status: Remote-maintenance studies such as Crofts and Harman (2014), *Maintenance Duration Estimate for a DEMO Fusion Power Plant, based on the EFDA WP12 pre-conceptual studies* (DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2014.01.038; arXiv:1412.4008), quantify major outage tasks, but complete hot-cell logistics remain an important plant-level constraint that has not been fully worked out.
solved_when: A hot-cell processing chain whose throughput matches the plant's maintenance schedule is demonstrated (by design, model, or prototype), with no stage of receipt, inspection, repair, detritiation, storage, or disposal limiting overall maintenance duration.
why: Fast in-vessel component replacement alone is insufficient if removed parts block the downstream processing chain; hot-cell capacity ultimately sets the plant's availability.
key_works: Crofts and Harman (2014), *Maintenance Duration Estimate for a DEMO Fusion Power Plant, based on the EFDA WP12 pre-conceptual studies*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2014.01.038; arXiv:1412.4008.

title: Remotely qualified pressure-boundary reconnection
open: Can the coolant and vacuum boundaries of a fusion power plant be reconnected entirely by remote handling, with leak tightness, structural integrity, inspectability, and repeatability that are verified rather than assumed — and can such connections be qualified for reactor service over many cycles?
status: Maintenance concepts for remote reconnection exist, but reactor-service qualification of repeated remote connections remains unresolved.
solved_when: A remote reconnection concept for coolant and vacuum boundaries demonstrates verified leak tightness, structural integrity, inspectability, and repeatable performance under reactor-service qualification, including repeated connect–disconnect cycles.
why: A single inaccessible leak in a remote connection can extend a plant outage dramatically, so unqualified remote reconnection directly threatens availability and economics of a fusion power plant.
key_works: Crofts and Harman (2014), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2014.01.038; Abdou et al. (2015), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: In-service inspection of activated structures
open: Can consequential cracks, thinning, delamination, and coolant problems in an operating fusion plant be detected without dismantling the plant or exposing personnel to activation?
status: Fusion materials qualification identifies lifetime uncertainty as a key issue (Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*), and reactor-compatible inspection is still needed to manage it operationally.
solved_when: A reactor-compatible inspection capability exists that detects cracks, thinning, delamination, and coolant problems in activated, assembled plant structures, without plant disassembly or personnel exposure.
why: It would allow safe operation without excessively conservative component replacement, turning lifetime uncertainty from materials qualification into a managed operational parameter.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, DOI: 10.1038/nphys3735; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: High-availability primary-loop machinery
open: Can the pumps, valves, seals, bearings, and instrumentation of a fusion primary coolant loop be qualified for long-term service in radioactive or reactive coolants, with maintenance access that reflects real plant conditions? The goal is an engineering qualification basis — not just component selection — for balance-of-plant machinery in fusion-specific service.
status: Blanket studies to date identify the thermofluid requirements of the primary loop, but qualification of industrial-duty machinery remains a separate, unaddressed layer; Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.
solved_when: A documented qualification of primary-loop machinery (pumps, valves, seals, bearings, instrumentation) is achieved under radioactive or reactive coolant conditions, with maintenance provisions consistent with realistic plant access.
why: These conventionally designed components can become fusion-specific bottlenecks, since ordinary balance-of-plant machinery has not been shown to survive the fusion coolant environment with maintainable access.
key_works: Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Pulse-to-steady power conversion
open: How can the pulsed heat and electrical output of a fusion power plant be smoothed into steady, grid-compatible power while keeping storage losses, component fatigue, and overall economics within quantified bounds?
status: Pulsed and steady-state plant concepts are both studied, but plant-specific buffering strategies and their associated cycling penalties remain unresolved; related work includes Schwartz et al. (2023), *The value of fusion energy to a decarbonized United States electric grid* (DOI: 10.1016/j.joule.2023.02.006) and Ellison et al. (2024), arXiv:2408.15206.
solved_when: A plant-level buffering design is demonstrated (analytically or experimentally) that converts pulsed fusion output to grid-grade steady power with quantified storage losses, thermal/cycling fatigue penalties, and an economic assessment of the conversion strategy.
why: The grid and turbine do not necessarily tolerate the plasma's preferred waveform; without adequate buffering, pulsed operation could impose unacceptable cycling damage and grid-integration penalties on an otherwise viable plant.
key_works: Schwartz et al. (2023), *The value of fusion energy to a decarbonized United States electric grid*, DOI: 10.1016/j.joule.2023.02.006; Ellison et al. (2024), arXiv:2408.15206.

title: Tritium-isolating power-cycle heat exchangers
open: Can a power-cycle heat exchanger transfer useful high-temperature heat from a fusion blanket while effectively isolating tritium from the conventional side of the plant? Formally, this means achieving acceptable tritium leakage, corrosion, pressure drop, and inspection burdens simultaneously in a single reactor-qualified component.
status: Blanket and tritium studies (e.g., Humrickhouse et al., 2017, *Tritium aspects of the fusion nuclear science facility*; Abdou et al., 2015, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021) identify these coupled constraints, but an integrated reactor-qualified solution remains open. Related directions include selective heat-transfer barriers and coupled mass- and heat-transport modeling.
solved_when: A heat exchanger design is demonstrated that transfers useful high-temperature heat while keeping tritium leakage, corrosion, pressure drop, and inspection burdens all within acceptable limits, and is qualified for integrated reactor use.
why: Without such a component, tritium contamination can spread from a compact nuclear island into a large conventional power system, coupling the entire balance of plant to nuclear regulation and maintenance.
key_works: Humrickhouse et al. (2017), *Tritium aspects of the fusion nuclear science facility*; Abdou et al. (2015), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2015.07.021.

title: Practical charged-particle direct conversion
open: Can a fusion plant convert the energy of its charged-particle exhaust directly into electricity at reactor-relevant conditions, rather than routing it through a thermal cycle?
status: Direct conversion is attractive for several alternative fusion concepts, but complete reactor-duty performance remains unestablished; Wurzel and Hsu (2025), *Continuing progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criteria*, arXiv:2505.03834, frame the broader progress context.
solved_when: A useful charged-particle energy distribution is converted to electricity with acceptable efficiency, lifetime, contamination tolerance, and auxiliary power draw under reactor duty.
why: Direct conversion could bypass some thermal-cycle losses, but achieving it requires particle-handling hardware far more demanding than conventional plant components.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2025), *Continuing progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criteria*, arXiv:2505.03834.

title: Safe black start, shutdown, and recovery
open: Can a fusion plant be taken through a full blackout, emergency shutdown, restart, and extended standby without ever entering an unsafe inventory or thermal state?
status: Plasma control and plant roadmaps address constituent systems (Ariola and Pironti, 2016; DOE, 2026 *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*), but integrated recovery behavior remains a qualification objective.
solved_when: Complete plant transitions — power loss, emergency shutdown, restart, and prolonged standby — are demonstrated end-to-end with no unsafe inventory or thermal states arising.
why: A plant must remain safe when its normal power and control assumptions fail; without demonstrated recovery behavior, no plant can be qualified.
key_works: Ariola and Pironti (2016), *Magnetic Control of Tokamak Plasmas*; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Auditable fusion capital-cost models
open: Can fusion power plant capital costs be estimated in a way that is traceable to real engineering quantities — materials, manufacturing processes, labor, construction sequencing, contingency, and uncertainty — rather than asserted as aspirational unit costs? In formal terms, the goal is a bottom-up, auditable cost model for first-of-a-kind fusion plants.
status: Systems and grid-value models exist, but first-of-a-kind cost credibility remains unresolved. Key works: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991; Schwartz et al. (2023), DOI: 10.1016/j.joule.2023.02.006.
solved_when: A capital-cost model exists whose estimates are decomposable into actual quantities, manufacturing processes, labor, construction sequence, contingency, and quantified uncertainty, with each figure traceable to its inputs.
why: Physics feasibility does not determine whether a plant can be financed; credible, auditable costs are what connect a working fusion design to investable deployment.
key_works: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*, DOI: 10.17226/25991; Schwartz et al. (2023), DOI: 10.1016/j.joule.2023.02.006.

title: Availability–lifetime–cost optimum
open: What combination of operating intensity, component lifetime, replacement frequency, and reserve capacity minimizes the cost of delivered electricity from a fusion plant? Formally, determine the coupled optimum over these deployment and maintenance variables rather than maximizing instantaneous fusion power.
status: Maintenance estimates and electricity-system models both exist, but their coupled optimization has not been performed for lack of reactor operating evidence (Crofts and Harman, 2014, arXiv:1412.4008; Schwartz et al., 2023, DOI: 10.1016/j.joule.2023.02.006).
solved_when: A tractable model yields the economically optimal operating intensity, component lifetime, replacement frequency, and reserve capacity, grounded in reactor operating evidence for the maintenance and availability terms.
why: Maximizing instantaneous fusion power can raise the cost of delivered electricity; the coupled optimum tells plant designers and fleet operators where to actually operate on the power–lifetime–cost tradeoff.
key_works: Crofts and Harman (2014), arXiv:1412.4008; Schwartz et al. (2023), DOI: 10.1016/j.joule.2023.02.006.

title: Fusion construction learning curves
open: Which parts of a fusion power plant's cost can realistically fall with each successive unit built, and which are pinned down by materials limits, site work, regulation, or fundamental physics?
status: No commercial operating fleet exists to supply an empirical fusion learning curve, so current claims about fusion cost declines remain prospective. Key works: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*; Hsu et al. (2026), *Retrospective on the Design and Implementation of the Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program…*, arXiv:2609.28398.
solved_when: An empirically grounded decomposition of fusion plant costs is available, identifying which cost components exhibit learning-curve behavior and which do not, ideally informed by data from operating units rather than projections.
why: Fleet economics cannot safely assume solar-like or aircraft-like cost reductions without evidence; credible deployment and investment decisions depend on knowing which declines are real.
key_works: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*; Hsu et al. (2026), *Retrospective on the Design and Implementation of the Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program…*, arXiv:2609.28398.

title: Fusion value in diverse future grids
open: How much is fusion power actually worth when embedded in a future grid — and how does that value shift across regions with different renewable mixes, storage costs, transmission limits, reliability standards, and competing firm low-carbon technologies? Formally, the question is to characterize fusion's system value as a function of these grid conditions rather than for any single scenario.
status: A 2023 study by Schwartz et al., *The value of fusion energy to a decarbonized United States electric grid* (DOI: 10.1016/j.joule.2023.02.006; dataset DOI: 10.34770/f8em-3c49), provides detailed U.S. modeling with public data; however, its results are conditional and should not be read as universal price forecasts.
solved_when: There exists an analysis of fusion's value spanning regional variation, renewable mixes, storage costs, transmission limits, reliability standards, and alternative firm technologies, yielding conditional results stated as functions of these grid parameters rather than single-scenario price estimates.
why: An economically sensible fusion plant specification — its capacity factor, ramping ability, and cost targets — depends on the system into which it will sell power, so generic value estimates cannot guide design or investment decisions.
key_works: Schwartz et al. (2023), *The value of fusion energy to a decarbonized United States electric grid*, DOI: 10.1016/j.joule.2023.02.006; dataset DOI: 10.34770/f8em-3c49.

title: Fleet-scale resource and lifecycle accounting
open: What does a realistic fusion deployment pathway actually demand in physical resources — and can we account for all of it coherently? The goal is a unified, uncertainty-aware accounting of lithium, beryllium, helium, superconductors, structural materials, energy inputs, water, waste, and component replacement flows across realistic fleet-scale deployment pathways.
status: Individual material and fuel constraints have been studied (e.g., Pearson et al., 2018, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2018.04.090; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*), but a harmonized, uncertainty-aware fleet account remains incomplete.
solved_when: A harmonized fleet-scale resource and lifecycle account exists that quantifies lithium, beryllium, helium, superconductors, structural materials, energy inputs, water, waste, and replacement flows under realistic deployment pathways, with uncertainties propagated throughout.
why: A technology's laboratory footprint can differ greatly from its fleet-scale footprint, so fleet-level resource demand could make or break deployment feasibility in ways single-plant studies cannot reveal.
key_works: Pearson et al. (2018), DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2018.04.090; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Competitive fusion process heat
open: Which industrial heat applications can fusion actually serve — where the temperature, availability, contamination barriers, and economics line up with what achievable fusion systems can deliver?
status: Electricity dominates many roadmaps (e.g., DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*; NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*), and non-electric applications still require their own integration and market evidence.
solved_when: Specific industrial heat applications have been identified and demonstrated whose temperature requirements, availability, contamination barriers, and economics match achievable fusion systems.
why: Some industrial users may value heat very differently from an electricity grid, so identifying them determines whether fusion has markets beyond power sales.
key_works: DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*; NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*.

title: Quantitative integrated fusion safety cases
open: Can accident models that couple tritium, activated materials, chemical energy, magnetic energy, coolant behavior, and confinement failures be validated as an integrated whole? In other words, is it possible to build a quantitative fusion safety case in which these interacting hazards are treated together rather than hazard by hazard?
status: Regulatory frameworks are advancing, with a proposed U.S. NRC rule on a regulatory framework for fusion machines (U.S. NRC (2026), Federal Register document 2026-03865), but plant-specific evidence remains necessary; related efforts include Abdou et al. (2015), probabilistic risk assessment, and coupled-hazard modeling.
solved_when: Integrated accident models covering tritium, activated materials, chemical energy, magnetic energy, coolant behavior, and confinement failures are validated against plant-specific evidence.
why: No single hazard category captures the full plant, so safety cases built from isolated hazards cannot establish the overall risk picture of a fusion facility.
key_works: U.S. NRC (2026), *Regulatory Framework for Fusion Machines*, proposed rule, Federal Register document 2026-03865; Abdou et al. (2015).

title: Tritium environmental-transfer uncertainty
open: How confidently can we predict the movement of released tritium through air, water, soil, and biota at a specific site? The goal is to reduce uncertainty in transport and dose models for both routine and abnormal releases.
status: Tritium management is established, but environmental consequences depend on chemical form, local conditions, and exposure pathways. Key works: Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*; NRC (2026), proposed fusion rule.
solved_when: Site-relevant atmospheric, water, soil, and biological transport following routine and abnormal tritium releases can be predicted with reduced, quantified uncertainty sufficient to support credible dose assessments and release limits.
why: Credible release limits depend on credible transport and dose models; without them, regulatory limits for tritium releases cannot be justified with confidence.
key_works: Glugla et al. (2023 report), *Tritium Technology for Fusion Devices—Status and R&D Needs*; NRC (2026), proposed fusion rule.

title: Activated-material recycling pathways
open: Can activated materials from fusion facilities be recycled or cleared for unrestricted use through routes that are both technically workable and regulatorily acceptable, with impurity and exposure accounting validated well enough to support licensing decisions?
status: Reduced activation is treated as a design objective, but it does not guarantee that all components qualify for unrestricted recycling; no fully accepted pathway currently exists. Key works include Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*, and Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*.
solved_when: Recycling and clearance pathways exist that are accepted by regulators, supported by validated impurity inventories and exposure assessments, for the activated material streams of a fusion device.
why: Waste pathways directly constrain material selection, plant cost, public acceptance, and the feasibility of decommissioning, so unresolved routes propagate into the whole plant design.
key_works: Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*; Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*.

title: Common-cause and compound hazards
open: Can fusion facilities be shown to withstand credible compound hazards — such as power loss combined with coolant failure, magnet faults together with structural motion, or fire accompanied by tritium release — rather than merely surviving each threat in isolation? Formally, the goal is analysis and testing methods that qualify integrated system response to such correlated event combinations.
status: Component protection exists, but it does not establish resilience to correlated failures; integrated qualification remains open. The NRC's proposed rule, *Regulatory Framework for Fusion Machines* (2026), and the DOE's *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap* (2026) frame the current regulatory and research landscape.
solved_when: Analysis and testing demonstrate credible combined scenarios — power loss plus coolant failure, magnet faults plus structural motion, and fire plus tritium release — with integrated qualification of system resilience to these correlated failures.
why: Independent safety layers can fail together when they share power, cooling, software, or physical space, so component-level protection does not establish resilience to correlated failures.
key_works: NRC (2026), *Regulatory Framework for Fusion Machines*, proposed rule; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Fusion-specific evidence standards for licensing
open: What body of validation, uncertainty-quantification, inspection, and operational evidence should regulators accept as sufficient to license novel fusion components and machine classes? A complete answer would specify fusion-specific evidence standards that carry the same predictability that established standards provide for fission licensing.
status: Regulatory work exists: the NRC published a proposed fusion-machine rule on February 26, 2026 (U.S. NRC (2026), *Regulatory Framework for Fusion Machines*, Federal Register document 2026-03865), so the gap is not an absence of regulatory activity but the undefined fusion-specific evidence standards themselves.
solved_when: A defined, accepted set of validation, uncertainty, inspection, and operational evidence requirements exists for licensing novel fusion components and machine classes, usable by both developers and regulators.
why: Without such standards, developers cannot know what safety case to build and regulators lack a predictable basis to evaluate it, stalling licensing of fusion machines.
key_works: U.S. NRC (2026), *Regulatory Framework for Fusion Machines*, Federal Register document 2026-03865.

title: Qualified fusion component standards
open: Can the fusion industry converge on shared, interoperable standards for the components that make a plant a plant — pressure boundaries, irradiation limits, remote joints, and functional materials? In formal terms, the goal is an agreed qualification framework covering fusion-specific design and manufacturing requirements for these component classes.
status: Existing industrial and nuclear standards provide the foundation, but fusion-specific qualification remains incomplete; recent policy moves — DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*, and the NRC (2026) proposed fusion-machine rule — are shaping the regulatory landscape in which such standards would sit.
solved_when: A set of interoperable fusion-specific design and manufacturing standards exists, covering pressure boundaries, irradiation limits, remote joints, and functional materials, such that components qualified under them are accepted across plants and vendors without bespoke re-qualification.
why: Today every plant must bespoke-qualify its components, which slows deployment and fragments supply chains; common standards let vendors build once and sell to many designs.
key_works: DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*; NRC (2026), proposed fusion-machine rule.

title: Evidence-based decommissioning provision
open: How can we estimate, and then validate against real fusion plants, the decommissioning methods, waste volumes, tritium cleanup requirements, schedules, and financial reserves that actual fusion architectures will require?
status: Materials and activation analyses — supported by tools such as the FENDL library (Schnabel et al., 2024) — currently inform decommissioning planning, and regulatory frameworks are being developed (NRC, 2026, *Regulatory Framework for Fusion Machines*), but no commercial fusion fleet yet exists to supply realized decommissioning costs.
solved_when: Decommissioning plans for concrete fusion architectures exist with validated estimates of methods, waste volumes, tritium cleanup, schedules, and financial reserves, grounded in realized data rather than assumptions alone.
why: If end-of-life obligations are underfunded, private fusion projects effectively shift cleanup costs onto the public or other parties; sound provisioning keeps the economics of fusion honest.
key_works: NRC (2026), *Regulatory Framework for Fusion Machines*; Schnabel et al. (2024), *FENDL: A library for fusion research and applications*.

title: Sustained funding for irradiation qualification
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: Can governments and consortia secure sustained, multiyear funding to build and operate shared irradiation and post-irradiation examination capacity, with operating schedules aligned to fusion component-development decision timelines?
status: The 2026 DOE roadmap (DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*) identifies enabling infrastructure, but roadmap publication is not equivalent to secured multiyear appropriations; materials-research needs are laid out in Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*.
solved_when: Shared irradiation and post-irradiation examination facilities are funded under secured multiyear appropriations — not merely named in a roadmap — and their schedules are aligned to component-development decisions.
why: Qualification bottlenecks at shared irradiation facilities can delay many otherwise independent fusion approaches at once, so sustained capacity functions as a public good for the whole field.
key_works: DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*; Knaster et al. (2016), *Materials research for fusion*.

title: Shared integrated blanket test loops
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: Can the fusion community establish shared, accessible test facilities that simultaneously reproduce the coupled conditions of a breeding blanket — relevant coolant chemistry, magnetic fields, heat flux, instrumentation, and component-scale geometry?
status: Specialized loops such as MaPLE exist, but comprehensive shared coverage of the coupled conditions relevant to integrated blanket testing remains incomplete. Key works: Smolentsev, ORNL research profile and MaPLE program; Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*.
solved_when: A facility (or coordinated network of facilities) exists that is openly accessible to multiple organizations and provides combined coverage of coolant chemistry, magnetic field, heat flux, instrumentation, and component-scale geometry in integrated blanket tests.
why: No single company can efficiently duplicate every enabling experiment on its own; shared loops spread the cost and capability needed to qualify blanket components.
key_works: Smolentsev, ORNL research profile and MaPLE program; Abdou et al. (2015), *Blanket/first wall challenges and required R&D on the pathway to DEMO*.

title: Public-interest access to pilot-plant evidence
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: How can agreements for publicly funded pilot plants be structured so that the performance, safety, failure, and qualification evidence they generate is reusable by the broader community, while still protecting legitimately proprietary information?
status: Public–private milestone programs exist, but evidence-sharing arrangements remain a policy-design problem. Hsu, Wurzel, and Subramanian (2026), *Retrospective on the Design and Implementation of the Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program of the U.S. Department of Energy*, arXiv:2609.28398.
solved_when: Concrete agreement or policy designs exist that make publicly supported pilot-plant evidence reusable outside the originating company, with a workable boundary between transferable evidence and protected proprietary information.
why: Public investment should generate transferable knowledge — evidence on what works, what fails, and what qualifies — rather than only isolated company assets.
key_works: Hsu, Wurzel, and Subramanian (2026), *Retrospective on the Design and Implementation of the Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program of the U.S. Department of Energy*, arXiv:2609.28398.

title: Tritium reserve and allocation governance
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: Who should own and control the world's scarce startup tritium, and by what rules should it be reserved, allocated, and contingently released among competing research and commercial users? A concrete governance answer would specify transparent ownership structures, reserve policies, allocation mechanisms, and contingency arrangements spanning all user classes.
status: Supply constraints are documented and technical breeding projections exist, but those projections do not determine allocation during shortages; no governance framework is established. Key work: Pearson et al. (2018), *Tritium supply and use: a key issue for the development of nuclear fusion energy*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2018.04.090.
solved_when: A transparent, implementable framework for tritium ownership, reserve sizing, allocation, and contingency arrangements exists and is accepted across research and commercial users, covering behavior under shortage conditions.
why: Without coordinated governance, uncoordinated procurement can strand fusion projects or undermine shared research; technical breeding projections alone cannot settle who gets tritium during shortages.
key_works: Pearson et al. (2018), *Tritium supply and use: a key issue for the development of nuclear fusion energy*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2018.04.090.

title: Milestone funding without continuity failures
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: Can a fusion funding mechanism be designed that pays out against rigorous technical milestones yet never leaves technically interdependent development stages stranded without support between them? In other words, is there a milestone structure whose disbursement schedule avoids destructive discontinuities in financing across dependent stages?
status: A September 2026 retrospective (Hsu et al. (2026), *Retrospective on the Design and Implementation of the Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program…*, arXiv:2609.28398) analyzes implementation experience of the DOE milestone program.
solved_when: A funding mechanism is specified that both (a) preserves rigorous, verifiable milestones as the basis for payment, and (b) demonstrably avoids financing gaps between technically interdependent development stages.
why: Stop–start financing can destroy teams and supply chains even when technical progress is real, so a mechanism that removes the gaps protects the very capabilities the milestones are meant to advance.
key_works: Hsu et al. (2026), *Retrospective on the Design and Implementation of the Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program…*, arXiv:2609.28398.

title: First-plant financing and insurability
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: Can the risks of a first-of-a-kind fusion plant — construction, performance, technology, fuel supply, and decommissioning — be allocated between public and private parties so that the project is genuinely investable without shifting unbounded liabilities onto the public balance sheet?
status: Strategies for financing pilot plants exist, but commercial underwriting still lacks evidence from an operating fusion fleet, leaving first-plant risk pricing unresolved. Key references: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*; Hsu et al. (2026), arXiv:2609.28398.
solved_when: A financing and risk-allocation structure exists for a first commercial fusion plant that is accepted as investable by private capital while placing explicit, bounded limits on public exposure across construction, performance, technology, fuel, and decommissioning risk categories.
why: A technically credible fusion design can still fail to reach construction if no party is willing to hold its risks; solving this is what converts engineering feasibility into a financed plant.
key_works: NASEM (2021), *Bringing Fusion to the U.S. Grid*; Hsu et al. (2026), arXiv:2609.28398.

title: Fusion qualification workforce
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: Can the fusion sector cultivate a workforce with the specialized expertise — tritium operations, remote handling, irradiation testing, nuclear quality assurance, superconducting fabrication, and plant commissioning — needed to qualify and operate fusion plants? In formal terms, the goal is a capacity-building program that develops these competencies at the scale and depth required for fleet deployment.
status: The 2026 DOE roadmap explicitly includes workforce development, and specialized capacity cannot be created by general hiring alone [DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*].
solved_when: A workforce pipeline exists that reliably produces qualified personnel in tritium operations, remote handling, irradiation testing, nuclear quality assurance, superconducting fabrication, and plant commissioning at the scale needed by the fusion industry.
why: Shortages in these shared specialties can delay an entire industry, since every fusion plant program competes for the same scarce qualified staff.
key_works: DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.

title: Falsifiable funding for underexplored concepts
subfield: Shared infrastructure, supply chains, and funding
open: How can fusion research funding be structured so that non-mainstream concepts compete for support on the strength of decisive, independently interpretable experiments rather than on indefinite promise? The goal is a funding mechanism that distinguishes genuine uncertainty from accumulating evidence of failure, without prematurely excluding unconventional approaches.
status: Cross-concept gain surveys show diverse development levels across fusion approaches, and it is recognized that funding design must distinguish uncertainty from evidence of failure.
solved_when: A funding design exists that competitively allocates support across fusion concepts at diverse development levels, tying continued funding to outcomes of falsifiable, independently interpretable experiments while limiting uninformative expenditure.
why: It preserves useful exploration of underexplored concepts while limiting spending that yields no informative evidence either way.
key_works: Wurzel and Hsu (2022), DOI: 10.1063/5.0083990; Ellison et al. (2024), *Opportunities in Pulsed Magnetic Fusion Energy*, arXiv:2408.15206.

title: Fusion propulsion with credible specific power
open: Can a fusion propulsion system be designed in which every subsystem — thrust, specific impulse, reactor mass, shielding, heat rejection, and auxiliary power — closes at once, rather than only in isolated concept studies?
status: NASA and other groups have published fusion-propulsion concepts, including NASA's 2012 *Z-Pinch Magneto-Inertial Fusion Propulsion Engine Design Concept* (NTRS:20120016553), but concept-level performance does not constitute integrated propulsion evidence.
solved_when: A complete propulsion architecture is demonstrated whose thrust, specific impulse, reactor mass, shielding, heat rejection, and auxiliary power all satisfy their requirements simultaneously.
why: In space applications mass and waste heat, rather than grid economics, are the dominant constraints, so a system that closes on all of them simultaneously is what distinguishes a viable engine from an attractive paper concept.
key_works: NASA (2012), *Z-Pinch Magneto-Inertial Fusion Propulsion Engine Design Concept*, NTRS:20120016553.

title: Efficient fusion magnetic nozzles
open: Can a fusion rocket turn its hot plasma into a genuinely directed exhaust stream — that is, convert fusion-plasma energy into thrust while keeping detachment controlled, divergence and electron losses low, magnetic reaction forces manageable, and hardware protected from the plasma?
status: Fusion-propulsion concepts, such as the NASA (2012) Z-Pinch Magneto-Inertial Fusion Propulsion Engine Design Concept (NTRS:20120016553), require this conversion, but complete reactor-compatible nozzle performance remains unresolved; related open issues include plasma detachment from magnetic nozzles and momentum conversion.
solved_when: A reactor-compatible magnetic nozzle demonstrates efficient conversion of fusion-plasma energy into directed exhaust, with controlled detachment, acceptably low divergence and electron losses, manageable magnetic reaction forces, and hardware exposure within survivable limits.
why: Producing energetic plasma is not the same as producing useful thrust; without this conversion step, a fusion reactor cannot serve as a propulsion engine no matter how well it confines its plasma.
key_works: NASA (2012), *Z-Pinch Magneto-Inertial Fusion Propulsion Engine Design Concept*, NTRS:20120016553.

title: Tenfold faster activated-component replacement
open: Can activated-component replacement in a fusion power plant be made ten times faster than today's estimated complete replacement outage time, counting inspection and recommissioning as well as removal and installation? Formally, the goal is a full maintenance scheme whose projected end-to-end replacement duration is at most one-tenth of a specified, reproducible baseline.
status: DEMO maintenance studies provide explicit baseline estimates for complete replacement outage time (Crofts and Harman, 2014, *Maintenance Duration Estimate for a DEMO Fusion Power Plant*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2014.01.038; arXiv:1412.4008), but the 10× target remains unmet, and it cannot be satisfied by speeding up only one robotic motion. Related directions include robotic assembly planning and parallel maintenance scheduling.
solved_when: A credible maintenance scheme, validated against a specified and reproducible baseline, achieves a 10× reduction in complete replacement outage time measured end to end, including inspection and recommissioning — not by accelerating a single robotic motion in isolation.
why: It offers a path to materially better plant economics that does not depend on improving plasma confinement, attacking downtime rather than physics performance.
key_works: Crofts and Harman (2014), *Maintenance Duration Estimate for a DEMO Fusion Power Plant*, DOI: 10.1016/j.fusengdes.2014.01.038; arXiv:1412.4008.

title: Hundredfold faster component qualification
open: Can the qualification of fusion components be made a hundredfold faster — or require a hundredfold less experimental burden — without sacrificing independently validated confidence in lifetime and safety? That is, for a well-defined component class, achieve the proposed 100× reduction in qualification time or testing burden while retaining equivalent, independently validated lifetime and safety assurance.
status: The ingredients — accelerated testing, multiscale models, and surrogate approaches — are available, but demonstrating equivalent confidence remains the unresolved requirement. Key works include Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*; Yang et al. (2026), arXiv:2604.19647; and DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.
solved_when: A defined component class demonstrates a 100× reduction in qualification time or experimental burden, with lifetime and safety confidence independently validated at a level equivalent to current qualification practice.
why: For deployment, the speed at which components can be qualified may matter as much as the speed at which they are invented; slow qualification bottlenecks the translation of new materials and designs into operating fusion systems.
key_works: Zinkle and Snead (2014), *Designing Radiation Resistance in Materials for Fusion Energy*; Yang et al. (2026), arXiv:2604.19647; DOE (2026), *Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap*.
